title: New Mexico Late Fee Rules
bodyText: New Mexico allows a late fee only if the lease provides for one. The fee may not exceed 5% of the rent for each rental period the tenant is in default, and it is calculated only on rent, not on deposits, other fees or utilities. To charge it, you must give the tenant notice of the late fee no later than the last day of the next rental period after the one in which the rent was late. There is no required grace period. The 5% cap took effect June 20, 2025; leases written for the earlier 10% cap must not charge more than 5%.

title: Fees Are Not Rent in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico defines rent as the payments the lease requires for use of the home, not including deposits, and the three-day nonpayment notice is for unpaid rent. Late fees are calculated only on rent, and the act treats other fees and utilities separately. To be safe, put only unpaid rent in a three-day notice and collect fees and other charges as separate debts.

title: Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: To raise rent in a month-to-month tenancy, give the tenant written notice at least 30 days before the rental date on which the increase starts. In a fixed-term lease, give written notice at least 30 days before the end of the term; the increase takes effect for the period after the term. For a tenancy shorter than month-to-month, give notice at least one rental period before the first increased payment. An increase may not be made in retaliation for protected tenant activity, though a uniform increase for similar units, given with proper notice, is allowed.

title: Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: Since June 20, 2025, a landlord may raise a fee the lease provides for only by written notice at least 60 days before the rental date on which the increase starts, or, in a fixed-term lease, at least 60 days before the end of the term. In a tenancy shorter than month-to-month, give notice at least one rental period before the first increased fee payment. This is longer than the 30 days required for a rent increase.

title: Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases
bodyText:
Since June 20, 2025, a New Mexico rental listing must disclose, in plain language, the base rent and an itemized description of every fee or charge that will be assessed during the tenancy. Charging an applicant any fee other than a screening fee or a deposit, or a fee not published in the listing, and charging a tenant any fee not included in the lease, are unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Unfair Practices Act.

Tenants can recover actual damages or $100 (up to triple or $300 for willful violations) plus attorney fees. You are not liable for a third-party website's failure to show all the costs you provided.

title: Application Screening Fees in New Mexico
bodyText: Since June 20, 2025, a New Mexico landlord may charge an applicant (including a guarantor or cosigner) a screening fee of no more than $50, and no other fee to process an application. You must give written or digital notice of the fee, get the applicant's written agreement to pay it, and give a receipt. You may not charge it when you know the unit is not available, and you must hold card payments or wait to deposit cash or checks until earlier applicants have been screened and rejected or have declined. Return the fee within 30 days if an earlier applicant takes the unit or you do not actually screen the applicant. Do not charge the same applicant twice within 90 days for properties under the same ownership. An unauthorized screening fee costs $250 plus a refund of all fees paid.

title: Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico
bodyText: You may require a background check of an applicant before signing a lease, but you must give the applicant a copy of any report you used to screen them. Screening criteria must not discriminate on a ground the New Mexico Human Rights Act protects. New Mexico has no state statute limiting the use of credit, eviction or criminal history in tenant screening beyond these rules.

title: No Local Rent Control in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico law bars cities, counties and other political subdivisions, including home-rule cities, from enacting rent control for privately owned property. The bar does not apply to housing that receives government benefits or funding to provide reduced rents for low- or moderate-income tenants. Other local rental rules, such as those in Albuquerque, Santa Fe or Las Cruces, are not covered here; check them separately.

title: Returned Checks in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico does not cap a returned-payment fee in a residential lease, but you may charge one only if the lease states it and your listing described it. Separately, if a tenant wrote a check knowing there were insufficient funds and intending to defraud, you may sue for the greater of $100 or three times the check (no more than $500 above the check amount), but only after sending a written demand by certified mail, return receipt requested and marked 'deliver to addressee only', warning that triple damages may be owed if the check is not paid within 10 days.

title: Applying Rent Payments in New Mexico
bodyText: Unless you and the tenant agree in writing, you may not apply a rent payment to deposits or damages. A lease could include that written agreement, but the library does not offer one: if you apply rent to damages and then sue for unpaid rent, the court must let the tenant pay within three days after judgment and avoid eviction. If you want such a clause, write your own and take advice first.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts in New Mexico
bodyText: Without a written agreement fixing a different rate, interest on money due under a contract in New Mexico may not exceed 15% a year, and court judgments generally bear 8.75% a year. A lease could set an interest rate on unpaid amounts, but the library does not offer one: interest on late rent can be argued to be a second late charge beyond the 5% late-fee cap. If you want an interest clause, take advice first.

title: Rent Receipts in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no general rule requiring a landlord to give rent receipts. Two exceptions: you must give a written or digital receipt for an application screening fee, and while an eviction appeal is pending, a tenant who pays rent directly to you is entitled to an immediate written receipt on demand. Keeping a record of every payment is still good practice.

title: Gross Receipts Tax and Residential Rent
bodyText: Receipts from leasing real property, including residential rent and furniture or appliances included in a rented home, may be deducted from New Mexico gross receipts. Receipts of hotels, motels, rooming houses and similar lodging from lodgers and guests are not treated as real property rent for this purpose. Local lodgers' taxes are not covered here.

title: No New Mexico Rule on Rent-Pricing Software
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute regulating the use of algorithmic or software-based rent-setting tools. General antitrust law still applies, and local rules are not covered here.

title: New Mexico Security Deposit Limits
bodyText: A deposit must be reasonable. If the lease runs less than one year (including a month-to-month tenancy), the deposit may not exceed one month's rent. Under an annual lease, a deposit larger than one month's rent is allowed, but you must pay the tenant interest on it every year, and that larger deposit may not be treated as prepaid rent. A refundable pet deposit counts toward these limits; last month's rent paid in advance under the lease does not.

title: Interest on Large Deposits in New Mexico
bodyText: Under an annual lease, if you take a deposit larger than one month's rent, you must pay the tenant interest on the deposit every year. The statute sets the rate as the passbook interest permitted to savings and loan associations in New Mexico by the Federal Home Loan Bank Board, an agency that no longer sets such rates, so the current rate is unclear; get advice on the rate or keep the deposit at one month's rent or less.

title: Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in New Mexico
bodyText: If you do not give the tenant an itemized written list of deductions and the balance due within 30 days, you lose the right to keep any part of the deposit, the right to counterclaim in the tenant's suit for it, and the right to sue separately for damage to the property, and you must pay the tenant's court costs and reasonable attorney fees. Keeping a deposit in bad faith adds a $250 civil penalty. If you do send a timely list, a 2025 Court of Appeals decision held that a landlord who complied could still bring a claim for damage not included on the list.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit in New Mexico
bodyText: A lease may require the last month's rent in advance, and that prepaid rent does not count toward the deposit limits. The statute says a deposit taken under an annual lease in an amount above one month's rent may not be treated as prepaid rent; whether a smaller deposit may be is not stated, so do not let a tenant use the deposit as the last month's rent unless you agree in writing.

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Fees in New Mexico
bodyText: A refundable pet deposit is a deposit under New Mexico law: it counts toward the one-month limit for a lease under a year (or the interest threshold under an annual lease) and is returned or itemized with the security deposit. Pet rent and other pet fees must be stated in the lease and described in your listing. Federal fair housing guidance treats assistance animals as an accommodation, not a pet, so the library charges no pet deposit, pet rent or pet fee for one.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold in New Mexico
bodyText: When you sell or otherwise transfer the property, the new owner becomes liable for all obligations under the lease and the act, including the deposit. You are relieved of liability only for events after you give the tenant written notice that your interest has ended, unless the lease says otherwise. After receiving that notice, the tenant pays rent to the new owner.

title: No New Mexico Rule on Where Deposits Are Held
bodyText: New Mexico does not require residential security deposits to be kept in a separate account, escrow or bank. You must still return or account for the deposit within 30 days after the tenancy ends.

title: Unclaimed Deposits in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's landlord-tenant law has no rule on a deposit the tenant never claims. Under the state's unclaimed property law, money owed that falls in no specific category is presumed abandoned five years after the owner's right to demand it arises, and must then be handled as unclaimed property. Mailing the itemized statement and any balance to the tenant's last known address within 30 days satisfies the deposit statute.

title: Holding Deposits in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute on holding deposits taken before a lease is signed. The 2025 law allows an applicant to be charged a screening fee or a deposit but bars any other application-processing fee, so a holding payment should be a true refundable deposit with written terms, not a fee. Once the lease is signed, money securing the tenant's performance is a deposit subject to the deposit limits.

title: No New Mexico Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: New Mexico does not require a move-in inspection, checklist or condition report, or a move-out inspection with the tenant present. Because you must prove any deduction from the deposit, documenting the condition at move-in and move-out (signed checklist, dated photos) is strongly recommended. At move-out the tenant must leave the unit as clean as at move-in, except for normal wear and tear; uncleanliness is not normal wear and tear.

title: Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico landlords must substantially comply with minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make repairs and keep the premises safe; keep common areas safe; keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, that you supply or are required to supply in good and safe working order; provide garbage receptacles and arrange removal; and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat (unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct utility connection).

A lease cannot waive these duties.

For a single family residence, the tenant may agree to take over garbage, water, hot water and heat duties and specified repairs, but only in a writing made for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your duties; for other units, the tenant may agree only to specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by consideration, made in good faith and not to evade your duties, and not affecting your duties to other tenants.

title: Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico
bodyText: If you fail to meet your repair duties, the tenant must give you written notice. For a material breach of the lease, or a violation of the act materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may give notice that the lease ends in at least 7 days unless you make a reasonable attempt to fix it. Or, if you do not fix a covered condition within 7 days of written notice, the tenant may withhold one-third of the daily rent from the notice date until it is fixed, or all of the rent if the home is uninhabitable and the tenant does not live there. The tenant may also sue for damages. These remedies do not apply to conditions the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused, or to amenities. New Mexico does not let tenants repair and deduct.

title: Tenant's Duties Under New Mexico Law
Utility Billing Rights in New Mexico
bodyText:
In multi-unit housing where each unit is separately metered, a tenant may ask you or your agent for a copy of the utility bill for the unit; if the unit is submetered, also the building's bill; any common-area bills whose cost is passed on, and your apportionment calculations. You may not allocate an empty unit's share of common-area costs to the other tenants. You may charge up to $5 per monthly request, but only if the lease includes that fee.

Supplying a utility only to your own tenants, without reselling it to others, does not make you a public utility, but a gas master meter at an apartment complex falls under the state's pipeline safety law (see "Submetering and Reselling Utilities to Tenants in New Mexico"). In a mobile home park, a park that provides utility services may charge only a reasonable administrative fee for doing so, stated in the rental agreement, with 60 days of written notice before an increase.

title: Municipal Utility Charges as a Lien on Rentals
bodyText: A New Mexico municipal utility charge is payable by the property owner and becomes a lien on the property served, even when a tenant ran it up. To avoid that, notify the municipality in writing, before the tenant's charges begin, that the renter's utility charges will not be your responsibility, and include the rental property's location.

title: Written Lease Required in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico landlord must give each tenant a written rental agreement before occupancy begins, and must give the tenant copies of the existing rules when the lease is signed.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes do not set a landlord-tenant rule for smoke or carbon monoxide alarms in rentals. Buildings with four or more units are subject to state rules requiring inspection and testing of fire and smoke dampers and smoke control systems by certified inspectors.

Alarm requirements come from the building, fire and housing codes that apply to the property, which a landlord must substantially comply with where they affect health and safety. For buildings with four or more units, the State Fire Marshal's fire code applies; an existing building generally must meet the alarm requirements in place when it was built.

The model codes setting those requirements were not available to this library (see "Which Fire and Building Codes Apply to New Mexico Rentals"). Check the state and local codes for your property.

title: No New Mexico Lock or Security Device Statute
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute requiring specific locks, deadbolts or rekeying between tenants. Changing or adding a lock to keep a tenant out without a court order is an unlawful lockout.

title: Entry Rules in New Mexico
bodyText:
The tenant must consent to entry to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit, but you must first give 24 hours' written notice stating the purpose, the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame. A written notice to a tenant must be hand-delivered or mailed (or posted and also mailed or hand-delivered).

No notice is needed to make repairs within 7 days of the tenant's request or when accompanied by an inspector or utility or cable representative. Try to accommodate a tenant's reasonable request for another time.

You may enter without consent in an emergency, after abandonment or surrender, or at reasonably necessary times during an absence of more than 7 days. A tenant who refuses lawful access can be made to allow it or have the lease terminated, with damages and fees; abusive or unlawful entry gives the tenant the same remedies.

The statute lets the lease set different entry terms, but the library keeps the statutory notice; take advice before changing it.

title: Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
If rent is unpaid when due, you may give the tenant written notice of nonpayment and of your intention to terminate. If the tenant does not pay within 3 days after the notice, you may terminate and seek possession; but if the tenant tenders the full amount due, in the way the notice states, before the 3 days run out, you cannot sue for that nonpayment.

A 2023 Court of Appeals decision held that the petition may be filed no earlier than the day after the third day.

The notice is effective only if hand-delivered, mailed, or posted on an exterior door, and must show the posting date. If the last day falls on a weekend or federal holiday, the period runs to the next day that is not a weekend or federal holiday.

The Supreme Court's Form 4-901 is the standard notice.

title: Seven-Day Notice for Other Lease Breaches
bodyText:
For a first material breach other than rent (or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties materially affecting health and safety), give written notice describing the breach, with dates and specific facts, stating that the lease will end on a date at least 7 days after the tenant receives it unless the breach is remedied in 7 days, and stating that the lease will end on a second material breach within 6 months. Give it within 30 days of the breach or of learning of it.

For a second material breach within 6 months, give a written notice with the same detail stating that the lease will end at least 7 days after receipt; no cure is allowed.

A court can grant relief only on the grounds stated in the notice.

title: Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation
bodyText:
If a tenant knowingly commits, or consents to another person in the unit or on the premises knowingly committing, a 'substantial violation', you may give a written notice specifying the time, place and nature of the act and stating that the lease will end at least 3 days after receipt.

Only the conduct listed in the statute counts: controlled-substance offenses other than misdemeanor possession and use; unlawful use of a deadly weapon; unlawful action causing serious physical harm; sexual assault or molestation; entering another's home or vehicle to commit theft or assault; theft by force or threat of force; and intentional or reckless property damage over $1,000, in the unit, on the premises or within 300 feet.

The tenant has defenses for domestic violence victims, for lack of knowledge, and for reasonable self-defense, and a frivolous or bad-faith action costs the landlord two times the monthly rent plus damages and costs.

title: Domestic Violence and Substantial-Violation Evictions
bodyText: In an eviction based on a substantial violation, it is a defense that the tenant is a victim of domestic violence. If the tenant has filed for or obtained a temporary domestic violence restraining order because of the incident behind the notice, or an earlier incident, the court may not issue a writ of restitution. In other cases where domestic violence is raised, the court has discretion to evict only the resident accused while letting the other residents' tenancy continue.

title: No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute letting a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking end a lease early or requiring a landlord to change locks for a victim. The act's only domestic violence rule is a defense to a substantial-violation eviction. Federal programs, such as housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, may have their own rules.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no just-cause or good-cause eviction statute: a fixed term ends on its end date, and a periodic tenancy can be ended by the required written notice without stating a reason. One exception: a mobile home park may end a tenancy for a mobile home lot only for the reasons the Mobile Home Park Act lists. Limits still apply: you may not end a tenancy, raise rent or cut services in retaliation for protected tenant activity within the last 6 months; a condominium conversion requires 60 days' notice and an offer to sell the unit to the tenant; a lease term letting a converting declarant end the lease early is unenforceable; and terminations for breach must follow the statutory notices.

title: When a Fixed-Term Lease Ends in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term. If the tenant stays without your consent after the term expires, you may bring an action for possession; no statute requires a notice to end a fixed term, but giving written notice that you will not renew avoids disputes. If you consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes month-to-month (week-to-week if rent is paid weekly), which then needs 30 days' (or 7 days') written notice to end. Rent and fee increases for the next term need notice before the term ends.

title: Holdover Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: If a tenant stays after the lease ends without your consent, you may bring an action for possession. Only if the holdover is willful and not in good faith may you also recover the damages you suffer and reasonable attorney fees. If you consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy continues month to month (week to week for weekly rent). If the tenant appeals an eviction judgment, the writ is stayed only if the tenant pays the rent into escrow or to you within 5 days of the appeal and keeps paying monthly.

title: Stipulated Holdover Rates in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico sets a damages measure only for a willful, bad-faith holdover (actual damages and attorney fees). A lease may fix a daily rate for holding over, and the library's holdover clause sets it at the Monthly Rent apportioned daily. A higher stipulated rate, such as one and a half or double rent, is not offered: a court may refuse to enforce a term it finds inequitable or a penalty. If you want one, take advice first.

title: Abandonment and Re-renting in New Mexico
bodyText: A tenant has 'abandoned' the unit only if absent, without notice to you, for more than 7 continuous days after rent became delinquent. Then you may take possession immediately, must store the tenant's property as the law requires, and may make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental; if you re-rent for a term starting before the lease would have ended, the lease ends when the new tenancy begins. Any party claiming damages must mitigate them.

title: Property Left After an Eviction in New Mexico
bodyText: After a writ of restitution is executed, you have no obligation to store property left more than 3 days, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, and may then dispose of it in any manner. Within those 3 days the tenant has a right to a reasonable opportunity to recover it, on paying reasonable moving and storage fees if you require them. You may not hold the tenant's property for other debts, and New Mexico gives landlords no lien on a residential tenant's belongings.

title: Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico
bodyText: If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the home, the tenant may move out and give written notice within 7 days ending the lease as of the move-out date, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced by the lost rental value. If the lease ends, you must return the balance of prepaid rent and the deposit as the deposit law provides. The tenant remains responsible for damage caused by the tenant's negligence. The statute gives the landlord no termination right; an optional lease clause can add a narrow one.

title: Damage a Tenant Causes in New Mexico
bodyText:
A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and a tenant who intentionally damages the premises is liable for two times the monthly rent; you may also recover damages for the tenant's noncompliance (whether both may be recovered for the same damage is not settled here). When the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused a condition, the tenant cannot use it to end the lease or withhold rent under the repair remedies.

But after a fire or casualty the tenant may still end the lease or reduce the rent even if the tenant was negligent, while remaining liable for the damage. A lease cannot take that casualty right away.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico
bodyText: You may not raise rent, decrease services, or bring or threaten an eviction because, within the previous 6 months, a tenant who is in compliance with the lease complained to a housing-code agency, joined or organized a tenants' union, exercised rights under the act in good faith (including a written repair request), filed a fair housing complaint, won or has pending a lawsuit against you about the tenancy, testified for another tenant, or lawfully abated rent. A violation makes you liable for two times the monthly rent and other remedies, and is a defense to eviction. Increases or service changes that are uniform for similar units and given with proper notice at the end of the term are allowed, and you may still evict for nonpayment, material noncompliance, a substantial violation or a code violation the tenant caused.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico
bodyText: Except after abandonment or surrender, you may not exclude or remove a tenant without a court order by fraud, changing or adding locks, blocking an entrance, interfering with utilities or services, removing the tenant's belongings, removing appliances or fixtures (except for legitimate repairs), or making the unit inaccessible or uninhabitable. A judgment for possession is not a court order permitting a utility shutoff before the writ is executed. You need not pay a tenant's own utility bills, but you may not direct a utility to cut service. The tenant may abate all rent for each affected day, recover two times the monthly rent and damages, and regain possession or end the lease.

title: No Landlord Lien on a Tenant's Belongings in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico gives a landlord no lien on a residential tenant's personal property for unpaid rent. You may collect a judgment for rent or damages only through the court's levy and execution process.

title: How Evictions Work in New Mexico
bodyText: After the required notice expires, an owner files a petition for restitution in magistrate or metropolitan court (a metropolitan court has the magistrate courts' jurisdiction) or district court, stating the facts, describing the premises and showing the notice was given. Trial is set 7 to 10 days after the summons is served, and the court may continue it up to 7 days for good cause. If the owner wins, the court issues a writ directing the sheriff to restore possession on a date 3 to 7 days after judgment. An owner or the property manager may appear without a lawyer in magistrate and metropolitan court. The Supreme Court's eviction prevention and diversion program was withdrawn for new cases in January 2023, but some of its forms remain in the rules.

title: Eviction Court Records in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute or court rule that automatically seals or limits access to eviction records. Court records are open to the public unless a court orders them sealed on a motion. The rules tell courts and parties to avoid including full Social Security, account and driver's license numbers and keep them off public court websites, but clerks do not screen filings for them.

title: Standard Notice Forms in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico prescribes no lease form, but the Supreme Court publishes standard forms for the act's notices: a 3-day notice of nonpayment of rent, a 3-day notice of substantial violation, a 7-day notice of noncompliance, a 30-day notice to terminate, and court forms for the petition, summons, answer, judgment and writ of restitution. Using them is the safest way to give the content the statute requires.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no special squatter-removal statute. A person who entered and occupied property without the owner's consent and refused to leave after notice can be removed by a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action, and knowingly remaining on property after consent is denied can be criminal trespass. Anyone who is a resident under a rental agreement, including an occupant the tenant allowed in, must be removed through the act's notice and court process, never by lockout.

title: Servicemember Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no state statute letting a servicemember end a residential lease early; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act provides that right. The New Mexico Human Rights Act bars housing discrimination because of military status.

title: When a Tenant Dies in New Mexico
bodyText:
If a tenant who is the sole occupant dies, you must turn the property in the home over to the tenant's named contact person, or another person lawfully entitled, if they ask before it is discarded, and refund the deposit less lawful deductions (including removal and storage costs). You may remove and store the property, require an inventory signature, and discard it only after a certified-mail request to the contact person and 30 days without removal or any claim. If you asked in writing for a contact person and the tenant gave none, you have no responsibility for the property.

The death does not end the lease by statute. A lease may set a different procedure, but the library uses the statutory one; take advice before changing it.

title: Sale of the Property or a New Manager in New Mexico
bodyText: When the property is sold or management changes, give the tenant written notice and keep the required owner and manager disclosures current; they bind any successor owner or manager. The seller is relieved only for events after the tenant receives written notice that its interest ended, the buyer takes on all lease obligations, and the tenant pays future rent to the buyer once notified.

title: Foreclosure and Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no state statute protecting residential tenants when a rental property is foreclosed; federal law may. If a lender with an assignment of rents sends the tenant a statutory notification, the tenant must pay rent to the lender, though a tenant who lives in the unit as a primary residence is still credited for rent paid to the landlord.

title: Condominium Conversion Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: A declarant converting a building to condominiums must give each residential tenant notice of the conversion and the disclosure statement at least 60 days before the tenant must vacate, and must offer to sell the unit to the tenant for 60 days. Failure to give notice is a defense to eviction, and a lease term letting the declarant end the lease early just because of the conversion is unenforceable.

title: Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico lease may not make the tenant (or the landlord) waive or give up rights or remedies under the law, so clauses saying the landlord is not liable, waivers of the notices the act requires before ending a tenancy or filing for possession, and similar terms are not allowed (the parties may agree to different entry-notice terms; see "Entry Rules in New Mexico"). A landlord who deliberately uses a lease containing terms known to be prohibited owes the tenant the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees. A confession-of-judgment clause signed before a claim arises is void, there is no landlord's lien on a tenant's belongings, and a court may limit any term it finds was inequitable when made.

title: Attorney Fees in New Mexico Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: In a suit by an applicant or a party to enforce the lease or the Owner-Resident Relations Act, the winning side is entitled to reasonable attorney fees and court costs. Fees also follow from specific violations, such as failing to return a deposit properly, a willful holdover, refusing or abusing access, a bad-faith counterclaim, or knowingly using prohibited lease terms. A lease may provide for prevailing-party fees, which matches the statute.

title: Inequitable Lease Terms in New Mexico
bodyText: If a court finds that any lease term was inequitable when made, it may limit the term to avoid an inequitable result, after giving the parties a chance to present evidence about the lease's setting, purpose and effect. Separately, an unconscionable trade practice in renting can violate the Unfair Practices Act.

title: Unfair Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act covers trade practices in connection with the lease or rental of property, and since June 20, 2025 it specifically lists charging an applicant an unauthorized fee, charging an applicant a fee not published in the listing, and charging a tenant a fee not in the lease. A tenant can recover actual damages or $100, up to three times damages or $300 for willful violations, plus attorney fees.

title: How to Serve Notices in New Mexico
bodyText:
A notice of nonpayment of rent is effective only if handed to the tenant, mailed, or posted on an exterior door of the unit. Any other written notice to a tenant may be posted only if it is also mailed first class or handed to the tenant. Every notice must state the posting date, which is its effective date; a posted notice must be taped on all sides or placed in a mail or notice receptacle.

If a mailed notice comes back or the tenant's last known address is the vacated unit, serve one more notice at any other address the tenant gave you.

E-mail does not replace these methods: New Mexico's electronic transactions law does not apply to default, eviction or right-to-cure notices for a primary residence.

title: Quiet Enjoyment in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's act protects a tenant's quiet enjoyment mainly through its entry rules and its ban on lockouts and service cutoffs: unlawful entries, unreasonable entries or repeated entry demands that interfere with quiet enjoyment let the tenant seek an injunction, end the lease and recover damages and attorney fees. There is no separate statutory covenant of quiet enjoyment in the act.

title: Accepting Late or Partial Rent in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's act has no section on whether accepting rent with knowledge of a breach waives the right to terminate. It does say that full payment, in the way the notice states, before a 3-day nonpayment notice expires bars an eviction for that nonpayment. If you accept partial or late rent and still intend to pursue termination, say so in writing at the time. Separately, cashing a check the tenant conspicuously marks as payment in full of a disputed amount can settle your claim under New Mexico's commercial code; see "Checks Marked "Paid in Full" in New Mexico".

title: Nuisance and Illegal Use of a Rental in New Mexico
bodyText: If a tenant is convicted of using the property as a house of prostitution or as a gambling place, or the property is adjudged a public nuisance (for a gambling place, adjudged a public nuisance on any ground), the lease is voidable by the landlord, who may regain possession as from a tenant holding over. Tenants must not disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment, and listed criminal conduct that the tenant knowingly commits or consents to is a substantial violation allowing a 3-day termination notice.

title: Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act
bodyText: The New Mexico Human Rights Act bars refusing to rent, discriminating in rental terms, conditions, privileges or services, and advertising or inquiring in a way that shows a preference, because of race, religion, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, pregnancy, childbirth or a related condition, spousal affiliation, physical or mental disability, or military status. The Act does not list familial status or age for housing; the federal Fair Housing Act protects families with children. Narrow exemptions cover some single-family homes rented by an owner of no more than three without discriminatory advertising, owner-occupied buildings of up to four units, and some religious organizations.

title: Source of Income in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico state law does not prohibit refusing a tenant because of a housing voucher or other lawful source of income. Some local governments may have their own rules; check your city and county. Refusing a voucher holder as a cover for a protected characteristic is still unlawful.

title: Assistance Animals in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText:
Treat a request to keep an assistance animal for a disability as a reasonable-accommodation request under fair housing law; do not charge pet fees for it. New Mexico's Human Rights Act bars disability discrimination in rental terms, conditions and services.

New Mexico's Service Animal Act requires admitting a person using a qualified service animal to any building open to the public and other public accommodations, which may include your leasing office and other areas open to the public, but it does not speak to a tenant's own unit; the White Cane Law likewise protects guide dogs in hotels, lodging places and places open to the public. Denying entry under either law is a misdemeanor (see "Penalties for Refusing a Service Animal in New Mexico"), and knowingly passing off an animal as a qualified service animal is a misdemeanor anywhere.

title: Misrepresenting a Service Animal in New Mexico
bodyText: It is a misdemeanor in New Mexico to knowingly present an animal as a qualified service animal (a trained service dog or miniature horse) when it is not one. Emotional support, comfort and therapy animals are not qualified service animals under the Service Animal Act, though a tenant may still need one as a disability accommodation in housing.

title: Cannabis in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: Adults 21 and older may lawfully use and grow limited amounts of cannabis at home in New Mexico (up to six mature and six immature plants per person, and no more than twelve mature plants per household). The act does not restrict a person's ability to prohibit cannabis conduct on the person's privately owned property, which the library reads as letting a rental owner ban it in the lease. No New Mexico statute protects a tenant's cannabis use from a lease prohibition.

title: Firearms and Rental Housing in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's constitution protects the right to keep and bear arms and bars cities and counties from regulating any incident of that right, but it restrains laws, not private landlords. No New Mexico statute limits a landlord's lease rules on firearms or requires landlords to allow them. Unlawful use of a deadly weapon on or near the premises is a substantial violation.

title: Towing From Rental Property in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico law expressly lets a property owner or parking-lot manager have a vehicle towed at the vehicle owner's expense for parking in, or blocking, an accessible space without a placard or plate. A vehicle is 'abandoned' only after law enforcement determines it was left unattended on public or private property for at least 30 days, and disposal requires a law-enforcement clearance.

Towing companies doing nonconsensual tows are regulated by the state. Under the Department of Transportation's towing rules, a towing service may not tow a vehicle illegally parked at an apartment property unless the property has visible signs telling the public that illegally parked vehicles may be towed and stating the exact hours when a vehicle is considered illegally parked. For each tow from private property, the towing service must first get written authorization signed by the property owner, lessee or agent, giving the location, how long the vehicle has been there, a description of it, the date and time of removal and a statement that it is illegally parked; it must photograph the vehicle (and, at an apartment, the signs), and it may not pay the property owner or agent anything for the right to tow there.

Separately, removing a tenant's belongings to force them out is an unlawful lockout.

title: No Duty to Disclose Deaths or Crimes in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico landlord has no duty to disclose, and is not liable for not disclosing, that a property was the site of a natural death, a homicide, suicide, assault, sexual assault or other felony, or was occupied by someone with HIV or another disease highly unlikely to be transmitted through occupancy. Failing to disclose these facts is not grounds to cancel the lease. Do not misrepresent them if asked.

title: Out-of-State Owners in New Mexico
bodyText: An owner who does not live in New Mexico, or a corporation not authorized to do business here, may designate a New Mexico agent for service of process by a written designation filed with the secretary of state. If none is designated, process may be served on the secretary of state with a copy mailed to the owner. New Mexico has no statewide landlord registration requirement, but an out-of-state limited liability company must register with the secretary of state, naming a New Mexico registered agent, before transacting business here, and an out-of-state corporation must obtain a certificate of authority. Until it does, it may not maintain an eviction or other suit in a New Mexico court, and it is liable for the fees it should have paid plus a civil penalty (up to $200 a year for a company, $200 an offense for a corporation); its leases stay valid, and an unregistered company is treated as having appointed the secretary of state as its agent for service of process on claims arising from its New Mexico business (NMSA 1978, §§ 53-19-48, 53-19-53, 53-17-1, 53-17-20). For a limited liability company, "owning, without more, real or personal property" is not transacting business, and the corporation statute has no such exception; whether renting out property is more than owning it is a case-law question, so get advice or register before you need to file (NMSA 1978, § 53-19-54(A)(9)). New Mexico's statutes contain no requirement for a business name to be filed before you rent under it; registering a name you use to identify your rental services as a service mark with the secretary of state under the Trademark Act is optional (NMSA 1978, § 57-3B-5).

title: Plain Language in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico has no plain-language statute for leases. The only plain-language rule is for listings: since June 20, 2025, a rental listing must disclose all costs, including base rent and an itemized description of every fee, in plain language.

title: No New Mexico Blank-Space Rule for Leases
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute barring blank spaces in a lease or requiring a copy at signing, other than the duty to give each tenant a written rental agreement before occupancy begins. Fill in every blank before the tenant signs anyway.

title: No New Mexico Rule on Security Cameras in Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute on security cameras installed by landlords or tenants in rental housing. Criminal voyeurism and privacy laws still apply, and recording inside a tenant's unit is never appropriate.

title: No New Mexico Tenant EV-Charging Right
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute giving tenants a right to install electric vehicle charging at a rental or setting rules for it; tax credits for charging units exist but impose no landlord duty. Any charging arrangement is up to the lease. New construction is different: since January 30, 2024, the state energy codes require new residential parking, including apartment parking facilities, to be built EV-ready or with charging equipment (see "EV Charging Rules That Apply to New Mexico Rentals").

title: No New Mexico Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose mold or setting mold standards for rentals. Mold that makes the home unsafe is still covered by your duty to keep the premises safe and in compliance with housing codes.

title: No New Mexico Bed Bug Rule
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute requiring bed bug disclosures or setting landlord and tenant duties for bed bugs. An infestation can still breach your duty to keep the premises safe and in compliance with housing codes.

title: No New Mexico Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute requiring a landlord to test for or disclose radon.

title: No New Mexico Methamphetamine Disclosure Rule
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose past methamphetamine manufacture or use at a rental, or setting cleanup standards for rentals. Contamination that makes the home unsafe is still covered by your duty to keep the premises safe.

title: No New Mexico Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose flood history or flood-zone status to a tenant.

title: Sex Offender Information and Rentals in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute restricting where a registered sex offender may rent or requiring landlords to disclose or check the registry. Registry information about certain offenders is publicly available from the sheriff, local law enforcement, the district attorney or the Department of Public Safety. State law takes over the field of sex offender registration and notification and bars cities and counties from adding their own restrictions on sex offenders, which this library reads as displacing local residency rules (no case read).

title: Immigration Status and Rentals in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute requiring or barring a landlord's inquiry into a tenant's immigration status. National origin and ancestry are protected under the Human Rights Act, so apply any identification requirement the same way to everyone.

title: No New Mexico Foreign-Ownership Rule for Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute restricting foreign ownership or leasing of residential rental property. The former constitutional restriction on aliens' land ownership has been repealed.

title: No New Mexico Rule on Tenant Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute protecting a tenant from eviction or penalties for calling police or emergency services. The act does protect tenants who are domestic violence victims in substantial-violation evictions, and retaliation for complaints to code agencies is barred.

title: Written Leases and the Statute of Frauds in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes contain no general statute of frauds for leases of real property, but the Owner-Resident Relations Act requires the landlord to give each tenant a written rental agreement before occupancy. Put every lease in writing, especially one longer than a year.

title: No Statewide Rental Inspection or Registration in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statewide rental registration, licensing or inspection program. Municipalities may adopt ordinances on repairing, closing or demolishing unfit dwellings, and local programs may exist; check your city or county.

title: No Guest Fees in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico landlord may not charge a tenant a fee for a reasonable number of guests staying a reasonable length of time. You may still charge for guests' use of premises or facilities other than the home itself (for example, a guest parking pass or amenity), if the lease includes that fee.

title: Waiving Repair and Habitability Duties in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico lease cannot remove or reduce your repair and habitability duties. The Owner-Resident Relations Act bars any rental agreement term by which the tenant (or you) agrees to waive or give up rights or remedies under the law. So a clause in which the tenant takes the unit "as is", gives up the right to repairs, or releases you from your duties is not allowed. Those duties are: substantially complying with housing codes materially affecting health and safety; making repairs and keeping the premises safe; keeping common areas safe; maintaining the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including any elevators, that you supply or are required to supply; providing garbage receptacles and arranging removal; and supplying running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat. The law allows only one narrower arrangement: the tenant may agree to do specified work. For a single family residence, that agreement must be in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your duties, and it may cover garbage removal, water, hot water and heat as well as specified repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodeling. For any other unit, it may cover only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling; it must be entered into in good faith and not to evade your duties, set out in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by consideration, and it must not affect your duties to other tenants. Even then your own duties are not reduced, and the tenant's failure to do the work is not a ground for eviction or a material breach (see the optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement, "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause). New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that lets a tenant accept a stated defect in exchange for a rent reduction. The heat and hot-water duty does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for it, or where the unit is built so that the heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection; that is the statute's own scope, not a waiver. If you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees.

title: Changing Habitability Terms by Agreement in New Mexico
bodyText: In New Mexico the lease can change who performs some upkeep tasks, but never the standard you must meet. The only agreements the law allows are these. For a single family residence, the tenant may agree, in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your duties, to handle garbage removal and the supply of running water, hot water and heat, and to do specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling. For any other unit, the tenant may agree only to specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, in good faith and not to evade your duties, in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by consideration, and the agreement may not affect your duties to other tenants. Any such arrangement leaves your own legal duties in place, and the tenant's failure to do the work is not a ground for eviction or a material breach. Use the Landscaping & Irrigation and Snow Removal clauses only for a single family residence, and the separate Tenant Maintenance Agreement for other units. Two limits are part of the statute itself, not agreements: you need not supply heat or hot water where the building is not required by law to be equipped for it, or where the unit is built so that the heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection; and where a minimum housing code applies, your maximum duty under this rule is to substantially comply with that code's requirements materially affecting health and safety. New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that lets the lease waive the water or hot-water duty for a unit without well or utility water.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in a New Mexico Lease
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires the lease itself to state that the home is fit to live in or that you will keep it so. Your repair and habitability duties apply whether or not the lease mentions them, and a lease cannot waive them (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). What the law does require: you must give each tenant a written rental agreement before occupancy begins, and at the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the rental agreement and your statutory duties; if you do not deliver possession, rent abates in full until you do, and the tenant may end the agreement on written notice or demand performance. The library's Maintenance & Repairs clause states your repair commitment in words that fit New Mexico law; you may use it, but it does not replace the statutory duties.

title: When a Repair Problem Is Material in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico measures your repair and code duties by whether a condition materially affects health and safety. You must substantially comply with minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety. When you fail to meet your repair duties, the tenant's right to end the lease on a 7-day notice arises for a material breach of the rental agreement, or for a violation of the Owner-Resident Relations Act that materially affects health and safety; you avoid termination by making a reasonable attempt to fix it within the notice period. The tenant may abate one-third of the daily rent for a violation of your repair duties that you do not remedy within 7 days of written notice, and all of the rent if the home is uninhabitable and the tenant does not live there because of it. An "amenity" is a facility or area you supply whose absence would not materially affect the tenant's health and safety or the home's habitability; a broken amenity gives no abatement. The same health-and-safety test applies to the tenant's own duties and to the tenant's protection from retaliation for a code complaint. The statute defines none of these words further, so whether a given defect is material will be decided by the court on the facts; treat any defect touching health, safety or habitability as material and repair it promptly.

title: No Habitability Presumptions in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law creates a presumption about habitability: for example, that a unit with a code violation is uninhabitable, that a landlord who fails to repair within a set time acted in bad faith, or that a landlord action soon after a tenant complaint is retaliatory. The Owner-Resident Relations Act bars retaliation for complaints, organizing, requests for repairs, abating rent and other protected acts within the previous six months, and a violation is a defense to an action for possession, but the act states no presumption, and who must prove what is left to the courts. The act also lets you bring a possession action despite a complaint where, for example, the code violation was caused mainly by the tenant's lack of reasonable care or the tenant is in default in rent. On heat, the compilation's annotation summarizes a 1981 New Mexico Supreme Court decision placing on the landlord the burden of showing a law that exempts the building from the heat duty. Cautious course: keep written repair requests, your responses and dates, because a dispute will turn on the evidence.

title: Habitability Rules New Mexico Does Not Have
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that provides any of the following, so do not expect them or build them into a lease: a presumption about habitability, bad-faith delay or retaliation ("No Habitability Presumptions in New Mexico"); a requirement that the lease state the home is fit to live in ("No Required Habitability Statement in a New Mexico Lease"); a tenant's right to repair and deduct, or a lead or health statute directing rent withholding ("Tenant Remedies When a New Mexico Landlord Breaches", "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico"); a way for a tenant to accept a stated defect for a rent reduction or to take the unit "as is" ("Waiving Repair and Habitability Duties in New Mexico"); or a statutory "warranty of habitability" under that name (the duties are the owner's statutory obligations in "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). Earlier New Mexico rows record other absences on habitability-related subjects: mold ("No New Mexico Mold Disclosure Rule"), bed bugs ("No New Mexico Bed Bug Rule"), radon ("No New Mexico Radon Disclosure Rule"), methamphetamine contamination ("No New Mexico Methamphetamine Disclosure Rule"), flood disclosure ("No New Mexico Flood Disclosure Rule"), locks and security devices ("No New Mexico Lock or Security Device Statute") and smoke and carbon monoxide alarm statutes ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms in New Mexico"); see each row for its scope. Local housing codes (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may add rules.

title: Rights a New Mexico Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: New Mexico has one non-waiver rule for residential leases, and it is broad: no rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to waive or give up rights or remedies under the law. It covers every right and remedy, not only those in the Owner-Resident Relations Act, and it binds both sides. It works alongside three other rules: the lease may include any terms the act or other law does not prohibit; a court may limit a term it finds was inequitable when made; and a landlord who deliberately uses a lease containing terms known to be prohibited owes the tenant the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees. Some default rules in the act are written to apply only "unless otherwise agreed" or let the agreement set the term, and an agreement on those is not a prohibited waiver (this library's reading): where and when rent is paid; applying rent payments to deposits or damages (only by written agreement); your liability after you transfer the property or a manager leaves; the 24-hour entry notice; use of the unit only as a dwelling, and a duty to give notice of an absence over 7 days; storing property after a writ of restitution; handling a deceased tenant's property (in a written rental agreement or other agreement); and having the tenant perform specified tasks (on the statute's conditions). After a dispute arises, a claim may be settled by agreement. No New Mexico statute sets a general non-waiver rule for a home sale-leaseback, but where a home in foreclosure is bought from its owner and leased back, the Mortgage Foreclosure Consultant Fraud Prevention Act may apply: it treats such a lease-back as a "foreclosure reconveyance", bars a foreclosure consultant from acquiring an interest in the home of an owner the consultant has contracted with, and makes any waiver by the owner of that act's provisions void; get advice before any lease-back with an owner in foreclosure. Mobile home park lots also follow the Mobile Home Park Act where it directly conflicts.

title: Changing the Showing Notice by Agreement in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico lets you and the tenant agree to entry-notice terms other than the statutory default. The tenant must consent to entry to inspect, repair, supply services, or show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, lenders, prospective tenants, workers or contractors; and unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, you may enter for those purposes only after 24 hours' written notice stating your intent, the purpose, and the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame. No separate document is required for such an agreement. The library does not offer a shorter-notice or showing clause: "Landlord's Entry" clause keeps the 24-hour written notice, because a shorter period is a choice to make with advice. You may add your own clause, for example a shorter written notice for showings in the last weeks of the term. Whatever you agree, these protections stay: you must not abuse the right of access; you must try to accommodate a tenant's reasonable request for another time where that is practicable or will not cause you economic loss; and unlawful entry, unreasonable entry, or repeated demands that unreasonably interfere with the tenant's quiet enjoyment let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover damages and attorney fees. A lease term that gave up those protections would be a prohibited waiver.

title: Landlord Liability Disclaimers in New Mexico Leases
bodyText: A New Mexico lease cannot make the tenant give up rights or remedies under the law, so a clause that releases you from liability for your own negligence or for failing to meet your repair and maintenance duties, or that makes the tenant hold you harmless for them, is not allowed. Your statutory repair duties do not change existing tort law, and the tenant may recover damages and get an injunction for your material noncompliance with the lease or your repair duties. If you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees. For this reason the library uses versions of its parking, storage, renter's insurance and services clauses without a "Landlord is not liable" sentence. A clause making the tenant pay for damage the tenant, a household member or a guest causes deliberately or negligently is different: the tenant owes that under the law. The law itself limits your liability in a few defined situations, with no lease clause needed: after a writ of restitution is executed you need not store property left behind for more than three days (unless you agree otherwise) and may then dispose of it without further notice or liability; property worth less than $100 left behind may be disposed of in any manner; if you fail to deliver possession but make reasonable efforts and return prepaid rent, deposits and fees within 7 days of the tenant's termination notice, you are not liable for damages for the failure; you are not liable for not disclosing that the property was the site of a natural death, a felony, or occupancy by a person with HIV or AIDS; after written notice that you have transferred the property or a manager's role has ended, you or the manager are relieved of liability for later events unless otherwise agreed; you need not pay utilities the tenant fails to pay; and you are not liable for a third-party website's failure to show the costs you gave it. In a mobile home park, a landlord's liability for removing a mobile home after judgment is limited to gross negligence or willful and wanton disregard of the owner's property rights.

title: Eviction Fees and Penalty Clauses in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law expressly bans, or expressly allows, a lease clause charging the tenant a set fee or penalty for being evicted. What the law provides instead: in a suit to enforce the lease or the Owner-Resident Relations Act, the winning side is entitled to reasonable attorney fees and court costs as the court assesses them; you may recover damages for the tenant's noncompliance; and the court may award fees and costs against a tenant whose defense or counterclaim is without merit and not in good faith. A fixed eviction charge is risky in New Mexico: any fee you charge a tenant must be included in the lease, a court may limit a lease term that was inequitable when made, and the rule against penalty clauses in contracts is case law. Cautious course: do not put a flat eviction fee or penalty in the lease; recover the fees and costs the court awards and your actual, documented damages. The fixed penalties the statute does set around possession run against the landlord: if a court finds an action for possession for a substantial violation was frivolous or brought in bad faith, the landlord owes a civil penalty of two times the monthly rent, plus damages and costs; and a landlord who removes or locks out a tenant without a court order, or retaliates (including by bringing or threatening an action for possession), is liable for two times the monthly rent.

title: Using a Lease With Prohibited Terms in New Mexico
bodyText: If you deliberately use a lease containing provisions you know are prohibited by law, the tenant may recover the damages the tenant suffered from the application of the illegal provision, and reasonable attorney fees. It is not a fixed sum: the recovery is measured by the harm the term caused. It reaches any provision prohibited by law, not only by the Owner-Resident Relations Act, and it sits alongside the act's bar on terms that waive rights or remedies and a court's power to limit a term that was inequitable when made. Mobile home park rental agreements have a parallel rule in the Mobile Home Park Act. Separately, the Unfair Practices Act makes it an unfair or deceptive trade practice to charge a tenant fees not included in the lease, and its general standards (such as stating that a transaction involves rights, remedies or obligations that it does not involve) may reach a lease that tells a tenant they have given up rights they keep (this library's reading; no case read). Several sections of the act carry their own fixed remedies (for example on deposits, lockouts and screening fees); no statute says those replace this remedy. Do not rely on a "nothing in this lease limits your rights" sentence to make a prohibited term safe; leave the term out.

title: Waiving Eviction Notices in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico lease cannot waive or shorten the notices the Owner-Resident Relations Act requires before you end a tenancy or seek possession. Those are: the 3-day written notice of nonpayment and of your intention to terminate (if the tenant tenders the full amount due, in the manner the notice states, before it runs, you cannot sue for that nonpayment); the 7-day written notice for a first material breach, which must let the tenant remedy it, and the 7-day notice for a second material breach within six months; the 3-day notice for a substantial violation; and the 7-day (week-to-week) and 30-day (month-to-month) written notices to end a periodic tenancy. These are rights of the tenant under the law, and the act bars any rental agreement term waiving them. Your petition for restitution must show you complied with the act's notice provisions, and the court may grant relief only on the grounds stated in the notice you served. If you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees. Serve each notice in a way the act allows (see "How to Serve Notices in New Mexico"). Mobile home park lots have their own notice rules in the Mobile Home Park Act. Federal law may require a longer notice for some properties ("Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Waiving Exemptions From Collection in a New Mexico Lease
bodyText: A New Mexico lease cannot make the tenant give up the exemptions that protect a debtor's property from a judgment creditor. New Mexico exempts listed property from attachment, execution, garnishment and levy, including household goods and furnishings, a motor vehicle, tools of the trade, many public and retirement benefits and a general amount of other personal property, many of them up to dollar limits that are adjusted for inflation every two years and published by the administrative office of the courts. It also gives a homestead exemption in a dwelling or land the person owns as a primary residence, and a person who owns no homestead gets an added exemption of real or personal property instead. These are rights under the law, and the Owner-Resident Relations Act bars any rental agreement term waiving them. For most tenants a homestead waiver would also be empty, since the homestead exemption covers a dwelling the person owns; it can matter for a tenant who owns a mobile home on a rented site. New Mexico gives you no landlord's lien on a tenant's belongings: you collect a judgment for rent or damages through the court's levy and execution, where the tenant may claim exemptions, and a creditor must give notice of the right to claim them. You may not keep exempt property left on the premises once an application for a writ of execution has been granted. If you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees.

title: Jury Waivers in New Mexico Leases
bodyText: Do not put a jury-trial waiver in a New Mexico lease. In metropolitan and magistrate court the right to trial by jury exists by statute in civil actions within the court's jurisdiction, and the New Mexico Constitution secures the right to trial by jury as it has existed. A jury is not automatic: a party must demand it (in metropolitan court, in the complaint or the answer) and pay the jury fee when demanding, or the jury is deemed waived; in district court a party may also waive by filing a waiver or by oral consent in open court. A lease clause in which the tenant gives up the jury in advance would be an agreement to waive a right under the law, which the Owner-Resident Relations Act bars any rental agreement from containing. New Mexico's statutes, constitution, 2025-2026 session laws and court rules do not address a jury waiver signed before a dispute; whether the bar reaches one is for the courts, and the cautious course is to leave such a clause out. If you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees. In arbitration, a clause in a standard-form lease that limits a tenant's procedural rights is unenforceable against, and voidable by, the tenant. Once a case is filed, either side may simply not demand a jury, or the parties may waive it in the ways the court rules allow.

title: Waiving Casualty Rights or the Duty to Mitigate in New Mexico
bodyText: A New Mexico lease cannot take away the tenant's fire and casualty rights or the duty to mitigate damages. If fire or another casualty damages the unit or premises so that the tenant's enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may move out and give written notice within 7 days, ending the lease as of the move-out date, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay rent reduced by the lost rental value; if the lease ends you must return the balance of prepaid rent and the deposit as the deposit law provides, and the tenant remains responsible for damage the tenant's negligence caused. Nothing in the Owner-Resident Relations Act lets a lease change these rights, and the act bars any rental agreement term waiving rights or remedies under the law. The library's optional casualty clause ("Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty" clause) adds only a narrow landlord termination right and keeps the tenant's rights. On mitigation, any party seeking damages under the act has a duty to mitigate them; after an abandonment you may make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental, and if you re-rent for a term starting before the lease would have ended, the lease ends when the new tenancy begins. A lease term saying you need not mitigate, or that the tenant owes all remaining rent however soon you re-rent, would have the tenant give up a remedy under the law, though that is for the courts to decide. New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that lets an express agreement override the tenant's casualty rights.

title: Liquidated Damages in New Mexico Leases
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law governs liquidated or agreed damages in a residential lease. New Mexico statutes allow reasonable liquidated damages, and void unreasonably large ones as penalties, only in other settings, such as sales and leases of goods and agreements with health care practitioners; those rules do not apply to a dwelling lease.

For a residential lease, the questions are left to general law: whether an agreed amount is an unenforceable penalty is case law; a court may limit a lease term it finds was inequitable when made; any party seeking damages under the Owner-Resident Relations Act must mitigate them; and any fee you charge must be stated in the lease.

Cautious course: recover your actual, documented damages and court-awarded fees and costs, and use an agreed amount only where the library offers a clause for it, stated in the lease as your figure (for example "Early Termination" clause).

The fixed amounts the act itself sets, such as the $250 civil penalty for a bad-faith deposit retention or two months' rent for certain violations, are statutory remedies, not agreed damages.

title: Tenant Remedies When a New Mexico Landlord Breaches
bodyText: If you breach the lease or the Owner-Resident Relations Act, a New Mexico tenant has these remedies, each on its own conditions. Repairs: after written notice, the tenant may give a notice ending the lease in at least 7 days for a material breach of the lease or a violation materially affecting health and safety, unless you make a reasonable attempt to fix it in time; or, if you do not fix a covered condition within 7 days of written notice, abate one-third of the daily rent (all of it if the home is uninhabitable and the tenant does not live there); the tenant may also sue for damages and an injunction for your material noncompliance. These repair remedies do not arise for conditions the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused, and where the problem comes solely from circumstances beyond your control the tenant gets only termination or abatement. Possession: if you fail to deliver possession at the start, rent abates in full and the tenant may end the lease or demand possession. Entry: unlawful or unreasonable entry, or repeated demands for entry that unreasonably interfere with quiet enjoyment, allow an injunction or termination, with damages and attorney fees. Lockouts and utility interference: the tenant may abate all rent for each affected day, recover restitution or end the lease, and recover damages and a statutory amount. Retaliation is a defense to your action for possession, and you are liable to the tenant for two times the monthly rent, plus attorney fees and costs if the tenant prevails. Fire or casualty: the tenant may move out or reduce rent. The winning side in a suit to enforce the lease or the act recovers reasonable attorney fees and costs. New Mexico gives no repair-and-deduct remedy, and no statute searched directs rent withholding or escrow for lead or other health hazards. See "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico" for the repair remedies in detail.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve in New Mexico
bodyText: In New Mexico a promise you make to a tenant to repair, clean or improve the unit is part of the rental agreement, and the tenant can enforce it. The rental agreement means all agreements between you and the tenant about the use and occupancy of the unit, and the tenant may recover damages and get an injunction for any material noncompliance by you with the rental agreement. Where the promise concerns your statutory repair duties, the tenant's 7-day termination notice and rent abatement remedies also apply. You must also deliver possession at the start of the term in compliance with the rental agreement. Representations about a rental may also be judged under the Unfair Practices Act, whose list of unfair or deceptive practices includes failing to deliver the quality or quantity of goods or services contracted for (whether that list reaches a dwelling lease is for the courts). No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a repair promise to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be given before the lease is signed. Cautious course: put any promise to repair, clean or improve in the lease or a signed addendum, saying what will be done and by when, and keep it.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Deposits in New Mexico Eviction Cases
bodyText: In a New Mexico action for possession for nonpayment, or an action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for any amount recoverable under the lease or the Owner-Resident Relations Act, but remains responsible for paying you the rent specified in the lease during the period of possession; judgment is entered according to the facts. On or before the appearance date the tenant may answer and raise any legal or equitable defense, setoff or counterclaim. In magistrate and metropolitan court no counterclaim is compulsory; in district court the general civil rules make a counterclaim arising from the same transaction compulsory. Other claims joined to a petition for restitution must be answered and tried separately if either party asks in writing. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule requires a tenant to pay rent into court or a court registry to raise a defense, to get a jury, or to obtain a continuance. Two related rules: if the tenant disputes the amount because the tenant abated rent (or because you applied rent to damages) and you win, the writ of restitution is conditioned on the tenant's right to pay the judgment within 3 days; and a tenant who appeals stays the writ only by paying, within 5 days of the notice of appeal, the rent coming due through the end of that rental period to you or a professional escrow agent, and then paying monthly rent as it falls due. A defense or counterclaim without merit and not in good faith lets you recover reasonable attorney fees and court costs, and the same applies against you for an action or reply without merit and not in good faith. The abatement section refers to an "abatement limitation of one month's rent" for subsidized rent, but the section states no such limit; do not assume one.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant in New Mexico
bodyText:
