New Mexico lets you shift specified maintenance work to the tenant only on the statute's conditions, and the shift never reduces your own duties.
- For a single family residence (a structure used as a single dwelling unit; a unit that shares walls with another still qualifies if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility or service with another unit), the tenant may agree in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your duties, to handle garbage removal and the supply of running water, hot water and heat, and to do specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling; that writing may be the lease itself, which is why the library's Landscaping & Irrigation and Snow Removal clauses bind only for a single family residence.
- For any other unit, the tenant may agree only to specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, in good faith and not to evade your duties, in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by consideration, which does not affect your duties to other tenants; use the optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement.

The statute requires consideration but does not say it must be a rent reduction. However the work is shifted, the tenant's failure to do it is not a ground for eviction or a material breach, and you remain responsible for your legal duties.

title: Deposit Rights a New Mexico Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: A New Mexico lease cannot make the tenant give up the deposit protections in the Owner-Resident Relations Act, because the act bars any rental agreement term waiving rights or remedies under the law. Those protections include: under a lease of less than a year, no deposit over one month's rent; under an annual lease with a deposit over one month's rent, annual interest at the statutory rate; no deduction for normal wear and tear; an itemized written list of deductions and any balance within 30 days after the lease ends or the tenant leaves, whichever is later; the consequences if you miss that deadline (you lose the right to withhold any of the deposit, to counterclaim in a suit for it and to sue separately for property damage, and you owe court costs and reasonable attorney fees); and a $250 civil penalty for a bad-faith retention. What a lease may lawfully do: require last month's prepaid rent (which is not the damage deposit), and, by written agreement, let you apply rent payments to deposits or damages. If you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover the resulting damages and reasonable attorney fees. See "Return of Security Deposit" clause and the deposit education rows.

title: Smoke Drift and Waivers in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: Do not ask a New Mexico tenant to waive claims about smoke drifting into the unit from other units or common areas. The Owner-Resident Relations Act bars any rental agreement term waiving rights or remedies under the law, which includes the tenant's remedies for your repair and safety duties, for nuisance, and for interference with quiet enjoyment. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects (including the fire marshal, construction and housing code parts, though not the model codes they adopt), addresses smoke drift between units. The Dee Johnson Clean Indoor Air Act makes it unlawful to smoke, including e-cigarettes and cannabis, in any indoor workplace or indoor public place; a private residence is a smoking-permitted area unless it is used commercially for child care, adult care or health care, and although the act's general definition of a smoking-permitted area adds that secondhand smoke must not infiltrate any area where smoking is prohibited, the private-residence listing applies "notwithstanding any other provision" of the act, so whether smoke drifting out of a unit makes smoking in it unlawful is not settled. An indoor workplace is any enclosed place where one or more persons work, including hallways, stairways, lobbies and elevators, whether or not work is going on at the moment, and an indoor public place is an enclosed area where the public is invited or permitted. Whether an apartment building's enclosed common areas fall within those definitions is not a settled rule. Cautious course: treat enclosed common areas where staff work or the public is permitted as smoke-free, and keep smoking a reasonable distance from their entrances, windows and vents. An employer must adopt and post a written smoking policy. The better tools are a no-smoking clause ("Smoking Policy" clause, which covers the whole property) and reasonable house rules ("Rules and Regulations" clause), together with the tenant's duty not to disturb neighbors. Local smoking ordinances may be stricter.

title: No Pre-Set Deposit Charges in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law lets a lease set in advance what you will charge against the security deposit for cleaning, carpet cleaning, painting or any other item, and none requires a special notice for such a list. The deposit statute decides what you may keep. When the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit to unpaid rent and to the damages you have actually suffered because the tenant did not comply with the lease or with the tenant's statutory duties, which include leaving the home as clean as it was at move-in, apart from ordinary wear and tear. You may not keep any part of the deposit for normal wear and tear, but dirt left behind is not normal wear and tear. If you keep anything, you must give the tenant an itemized written list of the deductions and any balance within 30 days after the later of the end of the lease or the tenant's departure. So a price list in the lease does not by itself let you keep the listed amount: deduct what the cleaning or repair actually and reasonably cost, and keep the invoices. Whether a court would enforce a pre-set charge as agreed damages is a question only case law could settle. For that reason the library offers no pre-set charge schedule for New Mexico; the deposit terms it uses are "Use of Security Deposit" clause and "Return of Security Deposit" clause.

title: No Deposit Installment Right in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, or requires you to offer a payment plan. You may require the whole deposit before the tenant moves in, or you may agree to installments. If you agree, put the schedule in writing, in the lease or a signed addendum: without a written agreement, a payment the tenant makes as rent may not be applied to the deposit. The deposit limits still apply to the total: for a lease of less than one year (including month-to-month) the deposit may not exceed one month's rent, and under an annual lease a deposit above one month's rent earns the tenant annual interest (see "New Mexico Security Deposit Limits" and "Interest on Large Deposits in New Mexico"). An unpaid deposit installment is not rent, so collect it as a separate debt rather than in a three-day notice for unpaid rent (see "Fees Are Not Rent in New Mexico").

title: No Deposit-Standards Posting Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to post, publish or give applicants the standards you use to set security deposits, whatever the number of units you rent, or requires one standard for every applicant. What the law does say: the deposit must be reasonable; for a lease of less than one year (including month-to-month) it may not exceed one month's rent; and under an annual lease a deposit above one month's rent earns the tenant annual interest (see "New Mexico Security Deposit Limits"). Your listing must disclose in plain language all costs of the rental agreement, so state the deposit there too (see "Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases"). Setting different deposits is lawful only on lawful grounds: the Human Rights Act bars discriminating in the terms or conditions of a rental because of race, religion, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, pregnancy, childbirth or a condition related to pregnancy or childbirth, spousal affiliation, physical or mental disability or military status (see "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act"). Using written criteria and applying them the same way to everyone is the safest practice.

title: Fees in Place of a Deposit in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law authorizes or regulates a fee, bond or insurance product offered in place of a security deposit. There is no offer-to-all rule, no right to switch to a deposit, and no special credit-reporting notice. General rules decide how such a payment is treated. Money a tenant hands you as a pledge to keep the lease's terms is a deposit, whatever you call it, so it counts toward the deposit limits and must be returned or itemized within 30 days after the tenancy ends. A nonrefundable fee is not a deposit: you may charge it only if the lease states it and your listing describes it, you may raise it only on written notice given at least 60 days before the periodic rental date or the end of a fixed term (one rental period ahead for a residency of less than a month), and you cannot apply it to damage or unpaid rent the way you apply a deposit. The tenant still owes you for damage and unpaid rent. Don't collect the fee from an applicant before the lease is signed: an applicant may be charged only a screening fee or a deposit. In a mobile home park, the park owner may not charge an entry fee of any type as a condition of tenancy. Whether a court would treat a particular deposit-alternative charge as a deposit is a question only case law could settle. The library does not offer a fee-in-lieu clause for New Mexico, because the terms depend on the outside product you use. If you want one, add your own clause, list the fee in "Fees and Charges" clause, and take advice first.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no rule that lets you make a security deposit, or part of one, nonrefundable, and so no notice that would do it (no New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law provides one). A deposit is money the tenant gives you as a pledge to keep the lease's terms. When the tenancy ends you may keep only what covers unpaid rent and damages you actually suffered, never normal wear and tear, and you must return the rest or send an itemized list within 30 days. Calling a deposit nonrefundable does not change that, and a lease may not take away the tenant's rights under the deposit law. If you want a charge you keep in every case, such as a pet fee or a cleaning fee, make it a fee, not a deposit: state it and its amount in the lease (the library's "Fees and Charges" clause), describe it in your listing, and don't call it a deposit. A fee is not part of the deposit and does not count toward the deposit limits; a refundable pet deposit does (see "Pet Deposits and Pet Fees in New Mexico").

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Fee Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico does not require a separate notice, document, signature or initials to disclose a nonrefundable fee or deposit (no New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires one). The reason is that a deposit cannot be made nonrefundable at all in New Mexico (see "No Nonrefundable Deposits in New Mexico"). A charge you keep in every case must be a fee, and the rule for fees is simpler: the fee must be stated in the lease and described in your listing. Listing each fee with its amount in the lease's fees section ("Fees and Charges" clause) meets that rule.

title: No Move-Out Notice Condition on New Mexico Deposit Refunds
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law makes the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, returning keys by a deadline or giving a forwarding address. Your 30 days to return the deposit, or to send an itemized list of deductions with any balance, run from the later of the date the lease ends and the date the tenant leaves. You meet the deadline by mailing the list and any payment to the tenant's last known address. If something you mail comes back undeliverable, or the last known address is the home the tenant has left, you must send at least one more notice to any other address the tenant has given you. That is why asking for a forwarding address in writing is useful, and the library's deposit clause ("Return of Security Deposit" clause) asks for one; but you may not keep the deposit, or delay the deadline, because the tenant did not give one. A tenant's notice ending a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy is a separate matter (see "Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause).

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law sets up a fast-track or early deposit procedure: there is no tenant request that shortens your time, no early-disposition election and no fee for one. The ordinary rule governs every case: within 30 days after the later of the end of the lease and the tenant's departure, return the deposit or send an itemized list of deductions with any balance. You may always do this sooner, for example right after a move-out inspection, but deductions are limited to unpaid rent and damages you can already show, and once you have returned the balance you cannot take later charges out of the deposit; a claim for damage found afterwards would have to be pursued separately, so inspect fully before you settle early. The library offers no fee for an early return: the deposit can be applied only to rent and damages, so a fee could not come out of it, and any fee must be stated in the lease (see "Fees and Charges" clause). For the deadline and penalties see "Return of Security Deposit" clause and "Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in New Mexico".

title: Alarm Tampering Charges in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the State Fire Marshal's 10.25 NMAC rules and the Construction Industries 14.7 NMAC building rules, but not the model fire and building codes those rules adopt by reference), contain nothing that sets or authorizes a fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm. So don't put a fixed tampering fee in a New Mexico lease.

Whether a court would enforce a set amount as agreed damages or strike it as a penalty is a question only case law could settle. Charge the reasonable cost of repairing or replacing the alarm instead, as the library's optional detector clause does ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors" clause).

The law does give you more. A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises, and a tenant who does so intentionally is liable for two times the monthly rent, in addition to your actual damages (whether a court would award both for the same act is for the courts; see "Damage a Tenant Causes in New Mexico"). Intentionally interfering with the proper functioning of a fire alarm system is also a misdemeanor; whether that reaches a single smoke alarm in a home is for the courts.

Which alarms the property must have comes from the building, fire and housing codes, not the landlord-tenant act (see "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms in New Mexico").

title: No Carpet-Cleaning Statute in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, forbids a lease term about it, or limits carpet or paint charges by the age of the carpet or paint.

The general rules decide it.

At move-out the tenant must leave the home as clean as it was at move-in, apart from ordinary wear and tear, and uncleanliness is not wear and tear. You may deduct from the deposit the cost of cleaning carpets the tenant left dirty, or of repairing carpets the tenant damaged, but never for normal wear and tear, and you must list the deduction in the itemized statement within 30 days.

A lease term requiring professional cleaning in every case, with its cost charged even when the carpets are as clean as at move-in apart from ordinary wear, is risky: that charge can look like a deduction for normal wear and tear, and outside a single-family home a term making the tenant do maintenance work may need a separate signed agreement. Either point is for the courts.

The library's optional carpet clause ("Carpets at Move-Out" clause) charges only the actual cost of cleaning or repairing carpets left substantially less clean or damaged. For worn carpet, no rule sets a useful life; charge only for damage beyond normal wear, taking the carpet's age into account, and keep move-in and move-out records (see "No New Mexico Move-In Inspection Rule").

title: Collection Fees in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that authorizes, caps or bars a lease charge for the cost of collecting rent or other money a tenant owes. Check whether the state's rules for licensed collection agencies limit what an agency may add to a debt. A lease may include terms the law does not prohibit, so a collection fee the lease states is not clearly unlawful. The library still does not offer one, for three reasons. First, any fee must be stated in the lease and described in your listing. Second, a collection charge triggered by late rent could be treated as a second late fee, and New Mexico caps late fees at 5% of the rent for each rental period, calculated only on rent. Third, whether a fixed collection fee is an unenforceable penalty is a question only case law could settle. What the law does give you: if you sue to enforce the lease or the Owner-Resident Relations Act and win, the court awards reasonable attorney fees and court costs (see "Attorney Fees in New Mexico Landlord-Tenant Cases"), and unpaid amounts can carry interest (see "Interest on Unpaid Amounts in New Mexico"). A licensed collection agency may also collect from the tenant the gross receipts tax on its own collection receipts, unless the agreement creating the debt or the agency's agreement with you expressly prohibits it. If you want a collection-fee clause anyway, write your own, state the amount or how it is calculated, list it in "Fees and Charges" clause and your listing, keep it off late rent, and take advice first. Federal debt-collection law may also apply to an agency you use.

title: Notice-Service and Filing Fees in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law authorizes, caps or bars a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice (such as the three-day notice for unpaid rent or the seven-day notice for another breach) or for filing an eviction. The library does not offer a notice-service fee, for three reasons. Any fee must be stated in the lease and described in your listing. A fee charged because rent is late could be treated as a second late fee beyond New Mexico's cap of 5% of the rent for each rental period. And whether a fixed fee for a breach is an unenforceable penalty is a question only case law could settle. Never put such a fee in a three-day notice for unpaid rent: that notice is for rent, and a fee is not rent (see "Fees Are Not Rent in New Mexico"). What the law does give you: if you sue to enforce the lease or the Owner-Resident Relations Act and win, the court awards reasonable attorney fees and court costs, and some violations carry their own fee awards (see "Attorney Fees in New Mexico Landlord-Tenant Cases"). How notices must be served is in "How to Serve Notices in New Mexico". If you want a notice-service fee anyway, write your own clause limited to your actual cost, list it in "Fees and Charges" clause and your listing, and take advice first.

title: Government Fines and Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that bars you from passing a government fine or abatement charge on to the tenant, limits a pass-through to fines the tenant caused, or makes the tenant liable for one automatically.

So the lease decides most cases: without a clause, you could recover such a fine only as damages for the tenant's breach of the lease or of the tenant's own statutory duties (such as complying with housing-code obligations placed on tenants or not damaging the premises), which you would have to prove. The library's optional clause ("Fines Caused by Tenant" clause) makes the tenant reimburse a fine or abatement charge you actually paid, but only for a condition or violation the tenant, the household or a guest caused or permitted, never for a condition you are responsible for, and never by taking it out of a rent payment.

Bill the amount you paid, with a copy of the citation or bill, and describe the possible charge in your listing.

Your own duties to keep the property up to code stay yours (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). Fines from a homeowners or condominium association follow the association-compliance clause ("Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause).

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statewide rental registration, licensing or inspection fee, and New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that lets or forbids passing a local government fee on to a tenant (see "No Statewide Rental Inspection or Registration in New Mexico"; check city and county programs). Because every fee must be in the lease, you may pass a local fee on only as a fee the lease states: list it with its amount in the lease's fees section ("Fees and Charges" clause) and describe it in your listing. If the city later raises it, you may raise your fee only by written notice at least 60 days before the rental date on which the increase starts, or, in a fixed-term lease, at least 60 days before the end of the term. A fee that is not in the lease can't be charged during it unless the tenant agrees in writing to add it. That is why the library doesn't use a clause that lets you bill whatever fee a government later assesses: it would charge a fee the lease never stated. A business improvement district may assess multifamily rental property with at least four units; such an assessment is your cost unless the lease states a matching fee.

title: Fees Your New Mexico Lease Must State
bodyText: New Mexico requires every fee to be in the lease: charging a tenant a fee the lease does not include is an unfair or deceptive trade practice, and your listing must describe, itemized and in plain language, the base rent and all fees and charges that will be assessed during the tenancy. The library's fees section is the lease text for this; list each fee with its amount and when or why it is due (see also "Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases"). You may raise a fee the lease provides only by written notice at least 60 days before the rental date on which it starts, or, in a fixed-term lease, at least 60 days before the end of the term; a new fee can't be added during the lease unless the tenant agrees in writing ("Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"). No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires the lease to show rent and fees as one labelled total, sets a general cap on markups for services billed through you, bars a fee for maintaining common areas, or sets a charge for partial payments. Two specific limits do exist in multi-unit housing: copies of utility bills on request cost no more than $5 per monthly request, and common-area utility costs that would fall on an empty unit can't be shifted to the other tenants ("Utility Bills and Allocation" clause). In a mobile home park, utility charges billed to residents may not exceed the park's cost per unit, and the park's utility administrative fee must be stated in the rental agreement, must be reasonable, and can be raised only on 60 days' written notice.

title: Late Fee Limit in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico caps late fees: a late fee is allowed only if the lease provides for one, may not exceed 5% of the rent for each rental period the tenant is in default, is calculated only on rent (not deposits, other fees or utilities), and may be charged only if you give notice of it by the last day of the next rental period. The full rule is in "New Mexico Late Fee Rules", and the lease clause is "Late Fee" clause. Nothing else in New Mexico's statutes, constitution or 2025-2026 session laws sets a different late-fee figure for a dwelling. The Mobile Home Park Act has no late-fee cap of its own, so the same 5% rule applies to park residents, because the Owner-Resident Relations Act governs parks wherever the park act does not directly conflict. The self-service storage law sets no late-fee figure. Late charges do appear in laws on rental-purchase agreements for goods, condominium assessments and licensing, none of which applies to renting a home.

title: Late Fees for Subsidized Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law sets a special late-fee rule for a tenant whose rent is partly paid by a housing voucher or other subsidy, so New Mexico's general rule applies: a late fee only if the lease provides for one, no more than 5% of the rent for each rental period in default, calculated only on rent, and only with notice by the last day of the next rental period (see "New Mexico Late Fee Rules"). New Mexico defines rent as the payments the tenant is to make to you under the lease. In a subsidized tenancy, the cautious reading is that the 5% is measured on the tenant's own share, not on the housing agency's payment, and that no late fee is charged because the agency paid late. Whether that reading holds is for the courts. Federal and housing-agency program rules, such as the voucher program's tenancy addendum, may limit or bar late fees further (see "Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease"). Check the program rules and your housing assistance contract before charging any late fee to a subsidized tenant.

title: Passing Tax Increases to Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or rule in the Taxation and Revenue Department gross receipts parts (3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.4 and 3.2.206 to 3.2.209 NMAC) regulates passing a property tax increase on to a residential tenant, requires a stated share or an abatement refund, or lets you take a tax share from the deposit. The library does not offer a tax pass-through clause for New Mexico. If the charge is rent, the statute's notice rule for a fixed-term lease is written notice at least 30 days before the term ends; whether a lease may build in a mid-term increase is not settled (the act's retaliation section speaks of increases made "as provided under the terms of the rental agreement"), so the cautious course is to raise rent only for the period after the term ("Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico"). If it is a fee, the lease must state it and you may raise it only on 60 days' written notice ("Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"). A clause billing a share of next year's tax bill during the term fits neither rule. In a month-to-month tenancy, cover a tax increase with an ordinary rent increase on 30 days' notice. The deposit covers only unpaid rent and damages, so a tax share cannot come out of it. Gross receipts tax: receipts from leasing real property, including a home or apartment and the furniture and appliances supplied with it, may be deducted, so ordinary residential rent normally carries no gross receipts tax to pass on. Hotel, motel, rooming-house and similar lodging receipts are not treated as real-property rent (see "Gross Receipts Tax and Residential Rent"). How the deduction treats fees charged alongside rent is set by Department rules; ask a tax adviser. Local lodgers' taxes do not reach a home that is the tenant's household or primary residence, and do not apply after 30 days' stay, or under a written agreement for 30 days or more, unless the lodging is temporary lodging near the tenant's job.

title: Fees for Services You Do Not Provide in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that says, in so many words, that a residential landlord may not charge a fee for a service or amenity it does not provide. Several rules point the same way. Every fee must be stated in the lease and described in your listing. New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act lists failing to deliver the quality or quantity of goods or services contracted for as an unfair or deceptive trade practice, in a definition covering the "sale, lease, rental or loan of goods or services" (whether that reaches a dwelling lease is for the courts); a tenant can recover actual damages or $100, more for a willful violation, plus attorney fees (see "Unfair Practices Act and Rentals"). So charge a fee only for something you actually provide, and stop or reduce it if the service ends. If you change a fee, give written notice at least 60 days ahead (see "Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"). Rent is different: a tenant may not abate rent because an amenity, such as a pool or fitness room whose absence doesn't affect health, safety or habitability, is unavailable. That rule covers rent only, not a separate amenity fee, and it never excuses the repairs you owe for essential services (see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico"). In a mobile home park, incidental charges are allowed only for services actually performed or agreed to in writing by the tenant, and a selling or transfer fee only for services both actually performed and agreed to in writing by the tenant.

title: Charging Separately for Parking in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to rent or price parking separately from the home, or stops you from including parking in the rent or charging for it separately. Local zoning or development rules may say more. If you charge separately for parking, the charge is a fee: state it and its amount in the lease's fees section ("Fees and Charges" clause), describe it in your listing, and raise it only on 60 days' written notice (see "Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases" and "Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"). You may also charge for a guest's use of parking or other facilities outside the home itself, if the lease includes that fee (see "No Guest Fees in New Mexico"). Parking rules you adopt after the tenant signs bind only on reasonable notice and only if they don't substantially change the tenant's bargain. The library's parking clauses for New Mexico are "Parking" clause and "Assigned Parking Space(s)" clause.

title: New Mexico Money Limits for Rentals
bodyText: These are the New Mexico limits on what a residential landlord may charge that this library has found, gathered in one place; each linked row has the detail. Security deposit: for a lease of less than one year (including month-to-month), no more than one month's rent; under an annual lease a larger deposit is allowed but earns the tenant annual interest ("New Mexico Security Deposit Limits", "Interest on Large Deposits in New Mexico"). In a mobile home park, one month's rent, or two months' for a multiwide home. Late fee: only if the lease provides for it, no more than 5% of the rent for each rental period in default, calculated only on rent, with notice by the end of the next rental period ("New Mexico Late Fee Rules"). Screening fee: no more than $50 per applicant, no other application-processing fee, and no second screening fee within 90 days for properties under the same ownership ("Application Screening Fees in New Mexico"). Utility bill copies: an administrative fee of no more than $5 per monthly request; in a mobile home park, utility charges may not exceed the park's cost per unit ("Utility Bills and Allocation" clause, "Fees Your New Mexico Lease Must State"). Guests: no fee for a reasonable number of guests for a reasonable time ("No Guest Fees in New Mexico"). Notice limits: rent increases need written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date, or in a fixed-term lease at least 30 days before the term ends (one rental period ahead for a tenancy of less than a month), and the cautious course in a fixed-term lease is to raise rent only after the term; fee increases follow the same pattern with 60 days' written notice ("Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico", "Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"). Interest: without a written contract fixing a different rate, interest on money due by contract may not exceed 15% a year; judgments generally bear 8.75% ("Interest on Unpaid Amounts in New Mexico"). Rent: cities and counties may not enact rent control on privately owned housing, except housing funded to provide reduced rents ("No Local Rent Control in New Mexico"). Fees generally: any fee must be stated in the lease and described in your listing ("Fees and Charges" clause). Penalties you can face: $250 for keeping a deposit in bad faith; $250 plus a refund of all fees for an unauthorized screening fee; two times the monthly rent for an unlawful lockout, utility shutoff or retaliation ("Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in New Mexico", "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico", "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"). A tenant who intentionally damages the premises is liable to you for two times the monthly rent ("Damage a Tenant Causes in New Mexico").

title: Who Keeps the Repair Duty When Someone Else Collects the Rent in New Mexico
bodyText: Some states say that whoever collects the rent keeps the landlord's repair duties, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law says that in those words. Other New Mexico rules do much of the same work. The Owner-Resident Relations Act puts its duties on the "owner": anyone holding all or part of the legal title, or all or part of the beneficial ownership with a right to present use of the premises, and their agents, and it expressly includes a mortgagee in possession and lessors. The manager you name in your required written disclosure becomes the agent of each owner for performing the owner's duties under the act and the lease. Unless otherwise agreed, if your interest ends by sale, assignment or otherwise, you are relieved only for events after the tenant gets written notice that it ended, and your successor takes on all of the lease and the act's obligations. A lender also has a claim to the rents: a mortgage or deed of trust creates an assignment of rents unless it says otherwise, and after your default (or as you agreed) the lender may notify the tenant to pay rent to it. A lender that collects rent that way need not spend it on protecting or maintaining the property, and collecting it does not make the lender a mortgagee in possession. But it collects subject to the lease and to any claim or defense the tenant has because you did not perform it, unless the tenant made an enforceable agreement not to assert them, and the tenant may still ask a court for a receiver or other relief if the lender's failure to pay upkeep has caused or threatens harm to the tenant's interest. A New Mexico lease cannot make the tenant give up rights or remedies under the law, so don't put a waiver of claims against a future assignee of rents in the lease. What to do: if a manager or master tenant collects rent for you, make the management agreement say who handles repairs, and keep your owner and manager disclosure current ("Management and Notices" clause). Rent receipts are covered in "Rent Receipts in New Mexico", and accepting late or partial rent in "Accepting Late or Partial Rent in New Mexico".

title: Checks Marked "Paid in Full" in New Mexico
bodyText: If a tenant pays you with a check or other instrument that says, or comes with a written note saying, conspicuously, that it is tendered in full satisfaction of what you claim, cashing it can settle your claim for less. Under New Mexico's commercial code, the claim is discharged if the tenant tendered the check in good faith, the amount was unliquidated or subject to a genuine dispute, and you obtained payment of it. Two ways out: you can repay the amount of the check to the tenant within 90 days after it was paid, unless you are an organization that sent the designated-address statement described next; and an organization can, a reasonable time beforehand, send the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including full-satisfaction checks, must go to a named person, office or place, which protects it if the check was not sent there. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed amount, knew a reasonable time before collecting it that the check was tendered in full satisfaction. Whether this rule applies to a residential rent dispute is for the courts; the cautious course is to treat it as applying. So don't deposit a check marked "paid in full" for a disputed balance you don't accept; return it, or repay it within 90 days. Separately, under the Owner-Resident Relations Act, a tenant who tenders the full amount due, in the manner your three-day nonpayment notice states, before the notice expires bars an eviction for that nonpayment (see "Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent" and "Accepting Late or Partial Rent in New Mexico").

title: Paying Rent in Installments in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico lets you and the tenant agree when rent is due, so the lease may split the monthly rent into installments on set days (use the optional Rent Paid in Installments clause).

Rent is due without any demand or notice on the agreed day. If the lease says nothing, rent for a term of one month or less is due at the start of the term, and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the start of each monthly period.

No New Mexico statute says whether a scheduled installment is a partial payment of rent, so say in the lease that it is not.

Late fees: you may charge one only if the lease provides for it, and it may not exceed five percent of the rent for each rental period the tenant is in default, so an installment schedule does not let you charge a late fee on each installment beyond that cap (see "Late Fee" clause).

One trap: if the lease has no fixed term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a tenant who pays weekly rent and month-to-month otherwise. Whether a monthly rent paid in weekly installments makes the tenancy week-to-week is not settled by any New Mexico statute; it is for the courts.

The cautious course for a month-to-month tenancy with weekly installments is to state the rent as a monthly rent and the tenancy as month-to-month, and to give the longer, month-to-month notices (written notice at least 30 days before a periodic rental date) before ending the tenancy or raising the rent (see "Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause and "Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico").

title: Rent Escalation Clauses in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute on rent escalation clauses. The lease may set the rent, and the tenant must pay rent as the lease provides. The only rule on raising rent works by notice: in a month-to-month tenancy, written notice at least 30 days before the rental date; in a fixed-term lease, written notice at least 30 days before the end of the term, so the new rent applies after the term (see "Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico"). That rule gives you no right to raise the rent by notice during a fixed term, so don't use a clause letting you raise rent mid-term at your discretion or to a market figure. Whether a step written into the lease at signing (a stated higher rent from a stated date during the term) counts as an increase under that rule is not settled by any New Mexico statute; it is for the courts. One New Mexico rule points toward allowing it: the retaliation statute lets you raise the rent upon appropriate notice at the end of the term or as the lease itself provides, if you can show the increase is uniform for similar units and not aimed at the particular tenant. Because the question is open, this library does not offer an escalation clause for New Mexico; you may add your own clause, ideally drafted by a New Mexico lawyer. The cautious course: use a fixed term at one rent and set any new rent at renewal, with written notice at least 30 days before the term ends. If you still want a step within the term, state each rent amount and the date it starts in the lease when it is signed (no index, formula or discretion), use the same schedule for similar units, and also give written notice at least 30 days before each step. Any increase made because the tenant complained to a code agency, joined a tenant group, exercised rights under the act or took other protected action in the previous six months is retaliation: it makes you liable to the tenant for two times the monthly rent and is a defense to an eviction. Fee increases follow a separate 60-day notice rule ("Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"), cities and counties cannot impose rent control ("No Local Rent Control in New Mexico"), and mobile home park lot rent follows the Mobile Home Park Act's own 60-day written disclosure rule.

title: Reporting Rent to Credit Bureaus in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to offer tenants positive rent reporting, sets up a state rent-reporting program, bars you from reporting rent payments, or requires a notice to the tenant before you report late rent to a credit bureau. So the lease need not say anything about rent reporting, and you may offer it if you choose. New Mexico's credit bureau law regulates the credit bureaus themselves: a bureau may report collection accounts and judgments for no longer than seven years (or until the statute of limitations runs, if longer), must delete derogatory items its source can no longer verify, and must let consumers see and dispute their files. If you send a bureau information about a tenant, you are its source of information: before the bureau gets written notice of an error, neither it nor its source is liable for damages from an unintentional error, so report only amounts you can document and correct errors promptly. Separately, a willful or negligent failure by a credit bureau or a user of its information to follow that law makes them liable to the consumer for actual damages and attorney fees, and for punitive damages if willful. If you screen applicants with credit reports, see "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico" and "Application Screening Fees in New Mexico"; federal law may also apply, including to anyone who furnishes information to a credit bureau (see "Federal Notice When a Screening Report Leads to a Denial" for the federal denial notice).

title: Rent Concessions in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law regulates rent concessions, so a free month, a move-in credit or a period of reduced rent is whatever the lease says.

Put it in the lease with the optional Rent Concession clause. Write it as a credit against the full Monthly Rent for named months, not as a lower rent that later goes up.

New Mexico's notice rule for a fixed-term lease is written notice at least 30 days before the term ends, it gives you no right to raise the rent by notice during the term, and whether a scheduled rent change written into the lease counts as an increase is unsettled ("Rent Escalation Clauses in New Mexico"); with a credit, the rent never changes.

Your listing must state the base rent and all fees in plain language ("Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases"), so advertise the full Monthly Rent and describe the concession accurately: a knowingly made false or misleading statement about a price reduction is an unfair practice under the Unfair Practices Act, which covers the "sale, lease, rental or loan of goods or services" (whether it reaches a dwelling lease is for the courts). Late fees: the late fee may not exceed five percent of the rent for the rental period, and whether that is measured on the full Monthly Rent or on what is due after a credit is unsettled; the cautious course is to keep any late fee in a credited month within five percent of the amount actually due that month.

This library does not offer a clawback (a term making the tenant repay the concession on default or early move-out). Some states allow one, but in New Mexico a sum payable on default that is not measured by your actual loss risks being refused as a penalty or limited as an inequitable term, and the act already lets you recover rent and damages, subject to your duty to mitigate. You may add your own clawback clause, ideally drafted by a New Mexico lawyer.

title: Demanding Rent for a Unit Needing Repairs in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law bars you from demanding or collecting rent, raising the rent, or serving a three-day nonpayment notice because the unit has code violations or is unfit. The tenant must pay rent as the lease provides. The condition of the unit works through the tenant's own statutory remedies instead. Repairs: if the tenant gives you written notice of conditions needing repair under your statutory duties and you do not remedy them within seven days, the tenant may abate one-third of the daily rent for each day from the notice until the repair, and all of the rent for each day if the unit is uninhabitable and the tenant does not live there because of it; there is no abatement for an amenity, and the tenant's repair remedies do not arise if the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the condition ("Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico"). Possession: if you do not deliver possession on the start date, all of the rent abates until you do ("Possession Delay" clause). Fire or casualty: if a fire or casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit and continued occupancy is lawful, a tenant who stays in part of it owes rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value ("Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico"). Lockouts and service shutoffs: all of the rent abates for each affected day ("No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico"). In court: in a nonpayment case the tenant may counterclaim for what the lease or the act allows, but must pay the lease rent while in possession; and if you win possession where the tenant disputed the amount because of a lawful abatement, the writ is conditioned on the tenant's right to pay the judgment within three days. Rent increases: you may not raise the rent to retaliate against a tenant who, in the previous six months, complained to a code agency, made a written repair request or abated rent under the act, though you may still sue for possession if the tenant is in default in rent ("Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico").

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, and a lease cannot create one. Except after abandonment or surrender, or as the Owner-Resident Relations Act otherwise permits, neither you nor anyone acting for you may knowingly exclude, remove, or threaten or attempt to remove a tenant without a court order by fraud, changing, adding, plugging or removing a lock, blocking an entrance, interfering with utilities or services, removing the tenant's belongings or appliances, or any other willful act that makes the unit inaccessible. There is no opt-in, advance-notice or key-access exception, and a lease term giving you one would be a waiver of the tenant's rights, which the act bars. A lockout lets the tenant abate all of the rent for each day of it, recover two times the monthly rent and damages, and regain possession or end the lease. For unpaid rent, serve a three-day nonpayment notice and, if it is not paid, file for possession in court ("Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent", "How Evictions Work in New Mexico"). Full detail: "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico".

title: No Truth-in-Renting Statement in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no truth-in-renting law. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a state-published statement of tenant rights to be handed over or posted, a lease notice that its terms must comply with state law or that the tenant may want to consult a lawyer, or a minimum type size or plain-language standard for the lease itself. What New Mexico does require at the start of a tenancy does the nearest work: a written rental agreement before occupancy and copies of the existing rules when the lease is signed ("Written Lease Required in New Mexico"); a written disclosure of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices and service of process ("Management and Notices" clause); and, in any published listing, the base rent and an itemized, plain-language description of every fee ("Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases", "Plain Language in New Mexico Rentals"). The act also lets the parties include any terms not prohibited by law, bars waivers of the tenant's rights, and makes you liable for damages and attorney fees if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited ("Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico"). Two narrow notices of this kind exist outside ordinary leases: a continuing care contract must say, in bold twelve-point type, that the person should consult a lawyer and a financial advisor, and a lender enforcing an assignment of rents must tell the tenant it may consult a lawyer.

title: Optional Lease Terms in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico lets you and the tenant put in the lease any terms and conditions not prohibited by the Owner-Resident Relations Act or other law, including the rent and the term. Three limits always apply: no term may make the tenant (or you) waive or give up rights or remedies under the law; a court may limit a term it finds was inequitable when made; and if you deliberately use a lease with a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover damages and attorney fees ("Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico"). The act itself names these lease-set choices. Where they serve you, this library offers them: rent amount, due date and payment methods ("Rent Payment" clause, "Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause); installments ("Rent Paid in Installments" clause); a late fee, which is allowed only if the lease provides for it; applying the tenant's rent payments to deposits or damages, which needs a written agreement ("Application of Payments" clause); last month's rent required in advance ("Amounts Due Upfront" clause, "Last Month's Rent and the Deposit in New Mexico"); fees, which must be stated in the lease and may be raised only on 60 days' written notice ("Fees and Charges" clause); tenant upkeep tasks, only in a writing supported by consideration and entered into in good faith and not to evade your duties, and, for a unit other than a single family residence, only specified tasks, in a separate signed writing, that do not reduce your duties to other tenants ("Landscaping & Irrigation" clause, "Snow Removal" clause, "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause); residential use only; notice of an absence of more than seven days ("Notice of Extended Absence" clause); a contact person if the tenant dies ("Contact Person if Tenant Dies" clause); rules and regulations; and the start date of occupancy ("Possession Delay" clause). Rent is payable at the unit unless the lease says otherwise, so name the place or method of payment in the lease. Two options are not offered: a shorter entry notice than 24 hours, which the act allows by agreement ("Entry Rules in New Mexico"), and a rent step written into a fixed-term lease, whose effect is unsettled ("Rent Escalation Clauses in New Mexico"); you may add your own clause for either with a New Mexico lawyer's advice. Lease with an option to buy: no New Mexico statute generally regulates residential lease-options or rent-to-own homes or requires a seller's property disclosure statement for them; but a lease or option given back to a homeowner whose home is in foreclosure can be a "foreclosure reconveyance" under the Mortgage Foreclosure Consultant Fraud Prevention Act, so get advice before any such deal. If the home is in a homeowner association, the seller must give the buyer the association's disclosure certificate at least seven days before closing when the option is exercised. And occupancy under a contract of sale is outside the act, unless the arrangement was created to avoid it.

title: Resolving Disputes Before Court in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that regulates a lease clause asking the parties to try to resolve a dispute before going to court, and none voids a term restricting resort to the courts as such.

Claims under the Owner-Resident Relations Act or the lease may be settled by agreement. The optional Informal Dispute Resolution clause asks each side to give written notice and offer to meet before suing, except in an action for possession, and does not delay any notice, deadline or remedy.

Keep it that way: don't make a meeting or mediation a condition you must satisfy before serving a three-day or seven-day notice or suing for possession, and don't make the tenant give up any right or remedy, which a New Mexico lease cannot do.

If you and the tenant agree in a signed record to mediate, New Mexico's Mediation Procedures Act makes what is said in the mediation confidential and unusable as evidence, subject to that act's and the court rules' exceptions, and a settlement signed by both of you is enforceable like any written contract.

Arbitration is a different matter: in an arbitration, a clause in a standard form lease that limits the tenant's procedural rights can't be enforced against the tenant, and this library does not offer an arbitration clause ("Why This Library Does Not Give You an Arbitration Clause for New Mexico").

Mobile home parks have their own rule: either the park or the resident may ask for mediation by a certified mediator before going to court, except for unpaid rent or utility charges or imminent danger to other residents, either may end it at any time, and the cost is split equally.

title: Which Code Edition Applies in New Mexico
bodyText: The Owner-Resident Relations Act makes you substantially comply with the applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and it defines codes broadly (building, housing, health and safety and sanitation codes, and any law, ordinance or regulation on fitness for habitation). It names no edition, so your duty follows whichever code applies to the property, at the edition that code's own adopting law fixes. Statewide building codes are frozen to named editions. The Construction Industries Division's rules adopt by reference, with New Mexico amendments, the 2021 International Building Code (the commercial building code), the 2021 International Residential Code (detached one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses up to three stories with separate means of egress), the 2021 International Existing Building Code, and the 2021 International Energy Conservation Code for residential and commercial work. Each applies to work performed on or after its own start date (July 14, 2023 for the commercial and existing-building codes, December 14, 2023 for the residential code, January 30, 2024 for the energy codes), unless the permit application was received earlier. The state fire code adopts the 2021 International Fire Code, and it does not apply to one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses built to the residential code unless used commercially. A newer edition published by the code council does not bind you until the agency adopts it by rule. Check their current editions with the Construction Industries Division. Cities: a city may adopt a building, fire, health or housing code by an ordinance that cites only the code's title and date, and that local code must be at least equal to state requirements; so the edition that binds you locally is the dated one in your city's ordinance. New Mexico's statute on reading laws also says a statute that incorporates a New Mexico rule does not pick up later changes to the rule, while a rule that incorporates another rule does.

title: Automatic Lease Renewal in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law regulates automatic renewal of a residential lease. There is no requirement of a separate reminder notice before an automatic renewal, no rule on bold or conspicuous renewal terms, and no limit on how early you may ask a tenant to commit to renewing.

So a renewal term is a matter of contract, and the lease may provide one (use the optional Automatic Renewal clause, "Automatic Renewal" clause).

The rules that do apply come from the Owner-Resident Relations Act: if the lease has a fixed term, give written notice of a rent increase at least 30 days before the term ends, and of a fee increase at least 60 days before; and a month-to-month tenancy, including one that continues after the term with your consent, ends only by 30 days' written notice before a rental date (7 days for week-to-week) ("Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico", "Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico", "When a Fixed-Term Lease Ends in New Mexico").

Without a renewal clause, a fixed-term lease simply ends at the end of its term.

New Mexico's only automatic-renewal statute is for service contracts (such as home warranties), which require a clear disclosure, the buyer's consent and a cancellation notice; it does not apply to leases. A tenant who misses a non-renewal deadline and is held to a long new term may argue the term was inequitable, which a court may limit, so keep renewal terms short or month-to-month, and send a reminder before the deadline even though no statute requires one.

If you are married and the property is community property, or you and your spouse own it together, have both of you sign a lease that renews automatically: a lease for an indefinite term, or one whose term with its renewals can exceed five years, is void unless both spouses join ("Long Leases, Married Owners and Recording in New Mexico").

title: Long Leases, Married Owners and Recording in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law sets a maximum term for a residential lease, requires a long lease to be under seal, or sets a homestead rule for leases. The statutes contain no statute of frauds for leases ("Written Leases and the Statute of Frauds in New Mexico"), but the Owner-Resident Relations Act requires a written rental agreement for every tenancy. Three rules do affect longer leases. First, married owners. If the property is community property, or separate property you and your spouse own together as joint tenants or tenants in common, both spouses must sign any lease whose initial term, together with any option or extension in it or agreed at the same time, exceeds five years, or that is for an indefinite term. A lease signed by one spouse alone in breach of that rule is void, unless it was signed under a validly executed and recorded power of attorney or the other spouse later ratifies it in writing; a minor spouse may join. Separate property you own alone needs no joinder. Whether a month-to-month tenancy, or a lease that renews automatically, is a lease for an indefinite term is not settled by statute; it is for the courts. The cautious course is to have both spouses sign, or act under a recorded power of attorney, whenever the lease is month-to-month, renews automatically, or could run more than five years. Second, recording. A lease whose initial term plus option terms exceeds five years, or a memorandum of its material terms, must be recorded with the county clerk where the property is; an unrecorded one does not affect a later good-faith purchaser, mortgagee or judgment lien creditor who did not know of it. A lease of any length may be recorded. Third, deposits. A deposit larger than one month's rent is allowed only under an annual lease and then earns interest; under a lease shorter than a year the deposit may not exceed one month's rent ("New Mexico Security Deposit Limits", "Interest on Large Deposits in New Mexico").

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that says whether a lease guarantor is liable for a renewal, an extension, a month-to-month continuation or a rent increase, lets a guarantor revoke a continuing guaranty, releases a guarantor when the lease changes without consent, makes you sue the tenant first, or requires a guaranty to state a maximum or an end date. Those questions turn on the guaranty's own words and on case law.

So say it in the guaranty: the optional Guaranty clause makes you choose whether it covers renewals, extensions and month-to-month continuations, including rent changes made under the lease, or ends with the original term. The cautious course is to have the guarantor sign again, or consent in writing, whenever the lease is renewed or the rent or other terms change, and to keep the guarantor's signature on the lease itself.

New Mexico does treat a guarantor or cosigner as an applicant. You may charge a guarantor no fee other than a screening fee (no more than $50, with written or digital notice, the guarantor's written agreement and a receipt) or a deposit, and no fee that was not published in your listing; you must give the guarantor a copy of any report used to screen them; and you may not charge more than one screening fee within 90 days for properties under the same ownership ("Application Screening Fees in New Mexico", "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico").

Whether a deposit taken from a guarantor counts toward the tenant's deposit limit is for the courts; the cautious course is to count it.

title: Ending a Lease to Move In Yourself in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives you a right to end a lease so that you or a family member can move in, limits that right, or sets a period you must live in the unit afterwards.

A month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy needs no reason: you may end it with written notice given at least 30 days before the periodic rental date it names (or, week-to-week, at least 7 days before the termination date it names) ("Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause).

A fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term, and you have no right to end it early to move in unless the lease reserves one. If you want that right, use the optional Owner Occupancy clause; a lease that is silent gives you none.

Whatever the lease says, you may not use the right to retaliate against a tenant for complaining to a code agency, joining a tenant group, exercising rights under the act or other protected activity in the previous six months (retaliation makes you liable for two times the monthly rent and is a defense to eviction); if the tenant does not leave, you must go to court; and the clause cannot be used for a space in a mobile home park, where the Mobile Home Park Act limits the grounds for ending a tenancy.

title: No Tenancy at Will Under the New Mexico Act
bodyText: The Owner-Resident Relations Act has no tenancy at will. If the lease does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a tenant who pays weekly rent and month-to-month in every other case, and either side ends it by written notice: at least 7 days before the termination date for week-to-week, and at least 30 days before the periodic rental date for month-to-month ("Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause). A tenant who stays after the lease ends with your consent becomes a week-to-week or month-to-month tenant on the same basis; one who stays without your consent may be removed only by an action for possession ("Holdover" clause, "When a Fixed-Term Lease Ends in New Mexico"). The older forcible entry and detainer law still speaks of a tenant at will, who must leave after 30 days' written notice to vacate, but it does not apply to a residential tenancy governed by the act. It matters only for arrangements outside the act, such as an employee whose written agreement ties occupancy to employment, a buyer in possession under a contract of sale, or agricultural premises ("What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers"). Mobile home park tenancies follow the Mobile Home Park Act, under which a park tenancy, including one at will, ends for nonpayment only after a written notice giving at least three days to pay or remove the home.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no seasonal tenancy. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law creates a seasonal or vacation lease category, a different deposit rule or eviction track for one, or an exemption from the Owner-Resident Relations Act for a seasonal rental. If you rent a house, cabin or apartment for a season to someone who lives in it, it is an ordinary tenancy under the act: a written lease before occupancy, the deposit limit of one month's rent for a lease shorter than a year, your repair duties, the notice rules and the court eviction process all apply. The act's exemption is narrower than it sounds: it covers transient occupancy in a hotel or motel, and transient occupancy means rent paid on less than a weekly basis or a guest who has not shown an intent to make the unit a residence or household. Whether a nightly or weekly vacation rental of a house, as opposed to a hotel or motel room, is outside the act is for the courts. The cautious course is to follow the act for any stay of a week or more, or whenever the guest treats the unit as home. Short stays have tax consequences instead: a city or county lodgers' tax may apply to lodging at premises that are not the guest's household or primary residence, except for a guest who has been a permanent resident for at least 30 consecutive days or has a written agreement for at least 30 consecutive days (unless it is temporary lodging near the guest's job). See "Gross Receipts Tax and Residential Rent" for gross receipts tax.

title: Which New Mexico Notices Must Be in Writing
No Initialing Requirement for New Mexico Leases
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a tenant to initial any lease clause, or requires initials to make a clause enforceable. A signed lease is enough for its ordinary terms. Three things do need more than the lease signature, and they are worth signing separately: for a unit other than a single family residence, any agreement that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling must be in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by consideration and entered into in good faith and not to evade your duties ("Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause); for a single family residence, that agreement must still be in writing, for consideration and in good faith; and the tenant's authorization for you to deal with a contact person if the tenant dies is a statement the tenant signs ("Contact Person if Tenant Dies" clause). An applicant or guarantor must also agree in writing to pay a screening fee, and applying rent to deposits or damages needs a written agreement ("Application Screening Fees in New Mexico", "Application of Payments" clause). Initialing key clauses is still good practice as evidence that the tenant saw them, but it cannot save a term the law prohibits ("Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico").

title: Actual Notice and Agreed Notice Methods in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's Owner-Resident Relations Act defines notice itself. A person has notice of a fact if they actually know it, have received a notice of it, or have reason to know it from all the facts they know. A notice is given by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the other person in the ordinary course, whether or not they actually learn of it, and it is received when it comes to the person's attention. For written notices the act adds fixed delivery rules. A written notice to you is received when it is mailed or delivered at the place of business through which the lease was made or at any place you hold out for receiving communications, so the lease may name an address, or (on this library's reading; no case read) an e-mail address, where the tenant may send notices to you ("Management and Notices" clause, "E-mail Communications" clause). A written notice to the tenant is received when handed to the tenant or mailed to the place the tenant has designated, or else the tenant's last known residence. A nonpayment notice is effective only if hand-delivered, mailed or posted on an exterior door, and any other written notice that is posted must also be mailed first class or handed over. No New Mexico provision found lets the lease add a text message or e-mail as a way to give the tenant a written notice the act requires, and the electronic transactions law does not apply to notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence; so use e-mail or text only for routine messages or as an extra copy ("How to Serve Notices in New Mexico"). For a business, notice counts from when it is brought to the attention of the person handling the matter, or when it would have been with reasonable diligence, so make sure messages to a manager or office reach the person dealing with the tenancy. If you fail to give the required written disclosure of your manager and of an owner or agent for notices, the tenant is relieved of any duty to give you notice under the act.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law specifically bars renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or sets a special remedy for it. The general rules on delivering possession cover it. On the start date you must deliver possession to the tenant as the lease and your repair duties require. If you can't, for instance because you rented the unit to someone else or the last tenant is still there, all of the rent abates until you deliver possession, and the new tenant may either end the lease at once by written notice, in which case you must return all prepaid rent and deposits, or insist on the lease, sue anyone wrongfully keeping possession, and recover damages and attorney fees. You are not liable for damages if you make reasonable efforts to get possession and return the prepaid rent, deposits and fees within seven days of the tenant's termination notice. You may also sue anyone wrongfully in possession ("Possession Delay" clause, "Holdover" clause). Screening rules guard against double-booking at the application stage: you may not charge a screening fee when you know or should know the unit is not available, you must hold an applicant's fee until every earlier applicant has been screened and rejected or has declined, and you must return the fee within 30 days if an earlier applicant takes the unit ("Application Screening Fees in New Mexico"). Knowingly promising the same unit to two tenants may also be a false or misleading representation under the Unfair Practices Act ("Unfair Practices Act and Rentals").

title: No New Mexico Rule on Keeping Domestic Violence Information Confidential
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to keep confidential what a tenant tells you about domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or limits whom you may tell. New Mexico's confidentiality rules in this area bind others. Under the Confidential Substitute Address Act, the secretary of state and state and local agencies may not disclose a program participant's home or mailing address, phone number or e-mail address except under a court order, and anyone who receives that information through a court order may not pass it on except under a court order or after the participant leaves the program. If you are yourself a state or local agency (for example a housing authority), those duties bind you. Employers, medical personnel, victim counselors and insurers have their own confidentiality duties. A tenant in the program may give you a secretary of state address. The secretary of state is the participant's agent to receive mail, and to receive and forward service of process, notices and demands required or permitted by law. Whether a lease notice served there meets New Mexico's notice rules for tenants is for the courts; the cautious course is to serve every notice at the unit in the way the act requires (see "How to Serve Notices in New Mexico") and also mail a copy to the substitute address. As a cautious course, treat abuse information and any protection order a tenant gives you as confidential: keep it apart from the general tenant file, let only staff who need it see it, never share it with the person named in an order or with other tenants, and don't disclose it in reference or screening responses unless the tenant agrees in writing or a law or court order requires it. Federal law may also apply, for example in federally assisted housing. Related rows: "Domestic Violence and Substantial-Violation Evictions", "No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right in New Mexico".

title: No Domestic Violence Deposit Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no law letting a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking end a lease early (see "No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right in New Mexico"), so it has no special rule on when you return a deposit after a victim leaves. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law ties any deposit rule to domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking. The ordinary deposit rule applies. When the residency ends, you may apply the deposit to unpaid rent and to damages caused by the tenant's noncompliance with the lease or the tenant's statutory duties, but not to normal wear and tear. If you keep any part, you must give the tenant an itemized written list of deductions and the balance within thirty days after the rental agreement ends or the tenant departs, whichever is later; mailing the list and any payment to the tenant's last known address complies. Missing the deadline costs you the right to keep any of the deposit, to counterclaim in a suit for the deposit and to sue separately for damage to the property, and exposes you to court costs and attorney fees, and keeping a deposit in bad faith adds a $250 civil penalty (see "Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in New Mexico" and the clause "Return of Security Deposit"). The statute doesn't say how one deposit is split when one co-tenant (for example a victim who flees) leaves and the others stay, or whether the thirty days run from that one tenant's departure. Only case law could settle it. The cautious course: get a written agreement signed by all tenants on how the deposit will be handled; without one, treat the deposit as held for the tenancy as a whole until the rental agreement ends, and tell the departing tenant so in writing. A protection order may give one tenant sole possession of the home while it is in effect; New Mexico statutes do not say how such an order affects the lease or the deposit. Federal law may also apply in federally assisted housing.

title: No Domestic Violence Lock-Change Right in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking a right to have the locks changed, or says who pays for a lock change. What New Mexico law does provide: in a protection order case under the Family Violence Protection Act, the court may give the protected person sole possession of the residence while the order is in effect, order the restrained person not to make contact, order the restrained person to reimburse expenses reasonably related to the abuse (including replacing or repairing damaged property), and order other protective relief. On the victim's request, police must help place the victim in possession of the home and help enforce or serve the order. A short emergency order bars abuse and contact but does not itself award the home. You may not change, add or remove a lock to keep a tenant out without a court order (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico"). A protection order that gives your tenant sole possession of the home can be read as such a court order, though the point is for the courts. The cautious course: if a tenant shows you an order that gives the tenant sole possession, respect it. Don't let the restrained person in or give that person a key, even if he or she signed the lease, and cooperate with police enforcing the order. If the tenant asks you to change or rekey the locks to carry out that order, do it promptly and keep a copy of the order. Without such an order, don't lock out a co-tenant or household member who has a right to live there; an order that only bars abuse or contact is not enough. If you charge for a lock change, the charge must be stated in the lease (see "Fees and Charges" clause). New Mexico has no general lock or rekeying statute ("No New Mexico Lock or Security Device Statute") and no domestic violence lease-termination right ("No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right in New Mexico"). Federal law may also apply in federally assisted housing.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's protection-order law has not moved or been renumbered. It is the Family Violence Protection Act, in chapter 40, article 13 of the New Mexico statutes, in place since 1987; no 2025 or 2026 session law searched changes it. The one landlord-tenant cross-reference uses different words. The eviction defense in the Owner-Resident Relations Act (see "Domestic Violence and Substantial-Violation Evictions") bars a writ of restitution in a substantial-violation case if the tenant has filed for or secured a "temporary domestic violence restraining order". The Family Violence Protection Act does not use that phrase. Its orders are: an emergency order of protection, issued at a police officer's request and lasting about three days; a temporary order of protection, granted without notice to the other side when a victim files a petition showing probable cause, with a hearing within ten days; an order of protection after a hearing or by agreement; and, after a conviction for criminal sexual penetration, an extended order that can last for any length of time, even for life. It defines an order of protection as an injunction or a restraining or other court order granted to protect a victim of domestic abuse.
