Orders from other states and from pueblos, tribes and nations are enforced in New Mexico under a separate uniform act. The Owner-Resident Relations Act does not define domestic violence. The Family Violence Protection Act defines domestic abuse to include stalking or sexual assault by anyone, and listed acts (such as physical harm, threats, harassment, criminal trespass or property damage) between household members, who need not live together. Whether the eviction defense covers every kind of order, or an order from another state or a tribe, is a question only case law could settle, and none was read. The cautious course: treat a filed petition, or any emergency, temporary, final or extended order of protection, or a valid out-of-state or tribal protection order, connected to the incident in your notice or to an earlier incident, as meeting the defense, and don't proceed with a substantial-violation eviction against that tenant. See also "Documents That Trigger New Mexico’s Domestic Violence Eviction Defense".

title: Documents That Trigger New Mexico’s Domestic Violence Eviction Defense
bodyText: New Mexico has one domestic violence rule for tenancies, the defense to an eviction for a substantial violation (see "Domestic Violence and Substantial-Violation Evictions"), and it names one document. If the tenant has filed for or secured a temporary domestic violence restraining order because of the incident behind your substantial-violation notice, or because of any earlier incident, the court may not issue a writ of restitution. Filing for the order is enough; the tenant doesn't need to have received it. The law sets no time limit: the filing or order may come before or after your notice, and an earlier incident counts whenever it happened. Without such a filing or order, the defense still applies: in any substantial-violation case it is a defense that the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, and the court may then evict only the resident accused of the violation and let the other residents stay. The defense doesn't apply to an eviction for unpaid rent or for an ordinary lease breach. New Mexico has no domestic violence lease-termination or lock-change right (see "No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right in New Mexico" and "No Domestic Violence Lock-Change Right in New Mexico"), so it has no other list of qualifying documents, and New Mexico's statutes do not say what proof you may ask a tenant for. The statute's phrase doesn't match the protection-order law's own terms (see "Domestic Violence Law Citations in New Mexico"). The cautious course: if a tenant facing a substantial-violation notice tells you of domestic violence, or shows you a petition or any emergency, temporary or final order of protection (including a valid out-of-state or tribal order), don't proceed against that tenant; at most, proceed only against the person accused, and get legal advice. Federal law may set its own documentation rules in federally assisted housing.

title: Children and Families in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico's Human Rights Act doesn't list familial status (having children in the household) or age among the grounds on which you may not refuse to rent or set different terms. New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the Human Rights Bureau's rules), contain nothing that protects tenants because they have children, requires the lease to say anything about children living in the unit, or sets a persons-per-bedroom limit. Two state rules still reach families. The Act protects pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions, and spousal affiliation, so you may not refuse to rent to an applicant, or set different terms, because she is pregnant or has recently given birth. And in a mobile home park of twelve or more occupied homes, management must treat all persons equally in renting spaces, except that a park may be designated as housing for older persons after six months' notice to the residents and compliance with state and federal antidiscrimination procedures; where the Mobile Home Park Act conflicts with the general landlord-tenant act, the park act controls. Federal law may protect families with children. The cautious course is to treat refusing families, charging them more, limiting them to certain units or floors, or adding child-specific rules as barred unless you have confirmed a federal exemption applies. Any occupant limit in your lease ("Permitted Occupants" clause) should rest on the unit's size and safety, apply to everyone, and not stand in for a protected ground (see "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act"). Local ordinances may add protections; check your city and county.

title: Questions About Protected Traits in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful to use a rental application form, or to make any record or inquiry about a prospective rental, that expresses any preference, limitation or discrimination as to race, religion, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, pregnancy, childbirth or a related condition, spousal affiliation, physical or mental disability, or military status. The same rule covers ads, statements, publications and signs. For disability, the protection applies where the disability is unrelated to the person's ability to rent and maintain the housing. Military status includes veterans and the spouses and children of members and veterans, and race includes traits such as hair texture, protective hairstyles and cultural or religious headdresses. The Act bars inquiries and records that express a preference or limitation; it doesn't list particular forbidden questions. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects (including the Human Rights Bureau's rules), adds a list of questions you may not ask, or requires you to keep or destroy records about protected traits. Whether a neutral question about a protected trait is itself unlawful is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: don't ask about any protected trait on an application, in a showing or in screening unless a law or a government housing program requires it; keep any such information you must collect apart from the screening file; and ask every applicant the same questions. Owner-occupied buildings with no more than four units are outside the Act. A single-family home rented by an owner of no more than three such homes is outside it only if no notice, statement or ad indicates a preference based on race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, sexual orientation or gender identity (see "Owner-Size Thresholds in New Mexico Law"). Federal law may still apply to those homes. A person who believes you violated the Act may file a complaint with the state within 300 days; the commission may award actual damages and, if the complainant had private counsel, attorney fees. Related rows: "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act", "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico", "Immigration Status and Rentals in New Mexico".

title: Disability Accommodations in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico's Human Rights Act bars refusing to rent, or discriminating in rental terms, conditions, privileges, facilities or services, because of a physical or mental disability, where the disability is unrelated to the person's ability to rent and maintain the housing. But the Act's duty to accommodate a disability, and its definition of reasonable accommodation, are written for employers and the workplace. New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the Human Rights Bureau's rules), contain nothing that requires a landlord to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies or services, or to allow reasonable modifications of the unit, for a tenant with a disability. None requires the lease to state that a modification must be undone at move-out, or to hold a restoration deposit in a separate account. Federal law may impose accommodation and modification duties, and whether refusing a request is itself discrimination in rental terms or services under the state Act is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: treat every disability-related request (a different parking space, a rule exception, an assistance animal, grab bars or a ramp) as a reasonable accommodation or modification request; answer it promptly in writing; ask only for information needed to confirm the disability-related need when it isn't obvious; consider alternatives the tenant proposes; and refuse only for a clear, documented reason, such as a real safety threat or a cost or change you can't reasonably bear. Assistance animals: "Service and Assistance Animals" clause and "Assistance Animals in New Mexico Rentals". The lease's alterations clause ("No Alterations" clause) preserves any modification the law entitles a tenant to make. For new construction and some alterations, the state building codes adopt accessibility standards, including for dwelling units; under the White Cane Law the attorney general, a district attorney or a person with a disability may sue when a building was built or altered without meeting the required access standards, and if the court finds the owner was required to meet them and has not done so within a reasonable time, the person suing recovers court costs, attorney fees and an injunction. Related: "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act".

title: Penalties for Refusing a Service Animal in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has two criminal laws on denying entry to a person with a service animal, and both are written for places open to the public, not for a tenant's home. Under the Service Animal Act, a person with a disability using a qualified service animal (a dog or miniature horse trained to work or perform tasks for the person) must be admitted to any building open to the public and to all public accommodations, whatever the no-pets policy, without any extra charge; the person can be held liable for damage the animal does, as anyone else would be for similar damage. Entry may be refused only where the animal's use poses a direct threat of significant harm to others. Violating the Act is a misdemeanor, punishable by jail for a term of less than one year, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. Under the White Cane Law, a person who is blind or partially blind may bring a trained guide dog, without extra charge, into the public places it lists, which include hotels, lodging places and any other place to which the public is invited; anyone who denies or interferes with admittance there is guilty of a misdemeanor. Neither law says whether a leasing office, a building's common areas, a rooming house or a tenant's own unit counts. The cautious course: treat your leasing office, model units and any part of the property open to the public as covered and admit a service animal or guide dog there without charge; treat furnished rooms, a rooming house or short-term lodging you offer as a possible lodging place. Inside the rental itself, handle any assistance animal as a disability accommodation (see "Service and Assistance Animals" clause and "Assistance Animals in New Mexico Rentals"); a refusal there can lead to a civil discrimination complaint under the Human Rights Act ("Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act") rather than a criminal charge. Knowingly passing off an animal as a qualified service animal is itself a misdemeanor ("Misrepresenting a Service Animal in New Mexico"). Federal law may also apply.

title: Owner-Size Thresholds in New Mexico Law
bodyText: New Mexico's Owner-Resident Relations Act applies the same rules to every owner, whatever the number of units. It has no small-landlord exemption and no duty that switches on at a portfolio size; its exemptions turn on the kind of occupancy, not the owner's size (see "What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers"). Size thresholds appear in other laws. Human Rights Act (fair housing). The Act doesn't apply to a single-family home rented by its owner if two conditions are both met: the owner doesn't own or hold an interest in more than three single-family homes, and no notice, statement or ad for the rental indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. The three-home limit is written in terms of a "seller", and for sales by an owner who doesn't live in the home the exemption covers only one sale in 24 months; the cautious course is to apply the three-home limit to rentals too. The Act also doesn't apply to rooms or units in a building with living quarters for no more than four families living independently, if you actually live in one of them as your residence. Both conditions of each exemption must be met. Federal law has its own, different exemptions, so a home exempt under state law may still be covered federally (see "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act"). Mobile home parks. The Mobile Home Park Act applies to a park of twelve or more occupied mobile homes run for the owner's profit. Contractors' liens. A subcontractor or supplier who claims more than $5,000 normally must give the owner written notice of its lien rights within 60 days after first furnishing work or materials. That notice rule does not apply to residential property with four or fewer dwelling units, so on a small rental a lien can be claimed without that early warning; the Prompt Payment Act also does not apply to construction contracts for such property. Get lien waivers from subcontractors and suppliers when you pay a contractor. Business improvement districts. A city's business improvement district may assess its benefit fee on multifamily residential rental property with at least four units, but not on other residential property, apart from homeowners associations of multifamily ownership properties. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects, limits how many homes a landlord or investor may buy or own.

title: Tenant Organizing in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico doesn't give apartment tenants a general statutory right to organize, meet in common areas, or distribute literature in the building. It does protect organizing in three ways. First, you may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant who is complying with the lease has, within the previous six months, organized or joined a residents' union, association or similar organization. A violation is a defense to eviction and carries the act's retaliation remedies (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"); rent or service changes made with proper notice at the end of the term or as the lease provides are still allowed if you can show they are uniform for similar units and not aimed at the tenant. Second, in a mobile home park, management may not prohibit tenants' meetings about mobile home living and park affairs in the park's community or recreation hall, if there is one, when the hall is reserved under the park rules, the meeting is at a reasonable hour and the hall isn't otherwise in use; common areas must be open to residents at reasonable times, subject to the park's written rules. Third, residents of continuing care retirement communities have a statutory right to form a resident association. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law otherwise requires you to allow tenant meetings, door-to-door organizing or postings in common areas, or bars a lease rule on them. The cautious course: apply any common-area, posting or solicitation rule to everyone, never enforce it more strictly against organizers, and don't single out union members or leaders for rule enforcement, nonrenewal or rent changes. Local ordinances and federal law may add rules.

title: No New Mexico Rule on Campaign Access to Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to let candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration volunteers into a rental building, or limits your rules on door-to-door canvassing, solicitation or leaving literature in common areas. The state constitution protects free speech against laws that restrain it; whether it limits a private landlord's access rules is a question only case law could settle. A tenant controls who visits the tenant's own unit, and criminal trespass law lets an occupant, as well as an owner, refuse or withdraw consent to enter. If you adopt a no-solicitation or access rule for common areas, put it in your written rules (see "Rules and Regulations" clause), apply it the same way to every message and group, and don't use it to stop tenants from inviting visitors, talking with neighbors, organizing (see "Tenant Organizing in New Mexico") or complaining (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"). Local ordinances and federal law may add rules.

title: No New Mexico Religious Display Right for Tenants
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a tenant a right to put a religious or cultural item (such as a mezuzah, cross, wreath or other symbol) on a door, doorframe or outside surface, or limits lease rules on such displays. The Human Rights Act still applies: you may not set different rules or enforce them differently because of a tenant's religion, race, national origin or ancestry, and the Act treats cultural or religious headdresses as part of race. The state constitution protects religious freedom and says no one shall be molested in person or property for their mode of worship; whether that limits a private landlord's lease rules is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: if your lease restricts displays (see "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause), make the rule neutral, apply it the same way to religious and secular items, and allow small items on or beside the entry door; don't remove a religious item without notice. Remember that holiday or seasonal decorations, which are often religious, fall under the same rule. Local ordinances and federal law may add protections. Flags and signs: "No New Mexico Flag or Sign Display Right for Tenants".

title: No New Mexico Flag or Sign Display Right for Tenants
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a tenant a right to display a flag (including the United States flag), a political or campaign sign, or a banner on a rental against a lease rule, and none limits a homeowners' association's rules on what a tenant or other occupant may display. The state constitution's free-speech clause restrains laws; whether it limits a private landlord's lease rules is a question only case law could settle. Sign permits are a local matter; check your city and county codes. Your own ads and signs must not express a preference based on a protected trait under the Human Rights Act (see "Questions About Protected Traits in New Mexico Rentals"). The library's Use of Property & Common Areas clause lets you require consent for signs visible from outside while preserving any display the law entitles a tenant to make. The cautious course: if you limit displays, do it in writing, apply the rule to every message and viewpoint alike, and enforce it the same way for everyone. Federal law may also apply. Religious and cultural items: "No New Mexico Religious Display Right for Tenants".

title: Tenant Information and Privacy in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law generally bars you from sharing information about a tenant or applicant (for example with a lender, buyer, another landlord giving a reference, or a collection agency), or sets a consent form for doing so. Several rules still limit how you handle that information. Under the Data Breach Notification Act, if you hold a New Mexico resident's name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or other government ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, or biometric data, you must keep reasonable security for it, require any vendor you share it with (such as a screening company or software provider) to do the same by contract, and shred, erase or otherwise make it unreadable when you no longer reasonably need it. If it is breached, you must notify affected residents within 45 days of discovery unless an investigation shows no significant risk of identity theft or fraud, and notify the attorney general and the credit bureaus if more than 1,000 residents are involved. Under the Privacy Protection Act, a business may not make a whole Social Security number available to the public, and one that collects these numbers must limit access to the employees who need them. That act also limits requiring a Social Security number as a condition of leasing unless it will be used consistently with law (for example for a credit check) or the person consents; whether it covers residential leasing is not settled, so ask for consent on your application. You must give each applicant a copy of any report you used to screen them (see "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico"). The cautious course: share tenant information only for a business need, give references limited to facts you can document, and get written consent before releasing anything else. Federal law may also apply. Records duties: "Tenant Records and Data Security in New Mexico"; domestic violence information: "No New Mexico Rule on Keeping Domestic Violence Information Confidential".

title: Tenant Records and Data Security in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a ledger on request or with a notice, or keep tenancy records for a set number of years. The few record duties that do exist are specific: a written or digital receipt for an application screening fee, a copy to each applicant of any screening report you used (see "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico"), and an itemized written statement of deposit deductions within 30 days after the tenancy ends (see "Return of Security Deposit" clause). Rent receipts generally: "Rent Receipts in New Mexico". Data security does apply to tenant files. If you hold a New Mexico resident's name with a Social Security number, driver's license or other government ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, or biometric data, you must keep reasonable security for it, require vendors you share it with to protect it by contract, dispose of it by shredding or erasing when you no longer reasonably need it, and give notice within 45 days if it is breached (unless an investigation shows no significant risk of identity theft or fraud). See "Tenant Information and Privacy in New Mexico". If a licensed real estate broker manages the property for you, the Real Estate Commission's rules on property management records and trust accounts also apply. Good practice: keep a running ledger of every charge and payment, the lease and notices, inspection records and deposit statements for at least as long as a claim could be brought, and store identity documents securely.

title: No New Mexico Rule on Landlord Cooperation With Police
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to cooperate with police, report suspected crime by a tenant, join a crime-free housing program, or use a crime-free lease addendum, and none penalizes you or a tenant for calls to police. Some cities have their own crime-free or nuisance-property ordinances; check yours. The entry statute limits what you can do for police. You may enter a tenant's unit without consent only in an emergency, after abandonment or surrender, during an absence of more than seven days as the act allows, or by court order; otherwise entry needs the tenant's consent and, unless an exception applies, 24 hours' written notice (see "Entry Rules in New Mexico"). Whether you may let officers into a unit on a search warrant addressed to them, without the tenant's consent, is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: don't open a tenant's unit for police without the tenant's consent, an emergency, or a warrant or court order the officers show you; keep a copy of any warrant, and give the tenant written notice afterward. You may share information with police about crimes on the property, but treat tenant identity data with care (see "Tenant Information and Privacy in New Mexico"). Criminal activity in the unit can be a lease breach ("No Criminal Activity" clause) or a substantial violation ("Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation"). Calls for help: "No New Mexico Rule on Tenant Calls for Police or Emergency Help".

title: No New Mexico Drug-Free Lease Addendum Rule
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires, supplies or regulates a drug-free housing addendum. You may include a lease term against illegal drug activity, but New Mexico law decides what it can do. The fast three-day termination for a substantial violation applies only to the conduct the statute lists, which for drugs is possession, use, sale, distribution or manufacture of a controlled substance other than misdemeanor possession and use, occurring in the unit, on the premises or within 300 feet, that the tenant knowingly committed or knowingly allowed another person in the unit or on the premises to commit. A lease cannot add to that list. Other drug activity, including misdemeanor possession or use, is a lease breach only if the lease says so, and then you must use the seven-day notice and cure process (see "Seven-Day Notice for Other Lease Breaches" and "Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation"). The tenant keeps the statutory defenses, including domestic violence, lack of knowledge and self-defense. The library's optional No Criminal Activity clause covers drug crimes and follows these rules, so a separate addendum isn't needed. Cannabis is lawful for adults in New Mexico; a lease may still prohibit it (see "Cannabis in New Mexico Rentals" and "No Cannabis Cultivation" clause). Federally assisted housing has its own lease rules (federal law).

title: No New Mexico Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a landlord a tax credit, grant or other incentive for renting to veterans or servicemembers, or sets special lease terms for veteran tenants. What the law does: the Human Rights Act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, or advertising or inquiring in a way that shows a preference, because of military status, which covers active members and veterans of the armed forces or state defense force and their spouses and children (see "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act"). A servicemember's lease-termination rights come from federal law (see "Servicemember Tenants in New Mexico"). State and federal agencies run housing programs for veterans, and a veteran may pay rent with a housing voucher; New Mexico doesn't require you to accept vouchers (see "Source of Income in New Mexico"), but refusing one as a cover for military status or another protected trait is unlawful.

title: No New Mexico Screening Rule for Rental Housing Employees
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, requires you to run background checks on employees of an apartment building or other rental housing, such as maintenance staff, leasing agents or managers who hold keys. If you do screen job applicants, one state rule applies to you as a private employer: a written or electronic employment application may not ask about the applicant's arrest or conviction history. You may consider a conviction after reviewing the application and discussing the job with the applicant, and you may tell applicants that a certain criminal history can disqualify them for particular positions. An applicant may bring a complaint under the Human Rights Act. A separate statute applies only to care providers. If your property is also a licensed or covered care setting (such as a home for the aged, boarding home, adult residential care home or group home), each caregiver with direct care or routine, unsupervised access to residents must submit to fingerprint-based nationwide criminal history screening before starting work (see "No New Mexico Work Card for Senior Housing Staff"). Good practice for staff with keys: screen consistently and in writing, follow the rules on employment background reports (federal law), and keep key and entry logs. Tenant screening is separate: "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico".

title: No New Mexico Work Card for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, requires a work card, fingerprint clearance card or background check for staff of age-restricted (55-plus or 62-plus) apartments or other senior housing that only rents homes. Screening is required only where the property is also a care provider: for example a home for the aged or disabled, a boarding home, an adult residential care home, a group home, an adult foster care home, or a private residence giving personal, residential or nursing care to two or more unrelated people. There, no caregiver whose work includes direct care, or routine and unsupervised physical or financial access to residents, may start work until the caregiver has submitted to fingerprint-based nationwide criminal history screening under the state health care authority's procedures; certain felony convictions disqualify a caregiver. For ordinary senior apartments, the private-employer rule still applies: your employment application may not ask about arrests or convictions (see "No New Mexico Screening Rule for Rental Housing Employees"). A mobile home park may be designated as housing for older persons only after six months' notice to residents (see "Children and Families in New Mexico Rentals").

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty for New Mexico Landlords
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell tenants or applicants whether a registered sex offender lives at or near the property, to put a registry notice in the lease, or to check the registry. Registry information about offenders convicted of certain sex offenses is public: anyone may request it from the county sheriff, the city's chief law enforcement officer, the district attorney or the Department of Public Safety, who must provide it within seven days, and the department posts it on a public website. The state has taken over the field of sex offender registration and notification, and the statute bars cities and counties from adding their own restrictions on sex offenders; that can be read as displacing local residency or notice rules, though whether it does is for the courts. You also have no duty to disclose that the property was the site of a sexual assault or other felony (see "No Duty to Disclose Deaths or Crimes in New Mexico"). Whether you could owe a duty to warn tenants about a known dangerous person is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: don't promise that the property or neighborhood is free of offenders; if asked, point the person to the public registry website rather than giving your own account; and apply any screening criteria the same way to every applicant (see "Sex Offender Information and Rentals in New Mexico" and "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico").

title: No Statewide Landlord Registration in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to register with the state, a county or a city, or to hold a rental license, before you rent out a home, and none lets a tenant end the lease because a landlord is unregistered. Two general state laws may still reach you. First, every New Mexico city, town or village must charge a yearly business registration fee (no more than $35) on each place of business within it that it does not license, and it may instead license and regulate a business by ordinance. The city can enforce either by court action, including by stopping the business or the occupancy of the building where it is carried on. State law does not say whether renting out a home is a business for this purpose; each city's ordinance decides that, so ask the clerk of the city where the property is. Second, a person who manages rentals for others for pay generally needs a New Mexico real estate broker's license; you and your own employees managing your own property do not. New Mexico's statutes do not stop a city or county from adopting its own rental registration or licensing rule, and the only statewide limit they place on local landlord rules is the ban on local rent control (see "No Local Rent Control in New Mexico"). Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and other local governments may have their own rental rules. For out-of-state owners, see "Out-of-State Owners in New Mexico"; for inspections, see "No Statewide Rental Inspection or Registration in New Mexico".

title: Recording a Lease in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no lease registry and no rule that a residential lease be registered with a state or local agency. Its recording law does reach long leases: a lease whose initial term plus any option terms is longer than five years, or a memorandum of its material terms (the names and mailing addresses of the parties, a description of the property if known, and the initial term and any renewal options), must be recorded with the county clerk of the county where the property is. A lease of any length may be recorded. Recording gives notice to everyone from the time it is recorded, and an unrecorded instrument that had to be recorded does not affect the rights of a later buyer, good-faith mortgage lender or judgment lien creditor who did not know of it. Whether a tenant's possession alone gives a later buyer or lender notice of an unrecorded lease is a case-law question; the cautious course for a lease that can run more than five years is to record it or a memorandum. See "Long Leases, Married Owners and Recording in New Mexico" for the other rules on longer leases, including when both spouses must sign.

title: No Required Rights and Responsibilities Guide in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule requires you to give a tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, before signing the lease or at renewal, or to get the tenant's signed acknowledgment of one. No state agency is directed to publish such a guide. What New Mexico does require at the start of a tenancy is a written rental agreement given to each tenant before occupancy (see "Written Lease Required in New Mexico") and a written disclosure of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices (see "Management and Notices" clause). A mobile home park lease must also include a statement of the resident's right to request alternative dispute resolution (see "Resolving Disputes Before Court in New Mexico"). Local ordinances (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may have their own notice rules. You may hand tenants a summary of your own, but it does not replace the lease or the required disclosures, and it should not misstate the law.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Statement in a New Mexico Lease
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule requires a state-agency statement of tenant rights to be attached to a lease, placed on its first page or signed by the tenant, and none bars you from suing until one is given. Two narrower rules exist. A mobile home park lease must include a statement explaining the resident's right to request alternative dispute resolution of disputes with the park, except over unpaid rent or utility charges or in a public safety emergency (see "Resolving Disputes Before Court in New Mexico"). And the Supreme Court's standard eviction notice forms carry their own explanations to the tenant (see "Standard Notice Forms in New Mexico"); its forms for the Eviction Prevention and Diversion Program, which "How Evictions Work in New Mexico" reports was withdrawn for new cases, had the landlord certify giving the tenant the court's Resource Information Sheet on rental and legal assistance. Those are notice and court-stage documents, not lease attachments. Local ordinances (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may have their own rules.

title: No State Limit on Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law limits renting out a house in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot, or sets a state lot-split or two-unit program with an owner-occupancy or minimum-rental-term condition. Zoning is local. State law lets each county and municipality regulate the density of population and the location and use of buildings and land for residence and other purposes, and divide its area into zoning districts. Whether a local zoning code may restrict rentals, for example by requiring owner occupancy or limiting short-term rentals, is a question of the local code and of case law. Before you rent a home, check the zoning and any rental or short-term rental rules of the city or county where it is (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others). A homeowners' or condominium association may also limit leasing (see "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause).

title: Accessory Dwelling Units and Casitas in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's building, fire, manufactured housing, utility, human rights and motor carrier parts, creates a right to build or rent an accessory dwelling unit or casita, bars a city from requiring owner occupancy, or sets a minimum rental term for one. ADUs are left to local zoning. The one related state rule: every county and municipal zoning authority must accommodate multigenerational housing, meaning people related by blood, common ancestry, marriage, guardianship or adoption, by creating a way, such as a conditional use permit, to allow up to two kitchens in a single-family zoning district. That rule speaks of related households and says nothing about renting; whether a second kitchen approved under it may be rented to an unrelated tenant is up to the local code. If you rent a casita or ADU, it is a dwelling unit under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act and every rule in the act applies, unless one of the act's exemptions fits (for example, occupancy by your employee under a written agreement that makes the right to occupy conditional on employment in and about the premises). It counts as a single family residence (which matters if you want the tenant to take on certain chores, see "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause) if it is a structure maintained and used as a single dwelling unit; a casita that shares a wall with another unit counts only if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares no heating, hot water or other essential facility or service with any other unit. The statute does not say whether a detached casita that shares the main house's heating or hot water counts; the cautious course is to treat it as a single family residence only if it meets both conditions. Building or converting one is construction under the state building codes; check permits and local zoning first.

title: No Health District Rental Rules in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's building, fire, manufactured housing, utility, human rights and motor carrier parts, creates a health district with rental housing regulations, requires you to give tenants health-agency rental rules on request, or sends tenants to a health district with complaints. The state Department of Health works through health regions with regional health officers, and the Environment Department and its Environmental Improvement Board make statewide rules on subjects such as nuisance abatement, vector control and septic (liquid waste) systems; New Mexico's statutes give them no rental-housing rules, so check their own rules. Housing conditions are enforced through the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act's repair duties, which include complying with applicable minimum housing codes (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"), and through city ordinances on unfit dwellings (see "City Repair, Closing and Demolition Orders for Unfit Rentals in New Mexico"). Check with local health or code departments (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others).

title: No State Lead-Safe Certificate for New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's building, fire, manufactured housing, utility, tax, human rights and motor carrier parts, requires a lead-safe or lead-free certificate for a rental, an inspection to obtain one, or attaching one to the lease. Those laws set up no state lead-based paint program for rental housing. For a home built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet still apply (see "Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause), and federal law may also govern renovation or repair work that disturbs paint in older housing.

title: No State Lead Notices for New Mexico Rentals
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's building, fire, manufactured housing, utility, tax, human rights and motor carrier parts, requires a state lead notice, certificate, pamphlet or packet to be given with a lease, beyond the federal disclosure.

For a home built before 1978, use the federal lead-based paint disclosure and give the federal pamphlet (see "Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause); New Mexico's statutes, constitution, session laws and the Administrative Code parts above add nothing to it. They also have no state blood-lead or lead-hazard reduction rule for rentals.

title: City Repair, Closing and Demolition Orders for Unfit Rentals in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statute that puts a substandard rental into receivership or lets a court collect rents to pay for code repairs, but cities can order repairs. A municipality that adopts an unfit-dwelling ordinance appoints a public officer who can charge a dwelling as unfit for human habitation (for example for dilapidation, fire hazards, lack of ventilation, light or sanitary facilities, overcrowding, or any violation of health, fire, building or zoning rules). The complaint goes to you, every recorded mortgage holder and everyone with an interest, including tenants in possession, with a hearing 10 to 30 days later. If the officer finds the dwelling unfit, the order tells you to repair it within a set time or to vacate and close it, or, if repair would cost too much relative to its value, to remove or demolish it. If you don't comply, the officer may do the work, and the cost becomes a lien on the property. Complaints and orders are posted on the property and filed with the county clerk, where they act as notice of a pending claim to anyone who buys or lends on it; you can appeal an order to district court. If the ordinance authorizes it, the officer may also enter to inspect, with a court order if entry is refused. Separately, a city council can, by resolution finding that a ruined, damaged and dilapidated building is a menace to the public comfort, health, peace or safety, order it removed: you have 10 days from service or posting to start removal or to object and ask for a hearing, and if you don't act the city may remove it at your cost, with a lien it can foreclose. State law gives counties the powers of municipalities except where limits on counties say otherwise. A tenant who is in compliance with the lease is protected from retaliation for complaining to a code agency, within the previous six months, of a code violation materially affecting health and safety (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"), and their own repair remedies are in "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico". Which cities and counties have adopted these ordinances, and their details (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others), is local law not covered here.

title: Telling Tenants About Code Orders and Condemnation in New Mexico
bodyText: For an ordinary rental under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, contain nothing that requires you to disclose to a tenant or applicant an outstanding inspection report, code violation, repair order or condemnation order. Two rules come close. First, mobile home parks: when a park owner is formally notified by a government agency that the park is the subject of a condemnation proceeding, the landlord must notify the tenants in writing of the terms of that notice within 17 days, and condemnation of the park is one of the grounds for ending park tenancies. Second, under a city's unfit-dwelling ordinance, the complaint goes to everyone in possession (your tenants included), and the complaint and any order are posted on the property and filed with the county clerk (see "City Repair, Closing and Demolition Orders for Unfit Rentals in New Mexico"). Separately, the Unfair Practices Act lists failing to state a material fact, where that deceives or tends to deceive, among the deceptive trade practices it defines by reference to representations knowingly made in connection with the sale, lease, rental or loan of goods or services in the regular course of trade or commerce (see "Unfair Practices Act and Rentals"); whether that definition reaches a dwelling lease, and whether keeping quiet about an open code or vacate order is such a failure, are case-law questions. The cautious course is to tell an applicant in writing about any open order affecting the unit before the lease is signed. Local ordinances (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may require more.

title: Rent When a New Mexico Rental Is Condemned or Uninhabitable
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, expressly bars you from collecting rent once a unit is condemned or a government vacate order is issued. Rent can still stop or shrink under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act. If your failure to meet your repair duties makes the home uninhabitable and the tenant moves out because of it, the tenant who gave you written notice may withhold all of the rent from the notice date until you cure the problem, if you haven't fixed it within 7 days of the notice. If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the home, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 7 days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay less rent in proportion; you must then return prepaid rent and deposits as the act provides. If, without a court order, you knowingly exclude or remove the tenant by a willful act that makes the unit uninhabitable or inaccessible, the tenant may withhold all of the rent for each day the tenant is denied possession, recover damages and hold you liable for two times the monthly rent (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico"). A court may also reduce rent on equitable grounds. Whether rent is owed for a period when a public order bars anyone from living in the unit is a case-law question. The cautious course: don't charge rent for any period a vacate or closing order is in effect, and refund rent the tenant paid for that period. See "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico", "Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico" and "City Repair, Closing and Demolition Orders for Unfit Rentals in New Mexico".

title: No Code Variance Notice to Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no state sanitary code for housing, and no New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's building, fire, manufactured housing, utility, tax, human rights and motor carrier parts, requires you to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a copy of a variance, exception or waiver from a housing, health, building or fire code. The state fire marshal may grant a variance from the fire code's requirements for existing buildings if it doesn't reduce overall protection from fire and similar emergencies; that rule applies to apartment and other buildings but not to detached one- and two-family homes and townhouses of up to three stories built to the residential code, unless they are used as commercial properties, and it has no tenant-notice requirement. Any variance you hold doesn't change your repair duties to tenants under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, which require you to comply substantially with applicable minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). City housing and health codes (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may have their own variance and notice rules.

title: No Lease Translation or Type-Size Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule requires a residential lease to be translated, to be in the language used to negotiate or advertise it, to follow prescribed wording, or to use a minimum type size. The language rules that do exist reach other transactions, not leases of a home: door-to-door sales contracts (which expressly exclude rentals of real property), rental-purchase agreements for goods advertised in another language, used car sales, and a foreclosure consultant's contract, which must be in the language the homeowner used to negotiate it (that rule covers the consulting contract, not a lease the homeowner signs to rent the home back). Practical points: if you negotiate in Spanish or another language, a tenant who did not understand the English lease may later dispute what was agreed, and only case law could settle how a court would treat that; the cautious course is to give the tenant a translation marked as a courtesy copy and keep the signed version. The Supreme Court's summons forms for the Eviction Prevention and Diversion Program (see "How Evictions Work in New Mexico") tell the tenant to ask the court clerk for language interpretation; interpreting at a hearing is the court's process, not a lease term.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Statute or Consumer Restrictions Statement in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law applies a plain-language or readability test to residential leases, requires a statement of consumer restrictions listing the rights a lease takes away, or offers Attorney General preapproval of lease forms. The one plain-language rule for rentals is for listings: since June 20, 2025, a published listing must disclose to applicants, in plain language, all costs of the rental agreement, including the base rent and an itemized, readily identifiable description of every fee or charge (see "Plain Language in New Mexico Rentals" and "Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases"). A consumer-restrictions statement would have nothing to list anyway, because a New Mexico lease may not make the tenant give up rights or remedies under the law (see "Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico"). Writing the lease plainly is still the cautious course: a court may limit a term it finds was inequitable when made (see "Inequitable Lease Terms in New Mexico").

title: No Recycling Notice Rule for New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's building, fire, manufactured housing, utility, tax, human rights and motor carrier parts, requires you to provide recycling at a rental or to tell tenants where and how to recycle. The state's Recycling, Circular Economy and Illegal Dumping Act deals with scrap tires, illegal dumpsites and grants to local governments; it puts no landlord-specific duty on you, though, like anyone, you must not engage in, maintain or allow illegal dumping. Under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act you must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for its removal; in a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not for the purpose of evading your obligations, that the tenant does this instead (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). That duty does not mention recycling; whether and how recycling is collected is set by your city, county or hauler. If you provide recycling or trash service, the lease or your written rules can tell tenants how to use it (see "Rules and Regulations" clause), and any charge for it must be stated in the lease (see "Fees and Charges" clause). Local ordinances (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may require more.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell a tenant about a move-in or move-out inspection, or to hold one, so there is no penalty for skipping that notice and no rule that you lose the deposit or pay a multiple of it for lacking an inspection (see "No New Mexico Move-In Inspection Rule"). The penalties that do exist are in the deposit law itself. If you don't give the tenant an itemized written list of deductions and the balance due within 30 days after the lease ends or the tenant leaves, whichever is later, you lose the right to keep any of the deposit, the right to counterclaim in the tenant's suit for it and the right to sue separately for damage to the property, and you owe the tenant's court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Keeping a deposit in bad faith adds a $250 civil penalty (see "Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in New Mexico"). Because you must justify every deduction, and the tenant must leave the unit as clean as at move-in except for ordinary wear and tear, a signed move-in condition checklist with dated photos is the cautious course (see "Existing Condition of Property" clause).

title: Inspections in Subsidized and Voucher Rentals in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law sets special inspection rules for subsidized or voucher housing, or special consequences when a tenant in such housing refuses an inspection. Voucher (Section 8) inspections and their deadlines come from federal program rules and your contract with the housing agency (see "Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease"). Under New Mexico law, every tenant, subsidized or not, must let you in to inspect on 24 hours' written notice stating the purpose, date and estimated time, unless you agreed otherwise; the 24-hour notice rule does not apply when you are accompanied by a public official conducting an inspection. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may ask a court to order access or end the rental agreement, and either way recover damages, reasonable attorney's fees and court costs. A city officer enforcing an unfit-dwelling ordinance may, if the ordinance gives the officer that power, get a court order to enter if entry is denied. What to do: give written notice of agency inspections, tell the housing agency promptly if a tenant blocks one so the failure isn't treated as yours, and keep copies.

title: Rent Abatement in Subsidized Rentals in New Mexico
bodyText: When a tenant whose rent is paid in whole or in part by a government agency uses the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act's rent abatement for an unrepaired condition (see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico"), the abatement is measured on the total monthly rent paid for the unit, not only on the tenant's own share. Where a third party pays rent, either that payor or the tenant may authorize the abatement and abate the rent payments. So a failure to repair after written notice can reduce what you receive from the housing agency as well as from the tenant: if you haven't fixed the condition within 7 days of the notice, one-third of the pro-rata daily rent for each day from the date of the notice until it is fixed, or all of the rent for each day from the date of the notice until the breach is cured if the home is uninhabitable and the tenant doesn't live there because of the condition. The statute refers to an "abatement limitation of one month's rent" that the abatement section does not itself state; don't assume a one-month cap applies. Voucher programs have their own federal rules on stopping housing assistance payments when a unit fails inspection (see "Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease"); how the state and federal rules interact is not settled by New Mexico's statutes or rules. Fix reported conditions within 7 days of written notice and keep records.

title: No Repair Escrow or Small-Landlord Opt-Out in New Mexico
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. New Mexico has nothing to opt out of in that way. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law lets a tenant pay rent into escrow until repairs are made, and none exempts small or owner-occupied buildings from the tenant's repair remedies or provides an exemption notice. The Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act's remedies (written notice, then rent abatement, termination or damages; see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico") apply to every rental the act covers, whatever its size; the act's only exemptions are for arrangements such as institutional residence, contract-of-sale occupancy, fraternal housing, transient hotel or motel stays, employee housing under a written agreement and agricultural premises (see "What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers"), and none applies if it was created to avoid the act. A lease term trying to waive those remedies is barred (see "Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico"). The one rent escrow in the act is on appeal: a tenant who appeals a possession judgment must pay the rent to you, or into an escrow account with a professional escrow agent, to keep the writ stayed. Don't add an exemption or waiver notice to the lease; answer repair requests promptly and in writing.

title: Certificates of Occupancy and Rentals in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that requires a lease to disclose whether a building has a certificate of occupancy or requires you to give the tenant a copy. But the building law itself reaches you: if a permit was issued to build a new residential building, the building may not be occupied until a certificate of occupancy has been issued certifying compliance with all codes and standards. So don't rent a newly built home until the certificate is issued. For a converted garage, an addition or other changed space, ask the building department whether a new certificate is needed. The state building codes send the certificate-of-occupancy procedure to the Construction Industries Division's permits and inspections rule, so check that rule for its details (including any posting rule); cities with their own building departments (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may have their own rules. Renting space that was never approved for living in can also breach your duty to comply with applicable housing and building codes affecting health and safety (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico").

title: No New Mexico Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that a home contains defective or corrosive drywall, or sets a drywall inspection or cleanup standard for rentals. Your general duties still apply: you must substantially comply with applicable minimum housing codes that materially affect health and safety, and make repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises in a safe condition (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). Separately, the Unfair Practices Act lists failing to state a material fact, where that deceives or tends to deceive, among unfair or deceptive trade practices; the act can be read as reaching leasing done in the regular course of trade, though a court could read it differently (see "Unfair Practices Act and Rentals"). Whether keeping quiet about a known building defect is such a practice is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: if you know the home has defective drywall, tell applicants in writing before they sign, and never misstate it if asked.

title: No New Mexico Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's utility, building-code and tax parts, requires you to tell an applicant or tenant, before signing, that the home is near a former military ordnance site, that you have applied for or plan a demolition of the building, or that the tenant's utility meter also serves another unit or a common area. Related rules you should know. Demolition: if complying with the building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the unit, you may bring an action for possession even though the tenant has recently complained or used a right the act protects, but you stay liable for your repair duties (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"). Ending the tenancy still takes the ordinary notice for a periodic tenancy ("Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause), and a fixed-term lease runs to its end unless it lawfully gives you an earlier way out. A city that finds a dwelling unfit for human habitation serves its complaint on the persons in possession as well as on the owner. Meters: in multi-unit housing, a tenant may ask for a copy of the utility bill for the unit if each unit is separately metered, the apartment's utility bill if the unit is submetered, and every common-area bill apportioned to tenants, with the calculations; a vacant unit's share of common-area cost cannot be passed to the others, and you may charge no more than $5 for each monthly request ("Utility Bills and Allocation" clause, "Utility Billing Rights in New Mexico"). Mobile home parks have their own utility billing rules. The state's commercial energy conservation code requires a separate electrical meter for each dwelling unit in an apartment house with an R-2 occupancy, for work under that code since January 30, 2024. If you know a fact of this kind that matters to an applicant, the cautious course is to say so in writing before signing (see "Unfair Practices Act and Rentals").

title: No New Mexico Chemical Exposure Warning Rule for Rentals
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warnings do not apply in New Mexico, and no New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to warn tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer, birth defects or reproductive harm, or to post such warnings at rental property. Federal rules still apply where they reach the home, such as the lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978. New Mexico also has no state radon, mold or methamphetamine disclosure rule ("No New Mexico Radon Disclosure Rule", "No New Mexico Mold Disclosure Rule", "No New Mexico Methamphetamine Disclosure Rule"). Your general duty to keep the premises in a safe condition still applies ("Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico").

title: No New Mexico Shoreline or Public-Access Disclosure
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a lease to disclose that a property is on or near a shoreline, beach, lake or stream, that the public may use a waterway or a path across the land, or any public access right. One rule matters for rentals along a stream or lake: nobody engaged in hunting, fishing, camping, hiking, boating or other recreation may walk or wade onto private property through non-navigable public water, or reach public water across private property, unless the owner, the lessee or the person in control of the land has expressly consented in writing. If your tenant will hold the land, say in the lease whether the tenant may give that consent, and tell the tenant of any recorded easement or path across the property that the tenant must not block.

title: No New Mexico Military Installation or Air Zone Disclosure
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that a rental lies near a military installation, a missile range or an air base, or within a military noise or accident potential zone, and none gives a tenant a right to end the lease on learning it. New Mexico's Military Base Planning and Impact Act (2025) gathers a state office and commission that date from 2003 with a new fund to support military bases and their communities; it places no duty on landlords or sellers. Airport zoning near public airports is a matter for local zoning boards and local ordinances. Federal or local rules may still apply. If the property is in a noisy flight path, telling applicants before they sign avoids later disputes (see "Unfair Practices Act and Rentals").

title: No Property-Tax-Share-of-Rent Statement in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell a tenant what part of the rent goes to property tax, or to give a tenant a statement or certificate of rent paid for a state tax credit or rebate. The one rent-based property tax rule is a tenant's own: a New Mexico resident aged 65 or older who files a New Mexico income tax return, is not someone else's dependent and rents a principal place of residence may, for the elderly property tax rebate on the state income tax return, calculate the property tax due as six percent of the gross rent for the taxable year. The law puts no duty on you for that rebate, but a tenant who claims it needs a record of rent paid, so giving receipts or a year-end rent statement on request helps (New Mexico has no general rent-receipt rule: "Rent Receipts in New Mexico"). Passing a property tax increase on to a tenant is covered in "Passing Tax Increases to Tenants in New Mexico".

title: No Pre-Lease Foreclosure Disclosure in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell an applicant or a new tenant, before signing, that the property is in foreclosure, that a foreclosure complaint has been filed, or that a foreclosure sale is scheduled, and none sets a lease form for such a disclosure. What New Mexico law does say about foreclosure and tenants is in "Foreclosure and Tenants in New Mexico" (no state tenant-protection statute; a lender enforcing an assignment of rents may notify the tenant to pay rent to it). Federal law protects bona fide tenants after a foreclosure sale ("Federal Tenant Protections After Foreclosure"). Separately, the Unfair Practices Act lists failing to state a material fact, where that deceives or tends to deceive, among unfair or deceptive trade practices, and the act can be read as reaching leasing done in the regular course of trade, though a court could read it differently ("Unfair Practices Act and Rentals"); whether staying silent about a pending foreclosure is such a practice is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: don't sign a new lease or take advance rent while hiding a foreclosure you know of that could end the tenancy; tell the applicant in writing.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice or Lease Type-Size Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a single-family home lease to carry an occupancy notice, to be notarized, or to be signed by a licensed property manager; none presumes that an occupant has no lawful right to be there unless the lease has some formality; and none sets a font size, boldface, capital-letter or first-page rule for any text a residential lease must contain. What New Mexico does require: a written rental agreement for every tenant before occupancy begins ("Written Lease Required in New Mexico"), and a written disclosure of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices and service, which the lease can carry ("Management and Notices" clause). The type-size rules in New Mexico law are for other contracts, such as rental-purchase agreements for goods and solar energy system agreements, not home leases (see also "Plain Language in New Mexico Rentals"). A person who occupies without your consent is removed through the court process, never by lockout ("Removing Unauthorized Occupants in New Mexico").

title: Association Documents and Your Tenant in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to disclose a homeowner or condominium association's obligations to a tenant, give the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules, or put an association statement in the lease. The tenant is bound anyway: the Owner-Resident Relations Act makes the tenant abide by the bylaws, covenants, rules and regulations of any applicable condominium regime, cooperative housing agreement or neighborhood association that are not inconsistent with your rights or duties, and the Homeowner Association Act makes a lot owner's tenants comply with that act and the association's community documents ("Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause; association fines and tenant suspensions: "Homeowner and Condominium Associations and Your Tenant in New Mexico"). Because the tenant is held to documents only you have, give the tenant a copy of the rules and any covenants that limit use of the home before signing; you may add your own acknowledgment of receipt. The disclosure certificate (homeowner associations) and resale certificate (condominiums) are owed by a seller to a buyer, not to a tenant. One likely exception for condominiums: the Condominium Act's purchaser is anyone who by a voluntary transfer acquires an interest in a unit other than a leasehold, including renewal options, of less than twenty years, and a unit owner must give a purchaser the declaration, bylaws, rules and an association resale certificate before conveyance unless an exemption in the act applies. That can be read as reaching a lease that can run twenty years or more, though a court could read it differently, so the cautious course is to deliver those documents before signing such a lease. A lease with an option to buy is covered in "Optional Lease Terms in New Mexico"; a condominium conversion in "Condominium Conversion Notice in New Mexico".

title: Every Disclosure New Mexico Requires of a Landlord
bodyText: These are the disclosures New Mexico law requires of a residential landlord; New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws require no others. Before signing: (1) every published listing must state in plain language all costs, including the base rent and an itemized description of every fee or charge that will be assessed during the tenancy ("Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases"); (2) before charging a screening fee, give written or digital notice of it and get the applicant's written agreement, give a receipt, and give the applicant a copy of any report used to screen ("Application Screening Fees in New Mexico", "Tenant Screening Rules in New Mexico"); (3) every fee you charge must be in the rental agreement, and charging an applicant a fee that is not a screening fee or deposit, or a fee that was not published in the listing, is an unfair or deceptive trade practice ("Fees and Charges" clause); (4) give each tenant a written rental agreement before occupancy begins ("Written Lease Required in New Mexico"); (5) in writing, at or before move-in, give the name, address and telephone number of the manager and of an owner or agent for service of process and notices, and keep them current ("Management and Notices" clause); (6) for housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure. During and after the tenancy: (7) written notice of a rent increase at least 30 days before the periodic rental date (month-to-month) or before the end of the term (fixed term), or one rental period ahead for a tenancy of less than a month ("Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico"), and written notice of a fee increase at least 60 days before the periodic rental date or before the end of the term, or one rental period ahead for a tenancy of less than a month ("Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"); (8) notice of a late fee no later than the last day of the next rental period ("New Mexico Late Fee Rules"); (9) in multi-unit housing, copies of utility bills and apportionment calculations on request ("Utility Bills and Allocation" clause); (10) an itemized written list of deposit deductions within 30 days ("Return of Security Deposit" clause); (11) if you are the declarant converting a building to condominiums, or a person in the business of selling real estate who will offer its units, a conversion notice to the tenants in possession ("Condominium Conversion Notice in New Mexico"). Notices the act requires for other purposes, such as entry, ending a tenancy, or a sale or change of manager, are in their own rows ("Entry Rules in New Mexico", "Sale of the Property or a New Manager in New Mexico"). You need not disclose that the property was the site of a natural death, a homicide, suicide, assault, sexual assault or other felony, or certain illnesses connected with the property ("No Duty to Disclose Deaths or Crimes in New Mexico"). Special cases. A mobile home park has its own written-disclosure rules under the Mobile Home Park Act. A subdivider selling or leasing land in a subdivision owes disclosure statements under the subdivision acts, which do not cover leasing apartments or similar space in a building; they can be read as reaching the developer of subdivided land, not the rental of an existing home, but that is for the courts, so get advice if you created the subdivision. A real estate licensee must give a landlord and tenant a list of the licensee's duties before presenting a written agreement; the duties and any rule on a licensee-landlord's own status are in Real Estate Commission rules. A lease with an option to buy brings in seller disclosures (an assessor's property tax estimate, a homeowner association disclosure certificate, a public improvement district notice, a condominium resale certificate); New Mexico has no general seller property-condition disclosure statute ("Optional Lease Terms in New Mexico"). When a seller duty attaches to a lease-option is not settled by statute; the cautious course is to deliver those items before the option agreement is signed.

title: No New Mexico Contamination Disclosure Rule for Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that hazardous substances, pollution or soil or groundwater contamination are on or under the property, or that it was used as a drug lab, and none requires a recorded environmental cleanup restriction to be written into a lease or handed to a tenant (see also "No New Mexico Methamphetamine Disclosure Rule"). Cleanup and water quality rules adopted by state environmental agencies are in the New Mexico Administrative Code; check whether one of them requires a recorded restriction to be passed to occupants. Your general duties still apply: keep the premises in a safe condition and comply with housing codes that materially affect health and safety ("Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). The cautious course: if the property is under a cleanup agreement or a recorded use restriction, or you know of contamination that affects the home, tell applicants in writing before signing and write any use limits (such as no digging, no well use or no gardening) into the lease.

title: No New Mexico Asbestos Disclosure Rule for Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the New Mexico Administrative Code's construction, utility, tax and other parts that bear on renting, requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that a building contains asbestos, to survey a rental for asbestos, or to give tenants notice before asbestos work. The only asbestos references are workers' compensation rules for asbestosis, public construction appropriations, and a residential building code rule on re-roofing over asbestos-cement tile. Asbestos removal and disposal are regulated by the state environment department and federal rules may also apply, so check them before any renovation or demolition that could disturb asbestos-containing material. Your general duty to keep the premises in a safe condition applies ("Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). The cautious course: if you know of damaged or friable asbestos material in the home, tell the tenant in writing and keep the tenant away from any work area.

title: Private Wells and Rental Homes in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to test a private or domestic well that serves a rental home, or to give a tenant or buyer well test results. Your general duties still apply: you must supply running water and a reasonable amount of hot water at all times (unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for it, or the hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection), and keep the plumbing and other facilities you supply or are required to supply in good and safe working order ("Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). One rule can apply to a larger rental: a water system that serves at least 15 service connections used by year-round residents, or regularly serves at least 25 year-round residents, is a community water system, which is a public water system regulated by the state environment department and the environmental improvement board.
