The drinking water rules for public water systems, including testing and notice to the people served, are in parts of the New Mexico Administrative Code, so if one well serves many units or tenants, check whether your system is a public water system and what those rules require. The cautious course for any rental on a well: test the water periodically and give tenants the results.

title: Telling Tenants About Proceedings Against the Property in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that the property is subject to a foreclosure, condemnation, partition, receivership, lien or other lawsuit that could affect the tenancy, outside two special cases: a condominium conversion ("Condominium Conversion Notice in New Mexico"), and a mobile home park owner formally notified by a government agency that the park is the subject of a condemnation proceeding, who must tell the tenants in writing of the terms of that notice within 17 days (a Mobile Home Park Act rule). Tenants may hear of a proceeding from others: a lender enforcing an assignment of rents may notify the tenant to pay rent to it ("Foreclosure and Tenants in New Mexico"); a city's complaint that a dwelling is unfit for human habitation is served on persons in possession; and a public agency that displaces residential tenants for a project must offer relocation advisory services. For foreclosure before signing, see "No Pre-Lease Foreclosure Disclosure in New Mexico". To learn of papers served at the property, use the tenant-forwarding clause "Notice of Proceedings Against the Property". The cautious course: tell tenants in writing promptly of any proceeding you know of that may end or disturb their tenancy.

title: Homeowner and Condominium Associations and Your Tenant in New Mexico
bodyText:
If the rental is in a homeowner association or a condominium, the tenant is bound by the association's rules. The Owner-Resident Relations Act requires the tenant to abide by the bylaws, covenants, rules and regulations of any applicable condominium regime, cooperative housing agreement or neighborhood association that are not inconsistent with your rights or duties, and the Homeowner Association Act requires each lot owner's tenants, guests and invitees to comply with that act and the association's community documents (use "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause in the lease).

Unless the community documents provide otherwise, a homeowner association may, after written notice and an opportunity to dispute an alleged violation other than failure to pay assessments, levy reasonable fines and suspend for a reasonable time the right of a lot owner's tenant to use common areas and facilities; before a fine or suspension the board must give the person 14 days' written notice of the chance to submit a written statement or have a hearing, and if the board or committee does not approve it by majority vote it cannot be imposed (no notice or hearing is needed for an imminent threat to public health or safety).

Since July 1, 2026, a homeowner association may not effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict use of a lot as a registered or licensed child care home, or charge it fees other lots don't pay, though uniform rules still apply ("Child Care Homes in New Mexico Rentals").

The Homeowner Association Act does not apply to condominiums, which follow the Condominium Act; a condominium declaration may require that tenants rather than owners vote on specified matters, and then the tenant gets notice of those meetings and access to records.

New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that regulates an association's power to restrict or approve leases, caps lease-approval fees, limits what tenant information an association may demand, or lets an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind; the declaration and bylaws control those questions. Before passing any association application or approval fee to an applicant or tenant, note that a screening fee is the only application fee an owner may charge and every fee must be itemized in any published listing and included in the lease ("Application Screening Fees in New Mexico", "Fees and Charges" clause); the cautious course is to pay association fees yourself.

This library does not offer a lease-approval contingency clause for New Mexico; you can add your own if your declaration requires approval.

title: Child Care Homes in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that requires you to let a tenant run a family child care home in a rental, or sets conditions (such as insurance or a liability waiver) on which you must allow it. Unless you agree otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit, and the library's "Residential Use Only" clause bars commercial use; whether a licensed child care home in which the provider lives breaches a residential-use term is a question only case law could settle, so if you will allow child care, say so in writing using "Home Business or Child Care (Landlord's Permission)" clause, and if you won't, say so plainly in the lease. Since July 1, 2026 (Senate Bill 96), other bodies may not stand in the way once you allow it: a registered child care home (up to four children), licensed family child care home (up to six) or licensed group child care home (seven to twelve), in each case run by a provider who lives in the home, is a residential use for zoning, permitted by right, and a city or county may not impose rules, reviews or permits on it that don't apply to other homes in the zone, charge any fee or tax for the privilege of operating it, or require more off-street parking than for a single-family home in the zone; the state fire rules may not regulate it more than other private residences; and a homeowner association may not effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict use of a lot as a child care home or charge it fees other lots don't pay, though uniform rules on parking, noise, safety, appearance and common areas still apply and the provider must follow association rules that don't conflict with licensing. These protections run against the association, local government and fire rules, not against you as landlord, and the Homeowner Association Act does not cover condominiums.

title: Home Businesses in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that gives a tenant a right to run a home-based business in a rental or makes a lease restriction on one unenforceable.

The default is yours to set: unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit and in compliance with the rental agreement. To keep business use out, use the "Residential Use Only" clause; to allow a particular business on conditions, add "Home Business or Child Care (Landlord's Permission)" clause.

Licensed and registered child care homes have their own protections against associations, zoning and fire rules (not against you): see "Child Care Homes in New Mexico Rentals". Local zoning and business licensing rules on home occupations are local matters, and a homeowner or condominium association's documents may also limit business use ("Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause).

title: Renting to Students in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law sets special rules for renting to students or for privately owned student housing. If you rent a house or apartment to students, the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act applies to the tenancy exactly as it does to any other tenant: deposit limits, notices, repairs, entry and eviction ("What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers"). The act exempts residence at an institution, public or private, where it is incidental to the institution's educational and similar services, which can be read as reaching dormitories and similar housing a school provides to its own students; whether a privately owned or master-leased student building can share that exemption is a question only case law could settle, and the exemption never applies to an arrangement created to avoid the act. The cautious course for a private landlord: treat every student lease as covered by the act. Roommate groups and parental guarantees are handled by ordinary lease terms ("Joint & Several Liability" clause, "Permitted Occupants" clause).

title: Housing an Employee in New Mexico
bodyText:
If you house your own employee, the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act does not apply to that occupancy only if a written rental or employment agreement specifies that the employee's right to occupy is conditional on employment in and about the premises, and the arrangement was not created to avoid the act. An employee who lives in a unit away from where the employee works, or who has no such written condition, is an ordinary tenant with all the act's protections ("What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers").

No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a separate signed disclosure to an employee-occupant, sets a move-out period after the job ends, or requires you to offer a regular rental agreement when employment ends. How an exempt employee-occupant is removed after the job ends is not settled by any New Mexico statute; the cautious course is written notice and a court action, never a lockout.

Rent and wages: the minimum-wage law expressly lets an employer that furnishes housing to an employee engaged in agriculture deduct the reasonable value of the housing from wages; for any other employee, get advice before deducting rent from pay.

If you want the exemption, put the condition in writing; "Employee Occupancy Conditional on Employment" clause is the library's optional clause.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that decides whether you or your tenant holds the hunting or fishing rights on rented land; the lease decides. Rentals of premises used primarily for agricultural purposes are outside the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act ("What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers"), and agricultural leases are outside this library. New Mexico's hunting and trespass laws treat the owner and the lessee alike: either may post the land against hunting or fishing, entering posted land to hunt or fish without permission of the owner or lessee is a misdemeanor, no one may reach public water across private land without the express written consent of the owner, lessee or person in control, and discharging a firearm within 150 yards of a dwelling or building without permission of the owner or lessees is a crime. So a tenant in possession may be able to give or refuse permission. If you mean to keep hunting rights, or to forbid the tenant from allowing hunting, say so in the lease. An owner, lessee or person in control who lets people hunt or use the land for recreation free of charge does not thereby take on a duty to keep the land safe for them, though that protection does not cover permission given for a charge.

title: Leasing Land Grant Common Lands in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no general rule requiring government approval of a residential lease of communal land, but one kind of communal land has its own leasing rules: the common lands of a Spanish or Mexican land grant-merced. Only the grant's board of trustees can lease common lands, under the grant's bylaws. For the community land grant corporations governed by the 1917 act (chapter 49, article 2), a lease of common lands binds the grant only if a board resolution approves it by a two-thirds vote at a regular quarterly meeting; the resolution takes effect only after 30 days, during which anyone interested in the common lands may file a written protest; if a majority of the owners and proprietors protest, the board must call an election, and a majority vote of the owners and proprietors against the resolution voids it; and no lease of common lands may run longer than 20 years (oil and gas leases aside). A person who is not an heir and who leases property within a grant gets rights only in the land leased, not in the common lands. Leases of tribal or pueblo land are governed by federal and tribal law.

title: No Special District Statement in a New Mexico Lease
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a lease to state, or a landlord to represent, that the property lies in a public improvement district, tax increment development district, special assessment district or other special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge a district's taxes or levies. The public improvement district notice is a seller's duty to a buyer before accepting an offer to purchase residential property, and it expressly does not apply to a transfer of only a leasehold interest. If you sell to a tenant under a purchase option, that notice and the other seller disclosures apply then ("Every Disclosure New Mexico Requires of a Landlord"). District taxes and levies are the owner's obligation; if you want a tenant to bear any part of one, the lease must say so as rent or as a stated fee ("Fees and Charges" clause, "Passing Tax Increases to Tenants in New Mexico").

title: Leasing When You Hold Only a Life Estate or Shared Interest in New Mexico
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that New Mexico statutes do not use; no New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law mentions it. The closest New Mexico situations are a life estate (for example, a parent who holds the home for life while the children own the remainder) and property owned with a spouse. No New Mexico statute says whether a lease signed by a life tenant survives the end of the life estate. The act says that, unless otherwise agreed, when an owner's interest ends, by sale, death or otherwise, the owner is relieved of lease obligations for events after the tenant gets written notice, and the owner's successor in interest is liable for the rental agreement; whether a remainder owner is a successor in interest bound by a lease the life tenant signed is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course: tell the tenant in writing what interest you hold, and either keep the lease term within your interest or have the remainder owners sign the lease too. Spouses: for community property, or separate property spouses own together, both spouses must sign a lease whose term with options exceeds five years or is indefinite, or it is void ("Long Leases, Married Owners and Recording in New Mexico"). Whatever your interest, give the tenant the owner and manager disclosure ("Management and Notices" clause).

title: Submetering and Reselling Utilities to Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no law requiring a lease statement when you submeter electricity, gas or water, or bill tenants for it. Furnishing utility service to your own tenants does not by itself make you a regulated public utility: the Public Utility Act excludes a person, not otherwise a utility, who furnishes a service or commodity only to itself, its employees or its tenants when it is not resold to or used by others, and similar exclusions cover electricity sold to tenants from a self-source generation resource serving a large qualified microgrid (one capable of generating at least twenty megawatts) or from an on-site renewable distributed generation facility. That is one reading of the statutes, and billing tenants for submetered service may itself be a resale. The cautious course is to bill no more than the actual cost and to ask the commission before running a profit-making resale. Gas piped from one master meter is different: a gas system at an apartment complex or similar property that buys metered gas and resells it to the units, whether by meter or through the rent, is a "master meter" system under the Pipeline Safety Act, and its operator falls under the commission's pipeline safety program, with an annual fee of up to $100 per master meter. For the pipeline safety rules themselves (federal rules and the commission's own part), ask the commission's pipeline safety bureau before you operate one. What New Mexico gives a tenant in multi-unit housing is records on request: the unit's own utility bill if each unit is separately metered, the apartment's utility bill if the unit is submetered, the common-area bills being apportioned and your calculations (see "Utility Billing Rights in New Mexico" and the optional clause "Utility Bills and Allocation"). Any utility charge you bill a tenant must be stated in the lease ("Fees and Charges" clause). New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the Public Regulation Commission's residential, electric and water service rules 17.5.410, 17.9.560, 17.9.570, 17.9.572 and 17.12.760 NMAC), contain nothing that requires a submetering disclosure in the lease.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Costs Among Tenants in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico lets you pass shared or submetered utility costs on to tenants, but it does not set a formula. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects (including the Public Regulation Commission's utility service rules), makes unenforceable a term requiring a tenant to pay for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit, or regulates how gas or electricity may be priced into rent. Three rules apply. First, in multi-unit housing where common-area utility bills are apportioned among units and passed on to tenants, each tenant may ask for copies of all the bills being apportioned, and the calculations you use to apportion common-area and submetered costs must be made available to any tenant on request. Second, the share of common-area cost that would fall on an empty unit if it were occupied may not be allocated to the remaining tenants; you absorb it. Third, every utility charge you bill must be stated in the lease, so state the utilities billed and the method (for example, by submeter reading, or by square footage or number of occupants) in the Fees and Charges clause; you may charge up to $5 per monthly request for copies only if the lease includes that fee ("Utility Bills and Allocation" clause). In a mobile home park, the written rental agreement must also disclose all charges to the tenant other than rent, and a park that provides utility services may add only a reasonable administrative fee for doing so, stated in the rental agreement, with 60 days of written notice before any increase. The cautious course is to bill no more than the actual cost of the service. See "Utility Billing Rights in New Mexico" for the tenant's records rights and "Submetering and Reselling Utilities to Tenants in New Mexico" on whether billing tenants makes you a utility.

title: No Shutoff of Submetered or Landlord-Billed Utilities in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no procedure that lets a landlord interrupt electricity, gas or water it submeters or bills to a tenant because the tenant has not paid. Instead, except after abandonment or surrender, you (and anyone acting for you) may not knowingly exclude or try to remove a tenant without a court order by interfering with services or normal and necessary utilities to the unit, including electricity, gas, hot or cold water, plumbing, heat or telephone service. The statute does not make you pay the tenant's utility charges or prevent interruptions that result from the tenant's own nonpayment to the utility, but New Mexico's Court of Appeals held that this does not let an owner direct a utility to shut off water for unpaid water charges, and that a judgment and writ for possession are not a court order allowing it before the writ is carried out. If you shut off or diminish a service in violation of this rule, the tenant may abate all of the rent for each day it happens, recover two times the monthly rent and damages, and regain possession or end the lease. So do not disconnect, switch off or ask a provider to cut a submetered or landlord-billed utility for nonpayment; collect the charge as an unpaid lease charge, including from the deposit at the end of the tenancy. You may interrupt service temporarily while making legitimate repairs or inspections, giving the notice of entry the law requires. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects (including the Public Regulation Commission's utility service rules), sets a separate interruption regime for landlord-submetered service. See "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico".

title: Utility Disconnection Protections for New Mexico Tenants
bodyText: New Mexico limits when a regulated gas or electric utility (including a rural electric cooperative) may cut off a residential customer for nonpayment. These rules protect whoever holds the account, which is usually your tenant; they don't give you any power to shut service off (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico"). The customer has at least 20 days from the bill to pay before it is delinquent, and at least 15 more days before disconnection. The utility must first send a written 15-day notice in English and Spanish, and contact the customer again at least two days before the shutoff date. Disconnection may happen only from 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday through Thursday, and not within 24 hours before a weekend or holiday unless the utility's office is open to take payment and can restore service. From November 15 through March 15, a customer who qualifies for low-income home energy assistance (LIHEAP) and has no past-due charges on November 15, or is keeping up a payment agreement, may not be disconnected for nonpayment; other residential customers get added notice and assistance steps in that period. This is a winter moratorium for qualifying customers, not a general one. Service may not be cut off to a home where a seriously or chronically ill person lives if the account holder can't pay and a medical professional's certificate (with the rule's financial certification) reaches the utility in time. A utility also may not cut off a new customer for a previous occupant's unpaid bill unless a court has made the new customer liable or the previous occupant still lives there. During a governor's public health or other emergency order, the Public Regulation Commission may order regulated electric and water utilities to stop disconnections for nonpayment; it is not automatic (check the gas utilities' rule separately). No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects, bars disconnection during a storm or extreme-weather event as such. City-owned utilities are outside the commission's rules unless the city has opted in; a municipality may stop water service after charges go unpaid for 30 days. The regulated water utilities have their own customer service rules; check them.

title: Third-Party Notice of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's Public Regulation Commission requires every regulated gas and electric utility (including rural electric cooperatives) to offer residential customers a third-party notification program. A customer who asks in writing may name a specific person, organization or government agency that is ready, willing and able to help pay the customer's utility bills; the utility then may not disconnect that customer for nonpayment without contacting the named person at least 15 days before the shutoff and finding that the person has not committed to help pay within a reasonable time. The program is open to every residential customer, not only older or dependent customers, but it is built for someone who will help pay: a landlord who will not help is not the designee the rule describes, and whether a utility will accept such a landlord as the designee is not settled by New Mexico's statutes or the commission's rules.

Separately, a utility must give copies of a customer's records that relate to a matter in dispute, or for good cause, to any person the customer authorizes in writing.

No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects, lets an owner authorize a utility on its own to tell it of a tenant's pending disconnection, or requires the utility to copy shutoff notices to a landlord. The lease may still ask the tenant to list you as a contact and sign the provider's form, as long as it does not make you liable for the tenant's charges and does not require the provider to act: see the optional clause "Authorization for Utility Notices to Landlord".

These rules don't cover city-owned utilities, and the regulated water utilities have their own customer service rules.

title: Utility Accounts in the Landlord's Name in New Mexico
bodyText:
When a utility account for a rental is in your name, you are the utility's customer and you owe the bill. The Public Regulation Commission's residential protections (notice periods, winter moratorium, medical certification) are written for a customer who is liable for service for that person's own household, so whether they cover your account for a tenant's unit is not settled by New Mexico's statutes or the commission's rules; plan as if the utility may cut off your account after its ordinary notice.

If the service is one you must supply (running water, a reasonable amount of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, unless the building isn't required by law to have them or the heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection) or one the lease says you provide, letting it lapse is your breach. The tenant may then give you written notice. If the lapse is a material breach of the lease or materially affects health and safety, the notice may end the lease on a date at least seven days after you receive it unless you make a reasonable attempt to fix it within seven days. Instead, if you don't fix it within seven days of the notice, the tenant may abate one-third of the daily rent for each day from the date of the notice until it is fixed (all of it for days the unit is uninhabitable and the tenant stays out). For a material breach the tenant may also sue for damages and an injunction.

Letting service lapse to force a tenant out is barred self-help: the tenant may abate all rent for each affected day and recover two times the monthly rent and damages ("No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico").

A utility may not cut off a tenant's own account for a previous occupant's bill (unless a court has made the tenant liable or that occupant still lives there) or a bill the tenant guaranteed. For city-owned utilities, charges are your personal debt and a lien on the property unless you notify the city in writing, before the tenant's charges begin and naming the rental property's location, that you won't be responsible ("Municipal Utility Charges as a Lien on Rentals").

No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects, lets tenants pay a landlord's utility bill and deduct it from rent, lets tenants seek a receiver when the landlord doesn't pay a utility, sets liquidated damages for failing to identify tenants, or requires the utility or a master-meter owner to notify each unit before a building-wide shutoff.

title: Putting Utilities in the Tenant's Name in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, sets a deadline for a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's name, or lets you cut off a utility left in your name.

So the lease is the whole instrument: use the Transfer of Utility Accounts clause, which requires the tenant to open or transfer the accounts by a date you set and to reimburse what the provider actually charged while an account stays in your name. List that reimbursement in the Fees and Charges clause too, since every charge you bill must be in the lease; and don't add a late fee to it, because late fees may be charged only on rent.

Never shut off, interrupt or ask a provider to cut a service because the tenant hasn't transferred it or paid you back; that is barred self-help ("No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico").

Two utility rules help the tenant transfer: a regulated electric utility may not refuse a new customer because a previous occupant owes it money unless that occupant still lives there, and a regulated gas or electric utility may not cut off a residential customer for a previous occupant's debt unless a court has made the new customer liable or the previous occupant still lives there. For city-owned utilities, tell the city in writing, before the tenant's charges begin, that you won't be responsible, or the charges become your debt and a lien on the property ("Municipal Utility Charges as a Lien on Rentals").

A tenant deployed or on temporary duty with the armed forces, reserves or New Mexico National Guard for more than 30 days may suspend regulated utilities in the tenant's own name if, among other conditions, the lease does not preclude it and no one will be staying in the home; the Utility Service Continuity clause does preclude interrupting water, gas, electricity, sewer and trash.

No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law lets a court in a protective-order case move a utility account between household members.

title: Utility Allowances and Rebilling Limits in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, caps what you may charge a tenant for a utility you rebill, sets a penalty for charging more than the utility billed, or bars passing master-metered electricity to tenants except through a fixed rent.

So a utility allowance with tenant-paid overage is a lease choice: use "Utility Allowance with Tenant-Paid Overage" clause, which caps your share at a monthly allowance and has the tenant reimburse the excess on a copy of the provider's bill.

Three New Mexico rules shape it.
- Every charge you bill must be stated in the lease, so put the allowance figure and the overage in the Fees and Charges clause too.
- A late fee may be charged only on rent, and rent used to figure a late fee may not include utilities, so don't attach a late fee to the overage.
- And the allowance shares cost only: where you must supply running water, hot water and heat, you still supply them and keep the equipment in repair.

The cautious course is to bill only the actual cost the provider charged; billing above cost could raise whether you are reselling utility service (see "Submetering and Reselling Utilities to Tenants in New Mexico").

Tenants in multi-unit housing may ask for copies of the bills and your calculations ("Utility Billing Rights in New Mexico").

In a mobile home park, the written rental agreement must disclose all charges other than rent, and a park that provides utility services may add only a reasonable administrative fee for doing so, stated in the rental agreement, with 60 days of written notice before any increase.

title: Meter-Attached Energy Charges in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, creates a meter conservation charge or an on-bill energy-efficiency repayment that stays with a meter and passes to the next customer, requires you to tell a new tenant about one, or regulates surcharges on submetered water. So there is nothing to disclose in the lease on this subject. New Mexico does allow energy and water improvements on a building to be financed by a special assessment on the property: a county program for commercial, industrial, agricultural and multifamily property with five or more dwelling units, and local renewable energy financing districts. Those are liens and charges on the property that you, as owner, pay; they are not utility meter charges, and New Mexico's statutes require no notice to tenants about them. If you pass any part of such a cost to tenants, it is a fee that must be stated in the lease ("Fees and Charges" clause), and the cautious course is not to bill it as a utility charge.

title: Tenant Energy Data and Benchmarking in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, requires building energy benchmarking, gives an owner a right to a tenant's energy usage data, or says a lease clause can authorize the utility to release it.

The Public Regulation Commission's rule for regulated gas and electric utilities lets a residential customer get copies of the customer's own records, and requires the utility to give copies of records relating to a matter in dispute, or for good cause, to any person the customer authorizes in writing. So a release reaches you only through the tenant's own written authorization, and the utility applies its own test to it.

An optional clause in which the tenant agrees to sign the utility's release, may withdraw it without breaching the lease, and you limit how you use the data is lawful in New Mexico: see "Energy Usage Data Authorization" clause.

Grid-modernization laws direct the commission to consider customers' access to their own usage information; they give owners nothing.

title: Government Shutdowns and Rent in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a federal or other government worker extra time to pay rent, or protection from eviction, during a government shutdown or furlough. Rent timing, late fees and nonpayment notices follow the ordinary New Mexico rules and your lease. You may agree to a payment plan or delay with an affected tenant in writing; if you do, say whether a late fee is waived for the period. Federal law may also apply.

title: Deposits and Unpaid Utilities in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico expressly lets you keep part of a tenant's deposit at the end of the tenancy for unpaid utilities, as well as unpaid rent, repair work and other legitimate damages, but never for normal wear and tear. The usual rules still apply: list each deduction, including any utility charge, in the itemized written statement you send with any balance within 30 days after the lease ends or the tenant leaves, whichever is later, or you lose the right to withhold anything ("Return of Security Deposit" clause, "Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit in New Mexico"). Keep utility charges out of rent: a late fee may be figured only on rent, and the rent used for that figure may not include utilities. If you collect a separate "utility deposit" from the tenant, treat it as part of the security deposit for the New Mexico limits and return rules, since the law defines a deposit as money the tenant gives you as a pledge to abide by the rental agreement (a reading, not a settled rule; see "New Mexico Security Deposit Limits"). A deposit the tenant pays a regulated gas or electric utility for the tenant's own account is between the tenant and the utility: the utility may require one only in listed cases, may not ask more than one-sixth of estimated annual billings, must pay interest, and must refund or credit it after 12 months if the customer has not been chronically delinquent. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects, otherwise regulates a landlord-held utility deposit.

title: No Utility Disclosure Form Required in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, requires a separate utility disclosure form or attachment to a residential lease. What New Mexico requires instead: every utility charge you bill must be stated in the lease itself, which the Fees and Charges clause does, and in multi-unit housing a tenant may ask for copies of the utility bills and your apportionment calculations ("Utility Billing Rights in New Mexico", "Utility Bills and Allocation" clause). In a mobile home park, the written rental agreement must disclose all charges other than rent, including any administrative fee the park charges for providing utility services. State in the lease which utilities you provide and which the tenant pays ("Utilities Paid by Landlord" clause, "Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause); no particular form is required.

title: Which Fire and Building Codes Apply to New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: Your duty under New Mexico's landlord-tenant law is to substantially comply with the applicable housing, building, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety. Which fire and building codes apply depends on the building. The State Fire Marshal's fire code covers public occupancies, which include residential buildings with four or more family units. It adopts the 2021 International Fire Code with state amendments, does not apply to detached one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses of three stories or less with a separate means of egress, built to the state residential code unless they are used as commercial properties, and lets cities and counties adopt stricter requirements. An existing building generally must meet the fire requirements in place when it was built, not today's code; a change of occupancy brings it up to the current code, and a fire official who finds an immediate hazard can give the owner time to comply and then order the facility out of service. For construction and alteration, the state building codes are the 2021 International Building Code (apartment buildings and other buildings) and the 2021 International Residential Code (one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses), each with state amendments, plus the 2021 International Existing Building Code for work on existing buildings other than those houses. The state codes delete the model codes' property maintenance references, so the state building codes adopt no statewide property maintenance code; local codes may have one. If the building has an elevator or other conveyance (except one inside a single-family dwelling), you as owner or lessee must register it, have it inspected every year by a state-certified inspector, keep a current certificate of operation and fix listed violations within 60 days. Check the specific fire safety requirements for your building (exits, alarms, extinguishers and the like) with the State Fire Marshal or your local fire and building officials. New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, contain nothing that imposes a separate statewide fire-escape duty on residential buildings.

title: Fire Sprinklers in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico does not require you to add fire sprinklers to an existing rental. For houses, the rule is set by statute: the state construction industries commission may not require residential fire sprinklers in detached one- and two-family dwellings or townhouses of three stories or less with a separate means of egress, and the state residential building code says sprinklers are not required in them. For apartment buildings and other buildings under the state commercial building code, whether new construction needs sprinklers is set by the sprinkler section of the 2021 International Building Code that the state adopts (the state deletes that section's exception); ask the building official for a particular project. An existing building generally must meet the fire requirements in place when it was built; work that changes the occupancy, or that replaces, repairs or alters an existing fire protection system, brings it under the current fire code, and a fire official may order a facility that is an immediate hazard out of service after a period to comply. Sprinkler systems must be installed and serviced by licensed contractors holding the State Fire Marshal's certificate of fitness, and a regulated water utility may not charge you extra standby charges because the building has sprinklers. New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, contain nothing that sets a stand-alone high-rise sprinkler mandate or a retrofit deadline. Cities and counties may adopt stricter fire protection requirements for buildings the state fire code covers.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the State Fire Marshal's fire code or the state building codes), requires you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has fire sprinklers, or offers owners a grant, loan or tax credit for a voluntary sprinkler retrofit. For the model fire and building codes those rules adopt and for local ordinances, check with the local fire official if your building is a high-rise or otherwise unusual. You may still describe the building's fire protection in the lease if you wish, as long as the description is accurate. See "Fire Sprinklers in New Mexico Rentals" for when sprinklers are required.

title: Heat in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText:
You must supply reasonable heat, and a reasonable amount of hot water at all times, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or the unit is built so that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection (for example, a furnace on the tenant's own gas meter). Even then, you must keep heating facilities and appliances you supply, or are required to supply, in good and safe working order.

The heat duty can be shifted to the tenant only for a single family residence, by a written agreement made for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your duties; for any other unit the tenant may agree, in a separate signed writing for consideration, made in good faith and not to evade your duties, only to specified repairs or maintenance tasks, not to supplying heat. Either way your own duties remain, and the tenant's failure to do the work is not a ground for eviction.

If heat fails, the tenant may give written notice and, if it isn't fixed within seven days of the notice, abate one-third of the daily rent for each day from the date of the notice until it is fixed (all of it for days the unit is uninhabitable and the tenant stays out), or instead give notice ending the lease on a date at least seven days later unless you make a reasonable attempt to fix it within seven days, and may sue for damages; deliberately cutting heat to force a tenant out is barred self-help.

New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, contain nothing that sets a minimum indoor temperature or a heating season for rentals, or requires state inspection certificates for apartment boilers (a city may inspect and regulate steam boilers). Heating requirements for construction are in the residential and commercial building codes, which adopt model code sections, and in the state mechanical code; local housing codes may set a temperature.

See "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico" and, for a tenant who controls the thermostat, the optional "Heat and Freeze Protection" clause.

title: Water Heater Temperature in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects (including the state building and energy codes), requires you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in, or at any other time. The rules that would most likely address water heater and fixture temperatures are in the New Mexico Plumbing Code (14.8.2 NMAC) and the model codes it adopts, which may set a limit; ask the local plumbing inspector or the Construction Industries Division if you are installing or replacing a water heater. Your general duty stands: supply a reasonable amount of hot water at all times (unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for it, or the hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection) and keep a water heater you supply, or are required to supply, in good and safe working order ("Heat in New Mexico Rentals", "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). The cautious course is to check the setting at each turnover and keep it at a safe temperature.

title: Window Guards and Security Bars in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, requires you to install child window guards, give tenants a window-guard notice in the lease, or disclose a release mechanism on security bars. For new construction and alterations, the state residential building code adopts the 2021 International Residential Code's section on guards and window fall protection, amended only to require guards on open-sided walking surfaces more than 30 inches above the floor or grade below, and its emergency escape and rescue opening rules; when a bedroom wall is opened for alterations or repairs and the framing next to the window is exposed, the replacement window must meet the escape-opening rule. For a building project, the model code text (window sill heights, opening-control devices, escape-opening size, and how bars or grilles may cover an escape window) also applies; ask the building official. In any building, keep the premises safe and comply with codes materially affecting health and safety. The cautious course: never install bars or grilles over a bedroom or other escape window unless they open from inside without a key, tool or special knowledge.

title: Common-Area Lighting in New Mexico
bodyText:
You must keep the common areas of the premises in a safe condition and comply with codes materially affecting health and safety, but New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, contain nothing that sets a specific lighting standard for hallways, stairways, entrances or parking areas of a rental.

Lighting requirements for construction are in the model building codes the state adopts, and local codes may set more; adequate lighting is the cautious way to meet the safe-condition duty.

New Mexico does not bar wiring common-area lights to a tenant's own electric service, and no rule limits it to certain buildings or to new tenancies; if you do it, say so in the lease ("Common-Area Lighting on Tenant's Meter" clause), keep maintaining the fixtures yourself, and remember that in multi-unit housing tenants may ask for copies of any common-area utility bills whose costs are passed on to them ("Utility Billing Rights in New Mexico").

title: No Radiator Cover Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, requires steam radiator covers or a lease rider about them. If your building has radiators or other heating equipment you supply or are required to supply, keep it in good and safe working order and keep the premises safe; covers or guards on hot surfaces are a sensible precaution, especially where children live.

title: No Balcony Inspection Law in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, requires periodic inspection of balconies, decks, stairways or other exterior elevated elements of a rental, or reports on them. For construction and alterations, the state residential code requires guards on open-sided walking surfaces more than 30 inches above the floor or grade below, and the commercial and existing-building codes adopt model code provisions, so check those model codes. Your ongoing duty is general: make repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a safe condition, keep common areas safe, and substantially comply with codes materially affecting health and safety. The cautious course is to inspect balconies and decks yourself, or have them inspected, at reasonable intervals and after any sign of rot, rust or loosening.

title: Pool Safety Rules for New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico has no landlord-tenant pool rule: no statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects, requires a pool safety notice in a lease or makes a residential landlord fence a pool as such. Two sets of rules may still reach your pool. First, for pools, spas and hot tubs built at a one- or two-family dwelling under the state residential code (construction permitted on or after December 14, 2023), the code requires a barrier at least 48 inches high around an outdoor pool, with limits on openings, self-closing and self-latching pedestrian gates opening away from the pool, and, where a house wall forms part of the barrier, a powered safety cover, door alarms or another approved equal protection; a spa or hot tub with a compliant safety cover is exempt. Pools at apartment buildings and other buildings under the commercial code follow the 2021 International Building Code's swimming pool provisions. Second, the Environment Department regulates the sanitation of public swimming pools, public spas and other public water recreation facilities and the Environmental Improvement Board may assess their owners or operators an annual fee of up to $150. Whether a pool at an apartment complex or rental community is a public pool under those rules depends on the department's water recreation facility rules; ask the department before opening a shared pool to tenants. Keep any pool you provide, and its gates and fencing, in a safe condition.

title: When the Law Lets a Tenant End a New Mexico Lease Early
bodyText:
New Mexico gives a tenant no general right to end a lease early, but the Owner-Resident Relations Act lets a tenant end the rental agreement before its term runs out in these situations.
- (1) You fail to deliver possession when the lease says occupancy begins: rent abates in full until you do, and the tenant may end the agreement at once by written notice, and you must return all prepaid rent and deposits.
- (2) You materially fail to comply with the rental agreement, or fail to comply with the act in a way that materially affects health and safety: the tenant may give you a written notice stating that the agreement will end on a date at least 7 days after you receive it unless you make a reasonable attempt to remedy the breach within 7 days. This right does not arise if the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent caused the condition by a deliberate or negligent act or omission.
- (3) Fire or another casualty damages the unit so that the tenant's enjoyment of it is substantially impaired: the tenant may move out and notify you in writing within 7 days, and the agreement ends on the move-out date (see "Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico").
- (4) You enter unlawfully, enter lawfully in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that unreasonably harass the tenant.
- (5) You lock the tenant out, cut off utilities or services, remove belongings or otherwise try to remove the tenant without a court order (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico").

Your own statutory early-termination right, apart from the notices for breach (see "Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent", "Seven-Day Notice for Other Lease Breaches", "Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation"), is narrow: if the tenant refuses to allow lawful access, you may terminate the agreement or go to court to compel access.

New Mexico has no state statute letting a tenant end a lease early because of domestic violence or military service (see "No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right in New Mexico" and "Servicemember Tenants in New Mexico"; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act may apply).

No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a tenant a specific right to end a lease because the landlord made a fraudulent misrepresentation, makes a landlord forfeit rent or other money for leaving a prescribed statement out of the lease, or requires the lease to list these termination rights. The act does say that the general law of fraud, misrepresentation, mistake and duress supplements it, so a tenant misled into signing may still have remedies under general contract law; only case law could say what they are.

Cautious course: describe the unit, its condition and its charges accurately in writing, and if a tenant asks to leave because of something you misstated, consider a written release. A lease cannot take any of these rights away.

title: No Illness, Age or Care-Facility Lease Termination Right in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law lets a tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or a move into a nursing home, assisted living or other long-term care, and none says that a tenancy ends when a party becomes incapable of contracting. The Owner-Resident Relations Act says that the general law on capacity to contract supplements it, so whether a lease signed by a person who lacked capacity binds that person is a question for general contract law and case law. What applies instead: a fixed-term lease runs to its end unless you agree to release the tenant or another termination right applies (see "When the Law Lets a Tenant End a New Mexico Lease Early"); a month-to-month tenancy can be ended by either side on written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date, and a week-to-week tenancy on at least 7 days' written notice (see "Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause). A tenant's death does not end the lease by statute; the act's procedure for a sole tenant's belongings is in "When a Tenant Dies in New Mexico". Cautious course: if a tenant, a family member or a guardian asks to end the lease because the tenant needs care, deal through a person with legal authority to act for the tenant (for example, an agent under a power of attorney or a court-appointed guardian), consider a written release, and remember that you must try to re-rent and cannot simply collect rent for the rest of the term (see "Abandonment and Re-renting in New Mexico"). Disability discrimination rules still apply (see "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act"); federal law may also apply.

title: No Disaster or Environmental-Event Termination Rule in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives you or the tenant a special right to end a lease because of a natural disaster, wildfire, flood, contamination, an environmental hazard or a declared emergency. What New Mexico does have is the fire-or-casualty rule: if the unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty so that the tenant's enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may move out and give written notice within 7 days to end the lease as of the move-out date, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the unusable part and pay reduced rent (see "Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico"). The statute does not define casualty; physical damage from a flood, wildfire or similar event can be read as a casualty, but only case law could settle it. If an event leaves the unit in breach of your repair duties, the tenant's notice-and-termination and rent-abatement remedies also apply (see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico"). The statute gives you no termination right of your own. The library's optional "Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty" clause lets you end the lease after damage that substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment and leaves no part lawfully usable during repairs, and it covers damage from any casualty. The library does not offer a broader clause letting you end the lease because of an event that leaves the unit usable (for example, a nearby evacuation order or smoke): a court may limit a lease term it finds inequitable when made, and no lease term may take away the tenant's own rights. You may add such a clause yourself, ideally drafted by a New Mexico lawyer.

title: Your Remedies When a New Mexico Lease Ends
bodyText: When a New Mexico lease ends because of the tenant's breach or your proper notice, you are entitled to possession and may also have a claim for rent and a separate claim for damages for breach of the lease. Possession: you file a petition for restitution (see "How Evictions Work in New Mexico"). The petition may include your other claims relating to the residency, such as unpaid rent and damages, but if either side asks in writing, those other claims are answered and tried separately from possession. A judgment for possession declares the lease forfeited and leads to a writ setting a move-out date 3 to 7 days after judgment. Damages without ending the lease: you can recover damages, or get an injunction or other relief, for any breach of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties, without first terminating. Limits on what you collect: you must take reasonable steps to reduce your loss; after an abandonment you may try to re-rent at a fair rental, and a new tenancy that starts before the old lease would have ended ends the old lease from that date (see "Abandonment and Re-renting in New Mexico"). In a nonpayment case the tenant may counterclaim but remains responsible for the rent while in possession. Attorney's fees go to the prevailing party in a suit to enforce the lease or the act (see "Attorney Fees in New Mexico Landlord-Tenant Cases"). Acceleration: New Mexico's statutes and court rules contain nothing that allows or forbids a lease term making all rent for the rest of the term due at once on default. Because of the duty to mitigate and a court's power to limit lease terms that were inequitable when made, the cautious course is to claim rent as it falls due, less what you receive from re-renting, and not to rely on an acceleration clause. Which court: a magistrate court hears civil actions where the amount claimed is $10,000 or less, not counting interest and costs, and a metropolitan court has the same civil limit; larger claims go to district court. New Mexico has no separate small claims court, although a few older statutes still mention one. In metropolitan court, possession cases under the act are not recorded, and an appeal goes to district court for a new trial (it must be filed within 15 days after judgment).

title: No Hardship Delay of Evictions in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule lets a court delay or stay an eviction because moving out would be a hardship for the tenant (for example, illness, a school year or winter), and none provides a statewide eviction moratorium. The compilation's annotations do summarize a 1992 Supreme Court decision allowing equitable principles to prevent the eviction of a qualified low-income public-housing tenant held liable for back rent (see "Undoing a Lease Forfeiture After Judgment in New Mexico"); whether a court may delay or refuse an eviction on equitable hardship grounds in other cases is case law, so plan on the statutory timetable. The timing rules are fixed: trial is set 7 to 10 days after the summons is served, the court may continue the hearing for up to 7 days for good cause, and the writ restores possession on a date 3 to 7 days after judgment (see "How Evictions Work in New Mexico"). The only stay the act provides is on appeal: an appeal by the tenant stops the writ only if, within 5 days after filing the notice of appeal, the tenant pays you or a professional escrow agent the rent for the rest of the current rental period and then keeps paying the monthly rent when due; if a payment is missed you may serve a 3-day notice, and if it is still not paid the court holds a hearing within 10 days after it is notified of the failure to pay and lifts the stay unless the tenant shows a legal justification (see "Holdover Tenants in New Mexico"). The court may also require a deposit or bond to stay the money part of a judgment. The Supreme Court's pandemic-era stay of writs for nonpayment and its eviction diversion program are over for new cases, although some of their forms remain published. New Mexico law bars local rent control, but New Mexico's statutes do not bar a county or city from adopting an eviction moratorium. Federal law, such as the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act for a tenant in military service, may also delay a case.

title: Serving Eviction Papers on a New Mexico Tenant
bodyText: Who must be served: the summons and a copy of your petition must be served on each tenant you name, by the methods in the court's rules (see "How Evictions Work in New Mexico"). In magistrate and metropolitan court, for a tenant who is an individual, that means handing the papers to the tenant (a refusal to take them still counts); if the tenant is absent, leaving them with someone over 15 who lives at the tenant's home; and only if no one is available or willing, posting them in the most public part of the premises and also mailing copies to the tenant's last known mailing address. District court has no posting method: after trying personal delivery or signed-receipt mail, you may leave the papers with someone over 15 who lives at the tenant's home and also mail a copy to the tenant's last known mailing address, and only if that fails deliver them to the person in charge at the tenant's workplace and mail copies; any other method needs a court order. The compilation's annotation summarizes a 2021 Court of Appeals decision holding that posting without the mailing was not valid service, so the possession judgment was void. Metropolitan and district court rules also allow service by mail or courier if the tenant, or a person authorized by appointment or by law to accept service for the tenant, signs the receipt; magistrate court rules allow mail service only if the tenant signs and returns an acknowledgment. Naming an agent in the lease: New Mexico's statutes and court rules contain nothing that lets a lease name a person to accept eviction papers for the tenant, and the magistrate rule for serving an individual does not mention an agent at all. Whether a lease clause would make someone a person authorized by appointment is unsettled, so this library does not offer one; serve the tenant by the rule's methods. You may add your own clause, but don't rely on it alone. Your side: the lease or a written disclosure must name a person authorized to accept service of process and notices for you (see "Management and Notices" clause); an owner who lives out of state may also file a designation of a New Mexico agent with the Secretary of State (see "Out-of-State Owners in New Mexico"). Tenants in the address confidentiality program: the Secretary of State accepts service of process, notices and demands for a person certified in New Mexico's confidential substitute address program (for survivors of domestic violence and others) and forwards them, and service through the Secretary of State is complete 3 days after it is accepted. If a tenant gives you a program card, serve as the rules require at the unit and also serve through the Secretary of State, and ask the court clerk how to keep the tenant's address out of the public file; the program statute does not say how it fits with a petition that must describe the premises.

title: No Possession Bonds for New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule provides a bond that a tenant posts to guarantee giving up possession at the end of the term, a bond with a confessed judgment for possession, or any other possession bond in a residential tenancy. Don't put a confession of judgment or a power to confess judgment in a lease: New Mexico voids such provisions in a written contract to pay money when they are given before a claim arises, and procuring one is a misdemeanor (see "Confession of Judgment in a New Mexico Lease" and "Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico"). The bonds and deposits that do exist are court-procedure ones on appeal. If the tenant appeals a possession judgment, the writ is stayed only while the tenant pays the rent to you or a professional escrow agent as the act requires (see "No Hardship Delay of Evictions in New Mexico" and "Holdover Tenants in New Mexico"); to stay a money judgment, the trial court may require the appellant to deposit the judgment and costs or give a supersedeas bond, and any bond or deposit is not refundable while the appeal is pending. The court sets these amounts in its judgment or a separate order. The forcible-entry bond rules do not apply to your action against a residential tenant. To secure the tenant's performance, use the security deposit within New Mexico's limits (see "New Mexico Security Deposit Limits") and, if you need more, a guarantor.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction in New Mexico
bodyText: Before the notice runs out: if you give a 3-day notice for unpaid rent and the tenant tenders the full amount due, in the way the notice states, before the 3 days expire, you cannot bring an eviction for that nonpayment (see "Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent"). The court form for that notice lists the payment methods you will accept (cash, money order, cashier's or certified check, personal check), and the statute measures the tender against the manner your notice states. After the notice runs out: no New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule gives a tenant a general right to stop an eviction by paying everything owed later, for example up to a set time before the writ is carried out, and none bars the writ once a money judgment is paid. The one exception: when the dispute is over the amount owed because the tenant abated rent under the act or you applied rent to damages, a judgment in your favor must condition the writ on the tenant's right to pay within 3 days; if the tenant pays the judgment in that time, the writ is dismissed (see "Undoing a Lease Forfeiture After Judgment in New Mexico" and "Applying Rent Payments in New Mexico"). The compilation's annotations summarize a 1992 Supreme Court decision allowing equitable principles to prevent the eviction of a qualified low-income public-housing tenant held liable for back rent; how far that reaches is for the courts. Partial payments and third-party payments: none of the statutes, constitutional provisions, session laws or court rules named above prescribes words you must use to accept a partial payment without waiving the default, requires you to accept payment from a charity, government program or other third party, or limits the payment methods you may require for such payments (the only third-party payor rule concerns rent abatement for subsidized tenants). Cautious course: if you accept partial rent and still intend to proceed, say so in writing when you accept it (see "Accepting Late or Partial Rent in New Mexico"), and if you accept full payment of what the notice demanded, treat the nonpayment as cured. Accepting rental assistance paid for the tenant is usually the practical course.

title: Undoing a Lease Forfeiture After Judgment in New Mexico
bodyText: When you win a possession case, the court declares the rental agreement forfeited and issues a writ restoring possession to you on a date 3 to 7 days after judgment. New Mexico's statutes, constitution, 2025-2026 session laws and court rules contain nothing that gives a tenant a general right to undo that forfeiture afterward by paying what is owed. The act has three narrower rules. (1) Before the 3-day nonpayment notice expires, full tender in the manner the notice states bars the eviction (see "Paying to Stop an Eviction in New Mexico"). (2) If the tenant disputes the amount owed because the tenant abated rent under the act, or because you applied rent payments to damages, a judgment for you must condition the writ on the tenant's right to pay the judgment within 3 days; if the tenant pays in time the writ is dismissed, and if not you may have the writ carried out without a further order (see "Applying Rent Payments in New Mexico"). (3) The tenant may raise any legal or equitable defense at trial. The compilation's annotations summarize a 1992 Supreme Court decision that equitable principles may be applied to prevent the eviction of a qualified low-income public-housing tenant held liable for back rent, and that the act does not require a writ whenever a court enters a money judgment for back rent; how far equity reaches in a private tenancy is case law. Cautious course: decide before trial whether you want possession or only the money; if the tenant offers full payment after judgment and you accept it, put in writing whether you are reinstating the tenancy or still enforcing the writ.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments and Evictions in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule makes a late Social Security check, other government benefit, or housing voucher or subsidy payment a defense to an eviction for nonpayment, or requires the court to continue the case or reinstate the tenancy when such a payment is delayed. The nonpayment rules apply as written: you may give a 3-day notice once rent is unpaid when due, and full payment in the way the notice states before the 3 days run out bars the eviction (see "Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent" and "Paying to Stop an Eviction in New Mexico"). The court may continue a possession hearing for up to 7 days for good cause. The act does have rules for subsidized tenants in two places: a rent abatement is measured on the total monthly rent, not only the tenant's share, and either a third-party payor or the tenant may use the abatement remedy; and a subsidized tenant who appeals and wants to stop the writ pays no more than the rent the tenant actually pays. The compilation's annotation summarizes a 2013 Court of Appeals decision holding that a tenant whose rent was late because public assistance checks arrived after the due date, and who paid when they came, had not committed a serious violation of a federal Section 8 lease. The compilation's annotations also summarize a 1992 Supreme Court decision allowing equitable principles to prevent the eviction of a qualified low-income public-housing tenant held liable for back rent. Federal program rules may also apply to a subsidized unit. Cautious course: if you know a tenant's rent depends on a benefit or program payment that is late, document it, consider waiting or agreeing to a short payment plan in writing, and don't serve a notice that you would struggle to defend under a federal lease.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the Public Regulation Commission's utility customer rule, 17.5.410 NMAC), requires a tenant to warn you before moving out of, or leaving empty, a unit during cold weather, or sets any cold-weather rule for vacating. What New Mexico does have: if your lease requires the tenant to tell you about an absence of more than 7 days and the tenant willfully fails to, you may recover the damages that result; during any absence of more than 7 days you may enter the unit at times reasonably necessary; and a tenant who has been absent more than 7 days without notice after rent became delinquent has abandoned the unit, so you may take possession (see "Abandonment and Re-renting in New Mexico"). The library's "Notice of Extended Absence" clause uses that rule; it is how to ask for notice before a winter absence so you can protect pipes. Two cold-weather rules exist but are not about vacating: a utility may not cut off a qualifying low-income residential customer for nonpayment during the heating season, and in a mobile home park eviction the persons with a property interest in the home are responsible for protecting it from freezing (the park landlord and the sheriff may agree in writing to delay removal for weather).

title: Your Duties While a Notice to Vacate Is Pending in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule sets special rules for the period while a notice to vacate is running, such as a ban on alterations that make the unit unlivable during that time. The general rules already cover it, because the lease and your duties stay in force until the notice period ends: (1) you may not make the unit inaccessible or uninhabitable, remove appliances or fixtures except for necessary and legitimate repairs, or cut services to push the tenant out; temporary interference while you make legitimate repairs or inspections the act allows is permitted (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico"); (2) you must keep making the repairs the act requires (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"); (3) against a tenant who is complying with the lease and the act, you may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten a possession case (treat a notice to vacate as such a threat) in retaliation for protected acts in the previous six months, such as a code complaint or a written repair request (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"); (4) in a condominium conversion, tenants get at least 60 days' notice before they must vacate, and a lease term ending the lease early just because of the conversion is unenforceable (see "Condominium Conversion Notice in New Mexico"). What the notice itself must say: use the court's 30-day notice form for a month-to-month tenancy (or the one-week version for week-to-week), give it at least 30 days before the periodic rental date, and keep it unconditional. The compilation's annotations summarize a 1981 Supreme Court decision holding that a notice must be definite enough to tell the tenant you want them to leave, that a notice to quit coupled with an option to stay at a higher rent does not end the tenancy, and that a notice given too late takes effect on the next rental date (see "Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause). If you want a higher rent instead, give a rent-increase notice (see "Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico"). Cautious course: while a notice is pending, keep services and repairs going, schedule renovation for after the tenant leaves, and don't change the rent or other terms.

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants in New Mexico
bodyText: Age of majority: in New Mexico a person is an adult for all purposes at 18. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule lets a person under 18 make a binding lease simply because they are 18 to 20 or otherwise near adulthood, and none bars you from filing a possession case against a minor. Signing a lease with a minor: the Owner-Resident Relations Act leaves capacity to contract to general law, and only case law settles how far a minor's lease binds the minor. The exception the statutes do settle is an emancipated minor: a person 16 or older who is validly married (even if the marriage has ended), is on active duty in the U.S. armed forces, or has a court declaration of emancipation may be treated as an adult for purposes such as making a binding contract, suing and being sued, establishing a residence and buying or selling real property. Cautious course: lease to a minor only if the minor is emancipated (ask for proof), or have a parent or other adult sign as a tenant or guarantor. Who to name in a possession case: name the tenants, that is, the persons entitled under the lease to occupy the unit. Minor children living with an adult tenant are household members, not tenants; the court's writ directs the sheriff to remove the named defendants and restore possession of the premises to you. If a defendant is a minor: the papers are served on the minor's guardian or conservator if there is one; otherwise, in magistrate and metropolitan court, on the minor and also on the adult the minor lives with, and in district court on each person who has legal authority over the minor (or, if there is none, a person the court designates). A minor defends through a guardian or other representative, a next friend or a guardian ad litem the court appoints, and a parent who is not a lawyer may not act as the minor's attorney. Ask the court clerk before filing so the case is not delayed.

title: No-Trespass Notices at New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: You can use New Mexico's criminal trespass law against a person who is not your tenant, such as a former occupant who never had a lease, a person causing trouble on the grounds, or someone you have banned from the property. It is a misdemeanor to knowingly enter or remain on another's unposted land knowing that the owner or occupant has denied or withdrawn consent, to enter and remain after being asked to leave, or to enter posted land without written permission from the owner or person in control. Posting must follow the statute: legible English signs of at least 144 square inches at each road or other way of access and along the boundaries (every 500 feet if the land is not fenced), naming who posted the property or who can grant permission. Separately, a person who enters without permission and damages buildings or other improvements owes the owner, lessee or person in lawful possession double the value of the damage. Limits: the statute names the owner or the occupant as the person whose consent counts, and your tenant is the occupant of the unit. No New Mexico statute says whether you may bar your tenant's guest from the common areas a tenant must use to reach the unit, or gives a guest or invitee a stated defense; only case law could settle that.
