You may not charge or bar guests in a reasonable number for a reasonable time (see "No Guest Fees in New Mexico"). Trespass is never a way to remove your tenant or anyone entitled to occupy under the lease: they must be removed through notice and a court case (see "Removing Unauthorized Occupants in New Mexico" and "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico"). Cautious course: give the person a dated written no-trespass notice that names the property and the areas covered, deliver it in front of a witness or by a method you can prove, keep a copy, and call law enforcement to enforce it; tell the tenant whose guest it concerns, and don't block access to the tenant's unit. Mobile home parks have their own rule for buyers of a home who have not been approved as residents (see "What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers").

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule requires you to tell a tenant, in the lease or in a separate notice, whether the unit is covered by or exempt from a good-cause or just-cause eviction law. New Mexico has no statewide good-cause eviction law, so there is nothing to disclose: a fixed-term lease ends on its end date, and a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy can be ended by the required written notice without stating a reason (see "No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in New Mexico", "When a Fixed-Term Lease Ends in New Mexico" and "Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause). Limits still apply: no raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening a possession case in retaliation against a tenant who is complying with the lease and the act, for protected acts within the previous six months (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"); the condominium-conversion notice and purchase offer (see "Condominium Conversion Notice in New Mexico"); and the statutory notices for ending a lease because of a breach (see "Three-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent", "Seven-Day Notice for Other Lease Breaches" and "Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation"). A tenancy under a federal program, such as a Housing Choice Voucher lease, may limit ending the tenancy during its term to good cause under the federal addendum (see "Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease").

title: Entity Landlords in New Mexico Eviction Courts
bodyText: Court rules, not a statute, decide who may appear for a corporation, LLC or partnership landlord in a New Mexico possession case. Magistrate and metropolitan court: in a case under the Owner-Resident Relations Act, a non-lawyer may appear, prosecute and defend if the appearance is by the owner (as the act defines it) or by the person authorized to manage the premises. A corporation or LLC whose shares or memberships are held by one person or a closely knit group of natural persons all active in the business may also appear through one of them who has been authorized, and a general partnership with fewer than ten partners, all natural persons, may appear through an authorized general partner. The Supreme Court's forms for authorizing such an appearance are Form 4-403 (corporation or LLC) and Form 4-404 (partnership). A non-lawyer who appears may not be paid a fee for doing so; a salaried property manager may appear as part of the job but may not charge extra for it. District court: New Mexico's court rules contain nothing that lets a non-lawyer appear for an entity, and the statute on practicing law bars practicing in any court except a magistrate court without admission to the bar. An appeal from metropolitan or magistrate court is a new trial in district court. Cautious course: in district court, and on any appeal, an entity landlord should appear through a New Mexico lawyer; in magistrate or metropolitan court, send the property manager named in your owner disclosure (see "Management and Notices" clause) or file the Supreme Court authorization form for a qualifying owner or partner, and bring the rental agreement and notice to the hearing. An individual owner may always appear in person. If the entity is organized outside New Mexico, check whether it must register before filing (see "Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law").

title: Deadlines for Suing Over a New Mexico Lease
bodyText: New Mexico has no limitation period written for landlord-tenant claims; the general statute of limitations applies. Claims founded on a written lease (unpaid rent, damages for breach of the lease): 6 years. Claims on an oral lease or an account: 4 years. Claims for injury to property (for example, damage to the unit) and for fraud: 4 years, but a claim for property damage or fraud does not accrue until the damage or fraud is discovered. Claims for injury to a person: 3 years. A suit on a New Mexico court judgment: within 14 years from the date of the judgment. Which period governs a claim based only on the Owner-Resident Relations Act rather than the lease (for example, a deposit or lockout claim) is not stated in the statute; only case law could settle it. Restarting the clock: a contract claim is revived by any partial or installment payment, or by a written, signed admission that the debt is unpaid or a written, signed new promise to pay, and the period then runs again from that date. Time the debtor spends outside New Mexico, or concealed within it, is not counted. Periods for a minor or incapacitated person are extended to one year after the incapacity ends. A tenant may still raise a time-barred claim as a setoff or counterclaim against your claim if it was not yet barred when your claim arose, but cannot recover more than your claim on it. Cautious course: sue for unpaid rent and damages promptly (a possession case may include them; see "Your Remedies When a New Mexico Lease Ends"), keep the lease and ledger for at least 6 years after the tenancy ends, and get any payment promise in writing and signed.

title: Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: These points come from all of New Mexico's statutes, constitution, 2025-2026 session laws and court rules, not only the Owner-Resident Relations Act. (1) Squatters: no special squatter-removal statute. A person who entered without your consent and refuses to leave after notice can be removed by a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action, and remaining after consent is denied can be criminal trespass; anyone who occupies under a rental agreement must be evicted through the act's process (see "Removing Unauthorized Occupants in New Mexico" and "No-Trespass Notices at New Mexico Rentals"). (2) Cash rent receipts: no general receipt duty, cash or otherwise; you must give a receipt for a screening fee and, during an eviction appeal, an immediate written receipt on demand for rent paid to you directly (see "Rent Receipts in New Mexico"). (3) Registration before eviction: no statewide landlord registration or rental license, and no rule that a landlord must be registered or licensed before bringing a possession case (see "No Statewide Landlord Registration in New Mexico"). (4) Entities from other states: a foreign corporation, LLC, limited partnership or limited liability partnership that transacts business in New Mexico without registering may not bring a lawsuit, including an eviction, in a New Mexico court until it registers; its leases stay valid and it may still defend a suit. For an LLC, owning property without more is not transacting business; whether renting it out is more is a case-law question, so register before you need to file (see "Out-of-State Owners in New Mexico"). (5) Business names: New Mexico's statutes contain nothing that requires you to file an assumed or trade name before renting under it, and none bars a suit for failing to; a name used to identify your services can be registered as a service mark under the Trademark Act, which is optional. A licensed real estate broker managing for others must use the trade name registered with the Real Estate Commission. (6) Service on an out-of-state owner: an owner outside New Mexico may file a designation of a New Mexico agent with the Secretary of State; without one, the tenant may serve the Secretary of State and must immediately send a copy to you by registered or certified mail, and your lease or disclosure must name a person to accept service and notices for you (see "Out-of-State Owners in New Mexico" and "Management and Notices" clause). (7) Reporting duties that bind everyone, including landlords and managers: every person who knows or reasonably suspects that a child is abused or neglected must report it immediately to law enforcement or the Children, Youth and Families Department; any person with reasonable cause to believe an incapacitated adult is being abused, neglected or exploited must report it immediately to the Aging and Long-Term Services Department; and anyone who learns of a sudden, violent or untimely death, or finds a body when the cause is unknown, must report it immediately to law enforcement or the medical investigator. Failing to make the first two reports is a misdemeanor.

title: No Right to End a New Mexico Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law lets you end a lease early because repairs would cost too much, and the act's repair duties do not end because a repair is expensive (see "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"). What the law does provide: (1) If bringing the unit up to the building or housing code requires alterations, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of its use, you may bring a possession action even within six months after a protected tenant act such as a code complaint, which would otherwise be retaliation; but you still need a lawful ground to end the tenancy (for example, a proper 30-day notice for a month-to-month tenancy, or the end of a fixed term), and bringing the action does not release you from your repair duties (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico"). (2) A city may order the owner of a dwelling unfit for human habitation to repair it, or to vacate and close it, when repair can be made at a reasonable cost in relation to its value, and to remove or demolish it when it cannot; such an order is a matter of local ordinance. (3) After fire or casualty damage, the tenant has the statutory right to end the lease, and the library's optional "Landlord's Option to End the Lease After a Fire or Casualty" clause gives you a narrow termination right of your own when no part of the unit can lawfully be occupied during repairs. (4) If a breach results solely from circumstances beyond your control, the tenant's remedies are limited to ending the lease or abating rent, without damages or an injunction. Cautious course: in a fixed-term lease, if a major repair or renovation makes the unit unusable, offer the tenant a written mutual termination with a refund of prepaid rent and the deposit, or abate rent while the work is done; don't use the cost of repairs as a reason to stop repairing.

title: When a New Mexico Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule says what happens to a residential eviction, a writ of restitution or the lease when a tenant files for bankruptcy. Bankruptcy is federal law. A bankruptcy filing can affect whether you may start or continue a possession case, enforce a writ or collect rent, so when you learn that a tenant has filed, stop collection and court steps and get advice from a lawyer before you go further. State law adds only background points: the Owner-Resident Relations Act says the general law, including bankruptcy, supplements it; New Mexico's landlord lien on a tenant's belongings does not attach when the premises rented is a dwelling unit, so the statutory landlord's priority for up to six months' rent in a tenant's bankruptcy, which is tied to property liable to distress for rent, does not help a residential landlord (a reading, not a settled rule; see "No Landlord Lien on a Tenant's Belongings in New Mexico"); and if your own interest in the property ends through bankruptcy or receivership, then, unless otherwise agreed, you are relieved of obligations for events after written notice to the tenant, and the successor becomes liable (see "Sale of the Property or a New Manager in New Mexico").

title: Condemnation of a Rental in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's Eminent Domain Code does not say what happens to a lease when the property is condemned.

New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that ends the lease, stops or reduces the rent, lets the court cancel the lease, or divides the award between you and the tenant because of a taking; the lease and general law decide.

What the law does say: private property may not be taken or damaged for public use without just compensation; a condemnation petition must name as defendants everyone who owns or occupies the property or has an interest in it, and damages are assessed for each such person separately; and the court may order payment of rent and other charges out of the award and make orders about rents and liens. The compilation's annotation summarizes a 1966 Supreme Court decision holding that lessees' right to compensation is as fixed and complete as the owner's.

Tenants displaced by a government program or project may also be entitled to relocation help under the Relocation Assistance Act: moving expenses and, for a residential tenant who lawfully occupied the home for at least 90 days before negotiations began (or in other cases the displacing agency prescribes), a payment to rent a comparable home for up to 42 months, capped at $7,200 (the act is effective only while matching federal relocation funding is authorized). Mobile home park owners must notify tenants within 17 days after formal notice of a condemnation (see "What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers").

The library's optional "Condemnation" clause sets out what happens to the lease on a total or partial taking. It does not assign the tenant's share of an award to you, because a lease term making the tenant give up a right under the law is barred; if you want such a term, have a New Mexico lawyer draft it.

title: Liens for Tenant Work in New Mexico
bodyText:
Work a tenant orders can put a lien on your property in New Mexico.

Everyone who performs labor or furnishes materials for the construction, alteration or repair of a building or other improvement has a lien for that work, and the contractor or other person in charge of the work is treated as the owner's agent for this purpose. A lien reaches the land and improvements of the person who caused the work to be done; if that person (for example, your tenant) owns less than the whole property, only that person's interest is subject to it.

But when an improvement is built, altered or repaired with your knowledge, it is treated as built at your instance, and your interest is subject to the lien, unless within 3 days after you learn of the work, or of the planned work, you post a written notice in a conspicuous place on the land or the building saying that you will not be responsible for it. The compilation's annotations summarize New Mexico Supreme Court decisions holding that the notice cannot protect an owner who itself ordered or contracted for the work, directly or indirectly; that oral notice is not enough; that the notice must be posted in good faith and reposted if it is torn down; and, in a lease case, that a lessor who let the lessee live rent-free in exchange for repairs posted in time when the notice went up within 3 days after the work actually began.

New Mexico's statutes contain nothing that lets a lease keep your interest free of liens for the tenant's work just by saying so, and none makes a lease's no-lien clause bind a contractor.

Lien claims must be filed within the statutory time and enforced in court within 2 years after filing, and the advance-notice rule for larger subcontractor claims does not apply to residential property with four or fewer units.

What to do: in the lease, forbid alterations without your written consent ("No Alterations" clause) and use the optional "No Liens for Tenant Work" clause; when you learn that a tenant has hired anyone to work on the property, post a written notice of nonresponsibility on the property within 3 days and keep a dated photo; and if the work is a repair that is your duty, don't trade it for rent without the separate written agreement the act requires (see "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause).

title: No Duty to Provide Substitute Housing in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to provide, find or pay for a hotel room, another unit or other substitute housing while you make repairs, after a fire or other casualty, or while the home is uninhabitable, whether or not the tenant asks. The Owner-Resident Relations Act gives the tenant other remedies instead. Repairs: if you do not remedy a violation of your repair and maintenance duties (other than a defect in an amenity) within 7 days of the tenant's written notice, the tenant may abate one-third of the daily rent from the notice date until the condition is fixed, or all of the rent for that period if the home is uninhabitable and the tenant does not live there because of the condition. For a material breach of the lease, or a violation of the act materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may instead give written notice ending the lease on a date at least 7 days after you receive it unless you make a reasonable attempt to remedy the breach in that time (see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico"). These repair remedies do not arise for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent. Fire or casualty: if the damage substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the home, the tenant may move out and give you written notice within 7 days ending the lease as of the move-out date, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the part made unusable and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value (see "Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico"). New Mexico's Relocation Assistance Act provides relocation payments for people displaced by a government program or project; it can be read as not reaching a private landlord's own repairs, though a court could read it differently. You may still offer another unit or a temporary stay by agreement. If you do, put it in writing, and don't make it a condition of the tenant's rent abatement or termination rights, which the lease cannot waive.

title: Appliances You Supply and Items You Don't in New Mexico
bodyText:
You must keep in good and safe working order and condition the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including any elevator, that you supply or are required to supply. You must also supply running water, a reasonable amount of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose or the heat or hot water comes from an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection.

New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that presumes that an appliance left in the unit is supplied by you, or sets rules for excluding one.

Whether you supply an item is a question of fact. An appliance a prior tenant left behind, or one the tenant owns, is not one you supply, and the optional Items Not Supplied by Landlord clause records it. Whether listing an item you yourself leave in the unit keeps it from being "supplied" is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course is to remove, before move-in, any item you do not intend to maintain, and to list what you do supply in the Appliances & Equipment Included clause.

The lease cannot waive your duty for anything you supply or are required to supply (for example by a local housing code). The tenant can take on specified repairs or maintenance only by the agreement the law allows: for a single family residence, in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations; for any other unit, in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations, and not reducing your duties to other tenants ("Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause). Even then your own duties remain.

Never remove or disable an appliance or fixture to force a tenant out, except for necessary and legitimate repairs (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico").

title: No New Mexico Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to supply a stove, range, oven or refrigerator in a rental home. If you do supply one, you must keep it in good and safe working order and condition, as with every facility and appliance you supply or are required to supply (see "Appliances You Supply and Items You Don't in New Mexico"). A local housing code may require kitchen appliances, and your duty reaches anything you are required to supply. The Owner-Resident Relations Act defines a "roomer" as a person occupying a unit that lacks a major bathroom or kitchen facility (for a kitchen, a refrigerator, stove or sink) in a building where major facilities are shared, but nothing in the act turns on that definition and it creates no duty to supply them. List the appliances you supply in the Appliances & Equipment Included clause. If the tenant brings their own stove or refrigerator, you may record it in the optional Items Not Supplied by Landlord clause; you then do not maintain it. You may not remove or disable a stove, refrigerator or other appliance you supply to force a tenant out, except for necessary and legitimate repairs.

title: Declared Disasters and Emergencies in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that ends a tenancy, suspends or excuses rent, bars evictions, or limits rent or price increases because the governor or a local government has declared a disaster or emergency. The ordinary rules of the Owner-Resident Relations Act apply. Damage to the home: if fire or another casualty damages the unit or premises so that the tenant's enjoyment of the home is substantially impaired, the tenant may move out and give you written notice within 7 days ending the lease as of the move-out date, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the part made unusable and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value; if the lease ends, you return the balance of prepaid rent and the deposit as the deposit law provides (see "Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico"). Flood, wildfire or storm damage can be read as a casualty, though a court could read it differently (see "No Disaster or Environmental-Event Termination Rule in New Mexico"). If the event leaves the home in breach of your repair duties, the tenant's written-notice remedies also apply: rent abatement after 7 days, or ending the lease on a 7-day notice for a material breach or a violation materially affecting health and safety; where the breach results solely from circumstances beyond your control, the tenant has those remedies but no damages or injunction (see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico"). A home that is undamaged but cannot be reached, for example during an evacuation order: no statute says whether rent is owed; only case law could settle it. The cautious course is not to charge rent, or to refund it, for any period a government order bars anyone from occupying the home. Rent increases during an emergency follow the ordinary notice rules (see "Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico"); local rent control is barred by state law, except for property funded under a government contract for the express purpose of providing reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants (see "No Local Rent Control in New Mexico"). Emergency orders: the governor directs emergency management under the All Hazard Emergency Management Act and may issue orders and rules to carry it out, and under the Riot Control Act may, in a proclaimed emergency, prohibit activities the governor reasonably believes should be prohibited to help maintain life, property or the public peace. A governor's or local emergency order can therefore add temporary rules. Federal disaster programs may also apply.

title: No New Mexico Rule on Housing Disaster-Displaced Guests
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives a tenant a right to house people displaced by a disaster or emergency, suspends your guest or occupancy limits during a declared emergency, or makes you accept displaced people in a vacant unit. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply as written (see the Guest Policy and Permitted Occupants clauses). One statutory limit applies at all times: you may not charge the tenant a fee for occupancy of the home by a reasonable number of guests for a reasonable length of time, though you may charge, if the lease includes the fee, for guests' use of premises or facilities other than the home itself (see "No Guest Fees in New Mexico"). Guest and occupancy rules must not discriminate on any ground the New Mexico Human Rights Act protects (see "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act"). If you choose to let displaced people stay, consider a short written guest or occupancy agreement stating who may stay and for how long. A related rule: a person who, voluntarily and without compensation, lets property be used to shelter people during a disaster is not civilly liable for negligently causing death, injury or property damage there, but only if emergency management authorities have approved the premises for that purpose. A governor's or local emergency order may add temporary rules.

title: Emergency Contacts and Contact Information in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws contain nothing that requires a tenant to give you an emergency contact, requires you to give tenants an emergency telephone number, or requires the lease to carry a management website or a social-services hotline notice.

What the law does require is that you disclose in writing, at or before the start of the residency, the name, address and telephone number of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent for service of process and notices, and keep it current (see "Management and Notices" clause).

An emergency contact you collect has two statutory uses. If the tenant abandons the home and your notice of intent to dispose of belongings is returned undeliverable, or the tenant's last known address is the vacated unit, you must also send at least one notice to another address the tenant gave you, including the address of a family member or emergency contact you have on record, and, if the tenant's last known address is the home, mail a copy of the accounting for property you sell or keep to such an address (see "Property Left After an Eviction in New Mexico" and "Handling of Property Left Behind" clause). Both uses need the contact's address, not only a telephone number.

Separately, you may ask, including in the lease, for a contact person to receive the tenant's belongings and deposit if the tenant dies ("Contact Person if Tenant Dies" clause, "When a Tenant Dies in New Mexico").

The optional Tenant's Emergency Contact clause collects a contact, limits how you use it and says the contact takes on no liability or right to enter. Do not give a contact access to the home or the tenant's information beyond what the clause and the law allow.

title: No New Mexico Key-Control Rule
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to keep a key-control policy or key log, limits who on your staff may hold master keys, requires rekeying between tenants, regulates a tenant's own lock changes, or requires background checks on employees who have access to units (see "No New Mexico Lock or Security Device Statute" and "No New Mexico Screening Rule for Rental Housing Employees").

The rules that do bear on keys: you may enter only as the Owner-Resident Relations Act allows (for the purposes the act lists, after 24 hours' written notice of your intent to enter, the purpose and the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise; without that notice to perform repairs or services within 7 days of the tenant's request or when accompanied by a public official conducting an inspection or a cable television, electric, gas or telephone company representative; without consent in an emergency; and otherwise only by court order or after the tenant abandons or surrenders the home or is absent more than 7 days, as the act provides) and must not abuse the right of access (see "Entry Rules in New Mexico"); and you may never change, add, plug or remove a lock, or block an entrance, to keep a tenant out without a court order (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico").

The library's Keys clause (`keys`) covers issuing, returning and replacing keys, and the optional Lock Changes clause requires the tenant's lock changes to have your written agreement, with an emergency exception.

Good practice: keep master keys secured and logged, limit them to staff who need them, and rekey after a tenant moves out or a key is lost.

A court order, such as a protection order giving one person sole possession of the home, overrides a lease term on locks or keys (see "No Domestic Violence Lock-Change Right in New Mexico").

title: No New Mexico Landlord Insurance Requirement
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to register proof of insurance, or to tell tenants in the lease whether you are insured. Whether to insure is your business decision, and your lender, a homeowners or condominium association, or a local government program may require it. Two points tie insurance to New Mexico rental law. Your repair and safety duties under the Owner-Resident Relations Act do not change existing tort law, so your liability for injuries on the property follows the general law of negligence. And a lease may not make the tenant give up rights or remedies, so a clause excusing you from liability for your own fault, or making the tenant's insurance the only source of recovery, is not allowed (see "Landlord Liability Disclaimers in New Mexico Leases" and "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause).

title: No New Mexico Parity Rule for Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law bars you from offering a month-to-month or week-to-week tenant different or more burdensome terms than a fixed-term tenant (or the reverse), or caps the difference in rent between lease types. You may price and structure each type as you choose, subject to the rules that apply to every lease: no waiver of the tenant's rights, every fee stated in the lease, no discrimination on a ground the Human Rights Act protects, and a court's power to limit a term it finds inequitable when made (see "Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico", "Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases", "Fair Housing Under the New Mexico Human Rights Act" and "Inequitable Lease Terms in New Mexico"). The Owner-Resident Relations Act itself treats the types differently in a few places. If the lease fixes no definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week where rent is paid weekly and month-to-month otherwise. Either side may end a week-to-week tenancy on 7 days' written notice and a month-to-month tenancy on written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date (see "Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy" clause). Rent increases need written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date in a month-to-month tenancy, or at least 30 days before the end of the term in a fixed-term tenancy, and at least one rental period before the first increased payment in a week-to-week or other periodic tenancy of less than a month (see "Rent Increase Notice in New Mexico"); fee increases need written notice at least 60 days before the periodic rental date or the end of the term, or one rental period ahead for a tenancy of less than a month (see "Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico"). Under a lease of less than one year, including a month-to-month tenancy, the deposit may not exceed one month's rent; under an annual lease a larger deposit is allowed but earns the tenant annual interest (see "New Mexico Security Deposit Limits").

title: No New Mexico Type-Size Rule for Leases
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule sets a minimum type size for a residential lease, or makes a lease printed in small type inadmissible or unenforceable. New Mexico sets type sizes only for particular consumer documents, such as rental-purchase agreements for goods, retail installment contracts, door-to-door sales contracts and foreclosure consultant contracts; none of these reaches an ordinary residential lease (a lease of furniture or other personal property that comes with the lease of a home, with no option to buy, is outside the rental-purchase act). Small or hard-to-read print can still hurt you: a court may limit a lease term it finds was inequitable when made, and a term the tenant could not fairly read invites that challenge (see "Inequitable Lease Terms in New Mexico"). The cautious course is a readable font (the library's documents use a standard size) and clear headings. New Mexico also has no general plain-language rule for leases; the plain-language rule applies to rental listings (see "Plain Language in New Mexico Rentals").

title: Elevators, Amenities and Other Facilities in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: Elevators and similar lifts: you must keep in good and safe working order any elevator you supply. Under New Mexico's Elevator Safety Act, the owner or lessee of a conveyance (an elevator, escalator, moving sidewalk, platform lift or stairway chair lift) must register each existing conveyance with the Construction Industries Division (the deadline was January 1, 2026), must obtain a certificate of operation before a new conveyance is used, must renew the certificate every year after an annual inspection by a division-certified inspector, must have required tests done by a certified mechanic with a certified inspector present, and must remedy any violations within 60 days of the inspection report. The division may order a dangerous conveyance out of use. Conveyances within a single family dwelling are exempt. The division's own elevator rules may add posting or other details. Other facilities: you must keep common areas safe and maintain the facilities and appliances you supply. A facility whose absence would not materially affect health, safety or habitability, such as a pool, gym, clubhouse or laundry room you offer as an amenity, is an "amenity": the tenant cannot abate rent because it is unavailable, though your duty to keep it safe while open remains. You may set reasonable rules for shared facilities that fairly distribute them among tenants (see "Rules and Regulations" clause), and you may charge for guests' use of facilities other than the home if the lease includes the fee (see "No Guest Fees in New Mexico"). In a mobile home park, common areas must be open to all residents at all reasonable times, subject to written park rules. For pools, see "Pool Safety Rules for New Mexico Rentals". No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, puts a special duty on a landlord for an automatic garage door or gate opener.

title: Parking Rules, Parking Fees and Towing in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the Department of Transportation's towing rules), sets rules written only for parking in a residential lease: none prescribes a heading or delivery form for parking rules, limits the vehicle information you may ask for, requires the lease to say whether parking is provided, or gives a waiting period or a registration-specific notice before towing a vehicle for expired registration (the general sign rule for towing below still applies).

Three general rules govern parking instead, and the state's towing rules set conditions on towing from your property.

Parking rules are rules: they bind the tenant only if they serve a permitted purpose, are reasonably related to it, apply fairly to all residents, are explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do and are not meant to evade your obligations. The tenant must be given a copy of the existing rules when signing the lease. A rule adopted later binds only after reasonable notice and only if it does not work a substantial modification of the tenant's bargain, so taking away a promised space or adding a new charge mid-lease is risky (see "Rules and Regulations" clause and "Assigned Parking Space(s)" clause).

Parking fees (space rent, permits, tags, gate remotes) must be included in the lease, and you may raise a lease fee only by written notice given at least 60 days before the periodic rental date, or at least 60 days before the end of a fixed term, or one rental period ahead in a tenancy of less than a month (see "Fees and Charges" clause and "Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico").

Towing: under the Department of Transportation's rules, a towing service may not tow a vehicle illegally parked at an apartment property unless the property has visible signs telling the public that illegally parked vehicles may be towed and stating the exact hours when a vehicle is considered illegally parked. For each tow from private property, the towing service must first get written authorization signed by you or your agent, giving the location, how long the vehicle has been there, a description of it, the date and time of removal and your statement that it is illegally parked. The towing service must photograph the vehicle (and, at an apartment, the signs) and may not pay you or your agent anything for the right to tow there.

Separately, you may have a vehicle parked in an accessible space without the required placard or plate towed at its owner's expense (see "Towing From Rental Property in New Mexico").

The library's Vehicle Rules clause does not tow for expired registration.

Never use towing, booting or blocking a tenant's vehicle as a way to force the tenant out or collect rent (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico").

title: Entry for Scheduled Services in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico lets you and the tenant agree to entry terms other than the statutory default, which can include a schedule for regular services such as filter changes or pest treatment. The default: the tenant must consent to entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services or show the unit, and, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, you may enter for those purposes only after 24 hours' written notice of your intent, the purpose, and the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame of the entry. The notice rule does not apply when you enter to perform repairs or services within 7 days of the tenant's request, or when you are accompanied by a public official conducting an inspection or a cable television, electric, gas or telephone company representative. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law says a scheduled-services entry term must be conspicuous or in a separate writing. The library does not offer a scheduled-services entry clause for New Mexico: its Landlord's Entry clause keeps the 24-hour written notice for every non-emergency entry, because shortening or replacing the notice is a choice to make with advice. You may add your own clause, for example listing each service and its schedule and giving written notice of each visit. Remember that a written notice to the tenant must be hand-delivered or mailed, or posted and also mailed or hand-delivered; the statute gives no exception by agreement, and whether an agreed entry term can change that delivery method is not settled, so the cautious course is to keep it (see "How to Serve Notices in New Mexico"). Whatever you agree, these protections stay: you must not abuse the right of access; you must try to accommodate a tenant's reasonable request for another time where that is practicable or will not cause you economic loss; and unlawful entry, unreasonable entry, or repeated demands that unreasonably interfere with the tenant's quiet enjoyment let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover damages (see "Entry Rules in New Mexico" and "Changing the Showing Notice by Agreement in New Mexico").

title: Permitted Use of a New Mexico Rental
bodyText:
Use of the home: unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit and in compliance with the rental agreement. The library's Residential Use Only clause keeps that default; to allow a particular home business, add "Home Business or Child Care (Landlord's Permission)" clause (see "Home Businesses in New Mexico Rentals").

Rules: any rule you adopt about the tenant's use of the premises is enforceable only if its purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the residents, preserve your property from abusive use or make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for residents generally, and it must be reasonably related to that purpose (see "Rules and Regulations" clause).

Prohibited uses: two criminal statutes make the lease voidable by you. If the tenant is convicted of using the property as a house of prostitution, or the property is adjudged a public nuisance for that reason, or if the tenant is convicted of using it as a gambling place or the property is adjudged a public nuisance, you may void the lease and regain possession with the same remedies as against a tenant holding over (see "Nuisance and Illegal Use of a Rental in New Mexico"). Knowingly entering into a lease for premises you own or control, knowing they are intended for prostitution, is itself a felony. Premises used unlawfully to sell, make, store, possess or consume alcohol in violation of the Liquor Control Act are a public nuisance, and a court may close them until a bond is posted.

Separately, under the Owner-Resident Relations Act, if the tenant knowingly commits or consents to a listed serious crime (a "substantial violation") in the unit, on the premises or within 300 feet, you may end the lease on a written notice of at least 3 days (see "Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation").

How voiding the lease under the criminal statutes fits with the act's own eviction procedure is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course is to use the act's notice and court process for possession in every case.

title: No New Mexico Renter's Insurance Rules
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law regulates a lease requirement that the tenant carry renter's insurance. None lets the tenant choose the carrier by statute, sets a deadline for proof, authorizes or limits force-placed coverage bought by the landlord, caps an administrative fee for it, or requires you to tell the tenant in writing that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings or to give a renter's-insurance or flood notice before signing.

You may require renter's insurance by lease (the library's Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance clause, "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause, and, for pets, "Pet Insurance Requirement" clause, which excludes assistance animals).

General limits still apply.
- The lease cannot excuse you from liability for your own fault or make the tenant's insurance the tenant's only remedy (see "Landlord Liability Disclaimers in New Mexico Leases").
- If you would charge the tenant for coverage you buy, or any related fee, the charge must be included in the lease; New Mexico makes charging a fee not included in the rental agreement an unfair or deceptive trade practice (see "Fees and Charges" clause).

Federal law may also apply in federally assisted housing.

title: Insurance Claims Between Landlord and Tenant in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law bars you or your insurer from recovering from a tenant for an accidental fire, gives your insurer or the tenant's insurer a statutory right of subrogation against the other party to a residential lease, or regulates a lease clause in which you and the tenant waive claims against each other for insured losses. What the Owner-Resident Relations Act says: the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and after a fire or casualty the tenant remains responsible for damage caused by the tenant's negligence, even while exercising the right to end the lease or reduce the rent (see "Damage a Tenant Causes in New Mexico", "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause and "Fire or Casualty Damage in New Mexico"). Your repair duties are not meant to change existing tort law. Whether your insurer, after paying you, may sue a tenant for a negligent fire, and whether the tenant counts as a co-insured under your policy, are questions only case law (and the policy) could settle. The library does not offer a mutual waiver of insured losses for New Mexico. A lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the law, and a waiver of the tenant's claims against you for losses the tenant's insurance covers could be read as such a waiver. If you want one, have a New Mexico lawyer draft it and make it mutual and limited to insured losses. Do report claims promptly under your own policy, and ask tenants to tell you promptly about damage.

title: Repair Requests and Written Notice in New Mexico
bodyText:
In New Mexico the tenant's repair remedies start with a written notice from the tenant. If you fail to meet your repair and maintenance duties, the tenant must give you written notice specifying the breach before ending the lease on a 7-day notice for a material breach or a violation materially affecting health and safety, and must give written notice of the conditions needing repair before abating rent; abatement is available only if you do not remedy the conditions within 7 days of the notice, and it then runs from the date of the notice. If the last day to remedy falls on a weekend or federal holiday, the period runs to the next business day.

Written notice to you counts as received when it is mailed or delivered to the place of business through which the lease was made or any place you held out for receiving notices, so keep your notice address current (see "Management and Notices" clause). If you never disclose in writing the manager and the owner or agent for notices, the tenant is relieved of the duty to give you the notices the act requires.

The law also protects the request itself: you may not retaliate against a tenant who is in compliance with the lease and the act by raising rent, decreasing services or bringing or threatening an action for possession because, within the previous six months, the tenant, acting in good faith to exercise rights under the act, made a written request or complaint to you to make repairs you are obligated to make, complained to a code agency of a code violation materially affecting health and safety, or abated rent under the act (a rent or service change on appropriate notice at the end of the term, or as the lease provides, is allowed if you can show it is uniform with similar units and not aimed at the tenant). A violation is a defense to an eviction, and an owner who retaliates is liable for two times the monthly rent (see "Retaliation Is Prohibited in New Mexico").

Entry to perform repairs or services within 7 days of the tenant's request needs no 24-hour notice (see "Entry Rules in New Mexico").

No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law prescribes the form of a repair request beyond these written-notice rules, requires the lease to state how to request repairs, or says that accepting phone or verbal requests waives the written-notice requirement. Your lease may ask for written repair requests (the library's Maintenance & Repairs clause does, "Maintenance & Repairs" clause, and "E-mail Communications" clause lets the tenant send notices by e-mail), but it cannot take away or narrow the tenant's statutory remedies.

Under the act a person also has notice of a fact they actually know or have reason to know, so a condition you know about is one you should fix whether or not a written request arrives. Whether accepting oral or portal requests excuses the tenant's written notice is a question only case law could settle; the cautious course is to act on every request and ask the tenant to confirm it in writing.

title: Who Makes Repairs in a New Mexico Rental
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law lets a tenant make repairs and deduct the cost from rent, lets a tenant choose who repairs your property, or requires you to name a repair contact or an approved repairer in the lease (see "Tenant Remedies When a New Mexico Landlord Breaches").

The tenant's statutory repair remedies are written notice followed by termination or rent abatement, and damages (see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico").

Who does the work is therefore yours to set, within the act's limits on shifting work to the tenant. You may arrange with a tenant to perform your obligations, but the arrangement does not reduce your duties, and the tenant's failure to do the work is not a ground for eviction or a material breach. An agreement that the tenant will take on specified repairs or maintenance tasks must, for a single family residence, be in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations; for any other unit it must also be in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by consideration, and may not reduce your duties to other tenants (see "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause).

You must disclose in writing the name, address and telephone number of the person authorized to manage the premises (see "Management and Notices" clause).

The optional Repair Requests and Approved Repairers clause names your repair contact, bars tenant-hired work and repair-cost deductions without your written agreement, and allows reasonable emergency steps when you can't be reached.

title: Pest Control Notices in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts on tenancy and related subjects or in the pesticide rules (21.17.50 and 21.17.51 NMAC), requires you or a pest control company to give tenants notice before a pesticide application, to post warning signs, or to give a pest-control disclosure before the lease is signed. The Pesticide Control Act lets the rule-making board require applicators to notify owners of adjoining property, or property in the immediate vicinity, of a proposed application where such notice is necessary to carry out the act, and to regulate how pesticides are applied; the board's pesticide rules contain no such notice requirement, but every applicator must follow the directions and precautions on the product label, which may include re-entry or ventilation instructions. Cities and counties may not adopt their own rules on pesticide use or application except as the act authorizes. Your own entry rules apply to any treatment inside the home: unless otherwise agreed, give at least 24 hours' written notice stating the purpose, the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame of the entry, unless you are treating within 7 days of the tenant's request (see "Entry Rules in New Mexico"). The cautious course is to tell tenants in writing before any treatment of their unit or of shared areas, name the product if they ask, and give the applicator's preparation instructions. Ask the applicator for the label's re-entry and preparation instructions and pass them on to the tenant. See also "No New Mexico Bed Bug Rule" and the optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause.

title: No New Mexico Bed Bug Cooperation Rule
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting, sets bed bug or pest duties between landlord and tenant: none requires the tenant to report an infestation, prepare the unit, or allow inspections, and none says who pays for treatment (see also "No New Mexico Bed Bug Rule").

The general rules decide it.
- An infestation can breach your duties to keep the premises safe and to comply with housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and the tenant's written-notice remedies (rent abatement or ending the lease) then apply, unless the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent (see "Tenant's Repair Remedies in New Mexico").
- The tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies as clean and safe as its condition permits and dispose of garbage cleanly and safely, and is liable for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes (see "Tenant's Duties Under New Mexico Law").

The optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause adds a reporting, access and preparation duty and puts the treatment cost on the tenant only where the tenant's household or guests caused the infestation through a deliberate or negligent act. Entry for treatment follows the act's notice rules (see "Entry Rules in New Mexico").

Local housing codes (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and others) may say more.

title: Smart Locks and Electronic Entry in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law regulates smart locks, keypads, key cards, fobs, app-based entry or other electronic access systems in rentals, requires you to offer a physical key or other non-electronic alternative, sets rules for entry logs, or lets a domestic violence survivor ask whoever manages a connected device's user accounts to cut off another person's access.

The general rules apply to an electronic system as they do to a key. Entering through the system is entry: you may enter only as the Owner-Resident Relations Act allows, which means 24 hours' written notice of your intent, the purpose, the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame (unless you and the tenant agree otherwise), with exceptions for repairs or services within 7 days of the tenant's request and for entry with a public official conducting an inspection or a cable television, electric, gas or telephone company representative; otherwise only in an emergency, by court order, after abandonment or surrender, or at times reasonably necessary during an absence of more than 7 days; and never abusing the right of access (see "Landlord's Entry" clause and "Entry Rules in New Mexico").

Cancelling or changing a tenant's code or credential to keep the tenant out is a lockout. Except after abandonment or surrender or as the act otherwise permits, you and anyone acting for you must not knowingly exclude a tenant without a court order by changing, adding or removing any lock or latching device, blocking an entrance, or any willful act making the unit inaccessible. A temporary interference while making legitimate repairs or inspections the act provides for is not a violation.

If you lock a tenant out, the tenant may withhold all of the rent for each day denied possession, recover the unit or end the lease, recover damages, and hold you liable for two times the monthly rent (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico").

A lock system you supply is very likely one of the facilities and appliances you must keep in good and safe working order (the statute does not name locks), so keep a backup way in for power, battery or network failures.

Fingerprint and face data: if the system stores measurements of a tenant's fingerprints, voice print, iris or retina, face or hand geometry used to confirm the tenant's identity at the door, together with the tenant's name, and the data is not encrypted or redacted, the Data Breach Notification Act applies to a person that owns or licenses it. You must keep reasonable security for it, require by contract that any service provider you disclose it to does the same, dispose of it by shredding, erasing or making it unreadable when you no longer reasonably need it, and notify affected tenants as quickly as possible, and no later than 45 calendar days after discovering a breach, unless an appropriate investigation shows no significant risk of identity theft or fraud (see "Tenant Records and Data Security in New Mexico").

Good practice: issue each adult occupant a credential, deactivate or change codes when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit or you recover possession by court order, keep entry records private, and use the optional "Electronic Entry System" clause.

Federal law may also apply.

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law regulates tenant portals or apps, bars you from asking tenants to pay rent online, requires you to offer a free non-electronic way to pay, or caps portal or convenience fees.

The general rules decide what a portal can do.

Payment: rent is payable at the time and place you and the tenant agree, and if the lease says nothing, at the dwelling unit. List the payment methods you accept in the lease ("Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause). A charge for using the portal or a payment method is a fee: it must be itemized in your published listing and included in the lease, stated as an amount (see "Fees and Charges" clause and "Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases"), and you may raise it only by written notice at least 60 days before the periodic rental date or, in a fixed-term lease, before the end of the term (one rental period ahead in a tenancy of less than a month) (see "Fee Increase Notice in New Mexico").

Applications: you may not charge any fee to process an application other than the screening fee of up to $50, so there is no separate online-application or portal fee. For a screening fee paid online you must give written or digital notice of the fee, get the applicant's written agreement to pay it, give a written or digital receipt, and place a hold on a credit card (or wait to deposit cash or checks) until earlier applicants have been screened and rejected or offered the unit and declined (see "Application Screening Fees in New Mexico").

Signatures and documents: under the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act a lease, signature or record may be electronic only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and their conduct (see "Electronic Signatures" clause). A tenant who agreed may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, and a lease term cannot waive that right. A term making the portal the only way to sign or receive documents is therefore risky against a tenant who later refuses; whether a monthly portal payment under an existing lease is an "other transaction" is for the courts, so the cautious course is to keep a paper route open for signatures and documents. Where the law requires you to give the tenant something in writing, an electronic record counts only if the tenant can keep it, and a record you stop the tenant from printing or saving is not enforceable against the tenant. Let tenants download and print the written lease you must give each tenant before occupancy and every document you post.

Notices: a portal message does not replace the notices the Owner-Resident Relations Act requires. The electronic transactions act does not apply to a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of an individual's primary residence; a nonpayment notice is effective only when hand-delivered, mailed or posted on an exterior door, and any other written notice to the tenant must be mailed first class or hand-delivered even if also posted (see "How to Serve Notices in New Mexico" and "E-mail Communications" clause). Mail the itemized deposit statement and any refund to the tenant's last known address, because mailing is what the act treats as compliance.

Data: bank or card numbers stored with the code that gives access to the account are personal identifying information under the Data Breach Notification Act when stored with the tenant's name and not encrypted or redacted (see "Smart Locks and Electronic Entry in New Mexico" and "Tenant Records and Data Security in New Mexico").

Federal law may also apply.

title: No Rent-Cap Law or Repeal Date for Tenant Statutes in New Mexico
bodyText: New Mexico has no statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law of the kind some states have adopted, so there is no core tenant-protection statute here running on a dated repeal clock. No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law sets a repeal or expiration date for the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, the Mobile Home Park Act or the state ban on local rent control, and the Owner-Resident Relations Act says it is not to be read as impliedly repealed by later legislation if that reading can reasonably be avoided. What New Mexico has instead: cities and counties, including home-rule cities, may not adopt rent control for privately owned property, except for housing that receives government benefits or funding to provide reduced rents for low- or moderate-income tenants ("No Local Rent Control in New Mexico"); and there is no just-cause eviction rule for ordinary residential tenancies ("No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in New Mexico"), though a mobile home park may end a lot tenancy only for the reasons the Mobile Home Park Act lists. What does change on set dates is the act itself when the Legislature amends it: the 2025 changes to listings, screening fees, fee increases and late fees took effect June 20, 2025 (see "Fee Disclosure in Listings and Leases" and "New Mexico Late Fee Rules").

title: No Tenant Right to Buy or Rent-Cap Notice in New Mexico (Except Condominium Conversions)
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires you to give tenants a notice of rent-cap or just-cause protections (New Mexico has no rent cap and, outside the Mobile Home Park Act's limited grounds for ending a lot tenancy, no just-cause rule; see "No Rent-Cap Law or Repeal Date for Tenant Statutes in New Mexico"), or gives residential tenants a right of first refusal, an opportunity to purchase, or advance notice before you sell the property. When you sell: the tenancy continues. Unless otherwise agreed, after you give the tenant written notice that your interest has ended you are relieved of liability for later events, the buyer is liable for all obligations under the lease and the Owner-Resident Relations Act, including the deposit, and once the tenant receives that notice the tenant pays future rent to the buyer. A tenant who paid rent to you before receiving notice of the transfer is not harmed by it (see "Sale of the Property or a New Manager in New Mexico" and "Deposits When the Property Is Sold in New Mexico"). The one statutory purchase right is a condominium conversion. A declarant converting a building, and anyone in the business of selling real estate for its own account who intends to offer units in it, must give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession notice of the conversion, setting out generally their rights, and the disclosure statement at least 60 days before they must vacate, hand-delivered to the unit or mailed. For 60 days after the tenant receives the notice, the unit must be offered to the tenant; if the tenant does not buy, it may not be offered to anyone else at a more favorable price during the next 60 days. The offer is not required for a unit that will be used only for nonresidential purposes or whose boundaries will not substantially match the old rental unit. Once the tenant accepts, the rent may not be raised unless the purchase falls through. Failing to give the notice is a defense to an action for possession, and a lease term letting the declarant end the lease early only because of the conversion is unenforceable (see "Condominium Conversion Notice in New Mexico"). Mobile home parks have notice rules but no purchase right: if you are formally notified of a condemnation of the park, you must tell tenants in writing of its terms within 17 days, and where zoning lets you change the land's use without the zoning authority's consent and the change would evict inhabited homes, you must mail each home owner written notice of intent to evict at least six months before the change. A lease may give a tenant an option to purchase or a right of first refusal as a private term. The library does not offer one: it transfers an interest in the property and needs its own terms (price, timing, recording and title), and an occupancy under a contract of sale, once there is one, falls outside the Owner-Resident Relations Act. Add your own clause with advice if you want one. Federal law may add rules for federally assisted properties.

title: No Rent-Cap Exemption Notice in New Mexico
bodyText: Because New Mexico has no statewide rent cap and no just-cause eviction rule outside the Mobile Home Park Act's limited grounds for ending a lot tenancy (see "No Rent-Cap Law or Repeal Date for Tenant Statutes in New Mexico"), no New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law requires a lease or a separate notice to tell a tenant that the unit is exempt from such a rule. The Owner-Resident Relations Act's own exemptions need no notice to the occupant. Unless an arrangement was created to avoid the act, it does not cover residence at an institution incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, counseling, religious or educational services; occupancy under a contract of sale by the purchaser; fraternal or social organization housing; transient occupancy in a hotel or motel; occupancy by your employee under a written rental or employment agreement that makes the right to occupy conditional on employment in and about the premises; or premises used mainly for agriculture (see "What the New Mexico Owner-Resident Act Covers"). The employee exemption depends on that written term, so put it in the employee's agreement. The exception from the state's rent-control ban for housing that receives government benefits or funding to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants is a limit on the ban, not an exemption you must announce (see "No Local Rent Control in New Mexico"). Federal programs may have their own notices.

title: What a Tenant Must Not Do Under New Mexico Law
bodyText:
New Mexico's list of what a tenant must not do is part of the tenant's statutory duties under the Owner-Resident Relations Act (see "Tenant's Duties Under New Mexico Law").

Two duties are phrased as prohibitions: the tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly permit anyone to do so; and must not knowingly commit, or consent to another person knowingly committing, a substantial violation, which means only the serious offenses the act lists (see "Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation"). The tenant must also conduct himself or herself, and require people on the premises with the tenant's consent to conduct themselves, so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises; follow the bylaws, covenants and rules of any applicable condominium, cooperative or neighborhood association that are not inconsistent with your rights or duties; and consent to entry made under the lease and the act's notice rules (see "Landlord's Entry" clause).

Consequences: for a breach of these duties materially affecting health and safety, or a first material breach of the lease, give the 7-day notice to remedy ("Seven-Day Notice for Other Lease Breaches"); for a substantial violation, the 3-day notice ("Three-Day Notice for a Substantial Violation"). A tenant who intentionally damages the premises is liable for two times the monthly rent ("Damage a Tenant Causes in New Mexico"). If a tenant refuses lawful access, you may seek a court order compelling access or end the lease, and recover damages.

No other New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law sets out acts a residential tenant must not do.

You may add further prohibitions as lease terms the law does not forbid, for example "Prohibited Acts by Tenant" clause (damage, interference and unreasonable refusal of entry), "No Disturbance or Nuisance" clause, "No Criminal Activity" clause and "No Cannabis Cultivation" clause.

Rules you adopt after the tenant signs bind the tenant only with reasonable notice and if they do not substantially modify the tenant's bargain (see "Rules and Regulations" clause).

title: Cable, Internet and Phone Access at New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law gives cable, satellite, internet or telephone providers a right of access to a rental or apartment building, gives tenants a right to choose a provider or to install equipment, bars charging subscribers different rent, or regulates exclusive provider arrangements or a phone company's carrier-of-last-resort duty in apartment buildings. Three rules do touch telecommunications at a rental. Entry: the 24-hour written notice rule does not apply when you enter accompanied by a cable television, electric, gas or telephone company representative (or a public official conducting an inspection). The entry must still be for a purpose the act allows, such as inspecting, repairs or supplying necessary or agreed services, and you must not abuse the right of access (see "Landlord's Entry" clause and "Entry Rules in New Mexico"). No interference: except after abandonment or surrender, you must not knowingly exclude a tenant, or try to remove or dispossess one, without a court order by interfering with services or normal and necessary utilities to the unit, which the act says include telephone service. You are not required to pay the tenant's own bills or prevent an interruption caused by the tenant's nonpayment. A violation lets the tenant withhold all of the rent for each affected day, recover damages and hold you liable for two times the monthly rent (see "No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs in New Mexico"). Installations: the lease may require your written consent before the tenant makes alterations or drills, nails or fastens anything to the property's surfaces ("No Alterations" clause, "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause), and damage beyond normal wear and tear that an installation causes can be recovered as damages (see "Damage a Tenant Causes in New Mexico"). Federal rules on over-the-air reception devices such as satellite dishes may limit how far a lease can restrict them, and both clauses yield to any installation right the law gives the tenant.

title: Solar Panels and Plug-In Solar at New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the Public Regulation Commission's electric service and net metering rules 17.5.410, 17.9.560, 17.9.570 and 17.9.572 NMAC), gives a tenant a right to install a solar panel, a plug-in (balcony or portable) solar device or a battery at a rental, or sets a procedure for asking. The Solar Rights Act declares a property right in solar energy, but it concerns an owner of real property protecting a collector's access to sunlight against neighboring structures, claimed and recorded by declaration; it gives a tenant no right to install anything. One statute does reach private instruments. A covenant, restriction or condition in a deed, contract, security agreement or other instrument affecting the transfer, sale or use of, or an interest in, real property that effectively prohibits the installation or use of a solar collector is void and unenforceable. The same statute's limit on cities and counties uses "solar collector" as the Solar Rights Act defines it, and that definition includes any device that collects solar energy for use in generating electricity; read with that definition, the covenant rule can cover a plug-in panel, though a court could read it differently. A lease is a contract affecting the use of, and an interest in, real property, so a flat lease ban on solar devices is very likely void. The attorney general has said restrictions that make installation or use unreasonably difficult or costly can also "effectively prohibit". The same statute bars counties and cities from restricting solar collectors except in historic districts. Cautious course: don't put a solar ban in a lease. You may require your written consent before anything is attached to the building or wired in, and set reasonable, specific conditions on placement, safety, licensed installation, insurance and removal, without making use unreasonably difficult or costly ("No Alterations" clause and "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause already require consent for alterations and attachments). The library does not offer a separate solar-conditions clause, because how far conditions may go before they effectively prohibit is unsettled; you may add your own with advice. Utility approval: the net metering rule says the utility authorizes interconnected operation of a customer's generating facility and that the interconnection standards are in 17.9.568 NMAC; check that part for whether a plug-in device that can feed power back needs the utility's approval, and tell tenants to follow the utility's interconnection requirements. Federal law may also apply.

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners in New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the building codes in 14.7 NMAC or the Manufactured Housing Division's rules in 14.12 NMAC), gives a tenant a right to install a portable or window air conditioner or an evaporative cooler, requires a lease that restricts window units to say so, voids a lease restriction on cooling devices, requires you to supply cooling, or sets a maximum indoor temperature. What the Owner-Resident Relations Act does require: you must keep in good and safe working order and condition the electrical, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply. If you supply a central air conditioner, a window unit or an evaporative (swamp) cooler, you must maintain it (see "Maintenance & Repairs" clause and "Landlord's Repair Duties in New Mexico"); no statute requires you to supply one, unlike heat, which you must reasonably supply in most cases (see "Heat in New Mexico Rentals"). The tenant must use the air conditioning and other facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner and must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises. A lease may require your written consent before a tenant installs a window unit or makes any alteration or attachment ("No Alterations" clause, "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause), and you may set conditions on electrical load, window security and condensation. New Mexico's rule voiding instrument restrictions applies to solar collectors only (see "Solar Panels and Plug-In Solar at New Mexico Rentals"), not to cooling devices. The building codes adopted by those rules incorporate model codes; for any construction requirement for cooling equipment, check those model codes. Federal law may also apply, for example to a disability accommodation.

title: EV Charging Rules That Apply to New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the building and energy codes in 14.7 NMAC and the Public Regulation Commission's electric rules), contain nothing that gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental (see "No New Mexico Tenant EV-Charging Right"), lets you or limits you in setting conditions on one (approval, licensed electrician, insurance, metering), or requires a landlord who sells charging to tenants to register a charger with weights and measures or collect a charging tax. What does apply: Building codes for new construction. For residential and commercial contracting work performed on or after January 30, 2024 (unless under a permit applied for before then; until July 30, 2024 a permit could still be issued under the earlier rules), the state energy codes require electric vehicle readiness for new parking. A new one- or two-family dwelling or townhouse with a designated garage or other onsite private parking next to the unit must have an electrical receptacle box wired with 8 ga. wire to a 50-amp breaker, both marked for future electric vehicle charging equipment. New apartment buildings and other R-2 parking facilities must have 5% of spaces with installed charging equipment and another 15% "EV capable" (a raceway or cable and electrical capacity in place for later charging), counted on the number of units or parking spaces, whichever is less, and rounded up; R-3 and R-4 buildings 2% and 5%, except a parking facility serving them with fewer than 10 spaces. These rules govern new construction and new parking; they do not require you to retrofit existing parking or give a tenant any right (one reading of the rules; a court could read them differently). They refer to model codes and electrical standards; check those for the details. Selling charging. A person not otherwise a public utility who engages in the retail distribution of electricity for vehicle fuel is not a public utility under the Public Utility Act (see "Submetering and Reselling Utilities to Tenants in New Mexico"). A charge to the tenant for charging is a fee: it must be itemized in your listing and included in the lease as an amount or rate ("Fees and Charges" clause). Maintenance and work. A charger you supply is very likely one of the electrical facilities and appliances you must keep in good and safe working order. Letting a tenant install a charger is letting the tenant make an alteration.
