For a single family residence, an agreement that the tenant do specified alterations is valid only in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations; for any other unit, only in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by consideration, entered into in good faith and not to evade your obligations, and without reducing your obligations to other tenants. Whether your simple consent to a tenant's own charger is such an agreement is for the courts, so the cautious course is to put the arrangement in that kind of separate signed writing (see "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause). Tax credit: a state income tax credit is available for buying and installing a charging unit before January 1, 2030 ($400 or the cost, whichever is less, for most chargers; up to $25,000 for a direct current fast charger), with certification by the Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department; ask your tax adviser. See also "EV Chargers in Shared Parking at New Mexico Rentals" and "Tenant EV Chargers When a New Mexico Tenancy Ends". Federal law may also apply.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking at New Mexico Rentals
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the building and energy codes in 14.7 NMAC or the Public Regulation Commission's electric rules), gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental (see "No New Mexico Tenant EV-Charging Right"), or sets rules for a tenant's charger in a shared parking area or common area, such as who may install it, who pays for power and insurance, or how the space is shared. General rules apply. You must keep common areas safe, and any charger you supply there is very likely one of the electrical facilities you must keep in good and safe working order. You may adopt rules for shared chargers, and they bind tenants only if their purpose is the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the residents, protecting your property from abusive use or making a fair distribution of facilities held out to residents generally; they are reasonably related to that purpose, apply to all residents fairly, are explicit, are not meant to evade your obligations, and tenants receive copies (a rule adopted later binds a tenant only on reasonable notice and if it does not substantially modify the tenant's bargain) (see "Rules and Regulations" clause). A charge for using a shared charger is a fee that must be in the listing and the lease ("Fees and Charges" clause). A tenant installing a charger in a shared area is making an alteration of your premises. For a single family residence, an agreement that the tenant do specified alterations is valid only in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations; for any other unit, only in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by consideration, entered into in good faith and not to evade your obligations, and without reducing your obligations to other tenants. Whether your simple consent to a tenant's own charger is such an agreement is for the courts, so the cautious course is to put the arrangement in that kind of separate signed writing (see "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause). New parking facilities built under the energy codes in force since January 30, 2024 must generally have a share of charging and EV capable spaces, with exceptions (see "EV Charging Rules That Apply to New Mexico Rentals"). In a condominium or planned community, the association's rules also bind your tenant where they are not inconsistent with your rights or duties (see "Homeowner and Condominium Associations and Your Tenant in New Mexico").

title: Tenant EV Chargers When a New Mexico Tenancy Ends
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the building and energy codes in 14.7 NMAC or the Public Regulation Commission's electric rules), gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental (see "No New Mexico Tenant EV-Charging Right"), or says who owns a tenant-installed charger at the end of the tenancy, whether the tenant must remove it, or who pays to restore the premises. General rules apply. At move-out the tenant must leave the unit as clean as at the start, except for ordinary wear and tear, and must not have deliberately or negligently damaged the premises; you may apply the deposit to damages caused by the tenant's noncompliance and must give an itemized statement within 30 days (see "Return of Security Deposit" clause). Under the "No Alterations" clause, an alteration you approve stays with the property at the end of the Term unless you require its removal. If a tenant leaves a removable charger behind, the act's rules for property left on the premises may apply (see "Handling of Property Left Behind" clause); whether an installed charger is the tenant's personal property or a fixture that belongs with the building is a question of case law. Cautious course: before any installation, agree in a separate signed writing who owns the charger, whether and how it will be removed, who pays for removal and restoration by a licensed electrician, and that you may deduct the actual, reasonable cost of restoring damage beyond normal wear and tear. Letting a tenant install a charger is letting the tenant make an alteration. For a single family residence, an agreement that the tenant do specified alterations is valid only in writing, for consideration, in good faith and not to evade your obligations; for any other unit, only in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by consideration, entered into in good faith and not to evade your obligations, and without reducing your obligations to other tenants. Whether your simple consent to a tenant's own charger is such an agreement is for the courts, so the cautious course is to put the arrangement in that kind of separate signed writing (see "Tenant Maintenance Agreement" clause).

title: Caring for a Tenant’s Animals When the Tenant Is Away in New Mexico
bodyText:
New Mexico's statutes, constitution, 2025-2026 session laws and court rules contain nothing that gives you a right or a duty to enter a rental to feed or care for a tenant's animal, lets a tenant name an animal caretaker, or says what happens to an animal left in a unit.

The general entry rules apply. You may enter with the tenant's consent under the lease after 24 hours' written notice of your intent, the purpose, the date and the estimated time frame (unless you and the tenant agree otherwise); without consent in an emergency; at times reasonably necessary during an absence of more than 7 days; and after abandonment or surrender; and you must not abuse the right of access (see "Landlord's Entry" clause). The act does not define an emergency; an animal whose life or health is in danger very likely is one, so enter only as far as the animal's care requires and keep a record.

The optional Animal Care clause ("Animal Care in Tenant's Absence" clause) lets the tenant name a caretaker you may let in, for that purpose only and after trying to reach the tenant, if the tenant is hospitalized, detained or otherwise absent and an animal is left without care; whether a lease may add this entry purpose is not settled, so use it when the animal's need is urgent or the tenant has been away more than 7 days, and get the tenant's consent at the time whenever you can reach the tenant.

Cruelty law: abandoning, or failing to provide necessary sustenance to, an animal under a person's custody or control is cruelty to animals, a misdemeanor. If you take a tenant's animal into your own custody you very likely take on that duty. A peace officer who reasonably believes an animal's life or health is endangered by cruel treatment may get a court warrant to seize it.

Cautious course: call the tenant's caretaker, then local animal control or a shelter, rather than keeping the animal yourself.

Animals left when the tenancy ends: the act's storage rules for belongings left behind are written for personal property and do not mention animals (see "Handling of Property Left Behind" clause); whether they apply to a live animal is not settled, and holding one for weeks without care risks cruelty liability, so arrange care through animal control or a shelter promptly and tell the tenant in writing (see "No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet in New Mexico"). If a tenant dies, a contact person the tenant named may be given access to remove belongings (see "Contact Person if Tenant Dies" clause).

Pets: "Pets" clause; assistance animals: "Assistance Animals in New Mexico Rentals".

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet in New Mexico
bodyText: No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision, 2025-2026 session law or court rule requires you to give a tenant a state fact sheet about pets and eviction, or sets special rules for animals during an eviction or after a writ of restitution. In those sources, the only animal-specific landlord-tenant statute is for mobile home parks: pets that comply with the park's existing rules are exempt from a new rule that would prohibit them, unless they are a nuisance violating the public peace, health or safety. After a writ of restitution is executed you need not store property left on the premises after three days, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise (see "Property Left After an Eviction in New Mexico"). That rule speaks of personal property and does not mention animals, and the cruelty law still forbids abandoning, or failing to provide necessary sustenance to, an animal under a person's custody or control. Cautious course: when you serve an eviction notice or obtain judgment, tell the tenant in writing to remove all animals; if an animal is left at execution of the writ, contact local animal control or a shelter at once rather than treating the animal as abandoned property (see "Caring for a Tenant’s Animals When the Tenant Is Away in New Mexico"). You may give tenants your own written information about pets and eviction; the library does not offer a fact sheet because New Mexico prescribes none.

title: No Waterbed Rule in New Mexico
bodyText:
No New Mexico statute, constitutional provision or 2025-2026 session law, and no rule in the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting (including the building codes in 14.7 NMAC), mentions waterbeds or liquid-filled furniture: none requires you to allow one, lets you refuse one, sets a deposit, fee or insurance requirement for one, or limits floor loads in rentals.

A waterbed is a lease matter. The NM-tagged "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause already bars a waterbed or other water-filled furniture without your prior written consent, and the optional "Waterbeds and Liquid-Filled Furniture" clause sets the terms if you consent (a frame and liner, an approved location, water-damage insurance of {{flotation_insurance_amount}}, and the tenant's responsibility for damage the item causes, but not for normal wear and tear).

The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and damage from the tenant's negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse is not normal wear and tear, so it can be recovered from the deposit with the itemized statement (see "Return of Security Deposit" clause).

If you want a separate waterbed deposit, it counts toward New Mexico's deposit limits (see "New Mexico Security Deposit Limits"), and any waterbed fee must be stated in your listing and in the lease (see "Fees and Charges" clause).

title: Access and Property-Use Rules New Mexico Does Not Have
bodyText: New Mexico's statutes, constitution and 2025-2026 session laws, and (where a row says so) the 57 New Mexico Administrative Code parts that bear on renting or New Mexico's court rules, contain nothing that provides any of the following, so do not expect them or build them into a lease: a smart-lock or electronic-entry statute, a physical-key alternative or a device-access request for domestic violence survivors ("Smart Locks and Electronic Entry in New Mexico"); a tenant-portal rule or a required non-electronic way to pay ("Tenant Portals and Online Payments in New Mexico"); a statewide rent cap, or a just-cause eviction rule outside the Mobile Home Park Act's limited grounds for ending a lot tenancy, a repeal date for the state's tenant statutes, or a notice of coverage or of an exemption ("No Rent-Cap Law or Repeal Date for Tenant Statutes in New Mexico", "No Tenant Right to Buy or Rent-Cap Notice in New Mexico (Except Condominium Conversions)", "No Rent-Cap Exemption Notice in New Mexico"); a tenant right of first refusal or opportunity to purchase when you sell, other than the condominium-conversion offer ("No Tenant Right to Buy or Rent-Cap Notice in New Mexico (Except Condominium Conversions)"); a cable, satellite, internet or telephone access rule for rental buildings ("Cable, Internet and Phone Access at New Mexico Rentals"); a tenant right to install solar panels or plug-in solar devices ("Solar Panels and Plug-In Solar at New Mexico Rentals", which also explains why a lease ban on solar collectors is very likely void); a tenant right to a window or portable air conditioner, or a cooling or maximum-temperature duty ("Window and Portable Air Conditioners in New Mexico Rentals"); a tenant right to install an electric vehicle charger, a shared-area charging rule or an end-of-tenancy charger rule ("EV Charging Rules That Apply to New Mexico Rentals", which also covers the energy-code EV readiness required in new construction, "EV Chargers in Shared Parking at New Mexico Rentals", "Tenant EV Chargers When a New Mexico Tenancy Ends"); an animal-care entry right or caretaker statute, or a pet and eviction fact sheet ("Caring for a Tenant’s Animals When the Tenant Is Away in New Mexico", "No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet in New Mexico"); or a waterbed rule ("No Waterbed Rule in New Mexico"). Earlier New Mexico rows record related absences: locks and security devices ("No New Mexico Lock or Security Device Statute"), security cameras ("No New Mexico Rule on Security Cameras in Rentals") and a tenant EV-charging right ("No New Mexico Tenant EV-Charging Right"); see each row for its scope. The tenant's prohibited acts are not an absence: they are the statutory duties in "What a Tenant Must Not Do Under New Mexico Law".

title: Confession of Judgment in a New Mexico Lease
bodyText: Don't put a confession-of-judgment or cognovit term in a New Mexico lease. New Mexico law makes it unlawful to include, in any written contract to pay money and before a claim on it has arisen, a provision letting someone appear for the person who owes the money, waive service of process or confess judgment against them without a court hearing after notice, and it declares any such provision void. A lease that obliges the tenant to pay rent is a written contract to pay money, so on the statute's terms a provision of this kind in it is void; how the statute applies to a lease is for the courts. Procuring a person's signature on such a provision is also a misdemeanor, with a fine of $50 to $500 and possible jail. Separately, the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act bars any rental agreement term by which the tenant gives up rights or remedies, and an owner who deliberately uses a lease containing a provision known to be prohibited is liable to the tenant for damages and reasonable attorney's fees (see "Prohibited Lease Terms in New Mexico"). A tenant may still agree to a judgment after a dispute arises, for example in a court settlement.

title: Why This Library Does Not Give You an Arbitration Clause for New Mexico
bodyText: This library does not offer a binding arbitration clause for a New Mexico lease. New Mexico's Uniform Arbitration Act generally enforces written agreements to arbitrate, but it singles out a "disabling civil dispute clause" in a standard form lease: a term that limits a tenant's procedural rights, for example by sending the tenant's claims to a forum less convenient, more costly or slower than a New Mexico court, or by making the tenant give up discovery, an appeal, a class action, or attorney fees, civil penalties or multiple damages. In an arbitration between you and a tenant, any such clause in the lease can't be enforced against the tenant, who may void it and ask a court to declare it unenforceable. Whether an ordinary pre-dispute arbitration clause in a form lease is itself such a clause, and whether it waives rights or remedies the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act forbids a lease to waive, are questions only case law could settle. New Mexico's appellate courts, as summarized in the compilation's annotations, have also held one-sided arbitration terms unenforceable, including terms that keep the drafter's own likeliest claims (such as collection or eviction) in court while sending the other side's claims to arbitration; a lease clause that keeps your eviction and rent claims in court but sends the tenant's claims to arbitration has that shape. If you use a lease that deliberately contains a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover damages and attorney's fees. The cautious course is to leave arbitration out and resolve disputes in court; if you want an arbitration clause anyway, have a New Mexico lawyer draft it.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: New Mexico follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (NMSA 1978, § 55-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (NMSA 1978, § 55-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: New Mexico's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (NMSA 1978, § 47-8-11). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
